Discharge Summary:
Patient: 45-year-old female
Diagnosis: Multiple myeloma, a type of blood cancer that affects the bone marrow

Hospital Course:
The patient came in with multiple purple and dark bruise-like patches on the skin. These patches appeared around the eyes, cheeks, and the front and back of the neck. The areas normally covered by clothing were mostly clear. These skin problems started 2 years ago. Even small bumps or injuries caused these patches to appear. The skin was very easy to damage in most areas. The patient also had several bouts of loose stools and fever over the past 6 months. A physical exam showed the patient was slightly pale and had swelling in both feet. A small sample of skin was taken and tested. It showed a blister-like problem with an abnormal protein buildup called amyloid. Blood tests and a bone marrow test confirmed the diagnosis of multiple myeloma. X-rays and other images of the bones looked normal.

Treatment:
The patient was sent to the blood cancer specialists. Treatment with cancer-fighting drugs was started.

Prognosis:
How well the patient does will depend on how the cancer responds to treatment. It will also depend on how far the cancer has spread. The patient should stay in close contact with the blood cancer care team.

Follow-up:
The patient should see the blood cancer specialists on a regular basis. The patient should also take all medicines as directed.

Discharge Summary:

Patient: 61-year-old male with a history of controlled type 2 diabetes, high cholesterol, and past smoking. He came to the hospital with lower back pain and weight loss.

Hospital Course: The patient was admitted to Internal Medicine because of lower back pain and weight loss. A CT scan showed broken bones and a growth near the left side of the spine. Doctors thought it might be cancer. More imaging tests showed a growth near the right lung and another in the upper left lung. There were also small spots that could be from infection or swelling. Doctors took a sample from the growth and found pus. Tests showed it contained tuberculosis bacteria. The patient started treatment with four medicines to fight tuberculosis, called HRZE. The patient also saw specialists for physical medicine and bone care. He received physical therapy to help him recover. After 25 days, the patient left the hospital. He was sent to continue physical therapy and to visit a special clinic for tuberculosis care.

Follow-up: The patient finished two months of treatment with four medicines. He is now taking two medicines to fight tuberculosis, called HR. The growths outside the lungs have gone away completely. A new CT scan of the lower back showed the growth there has gotten smaller.

Diagnosis: Long-term infection with swelling caused by tuberculosis.

Condition at discharge: Stable.

Hospital Course:

An 82-year-old woman came to the hospital because of weakness in her right arm muscles. A brain scan showed a growth in the left side of her brain. Doctors removed the growth through surgery that opened part of her skull. During surgery, doctors used two different tests to check how her nerves and muscles were working. The test results were not what doctors expected. One test showed no big changes while the other showed a major loss in nerve signals. Doctors repeated one of the tests several times but got the same unexpected results. After surgery, the patient had weakness in her right arm and right leg. Lab tests showed the growth was a very serious type of brain cancer called glioblastoma. The patient had a seizure after surgery. Because of this, doctors could not do a follow-up nerve test. The patient left the hospital 13 days after surgery. Her nerve and muscle problems were the same as right after surgery.

Discharge Diagnosis:

Glioblastoma, which is a serious type of brain cancer

Hospital Course Summary:

An 82-year-old woman with right arm weakness came to the hospital. Doctors found a tumor in the left side of her brain. The tumor was a serious brain cancer called glioblastoma. Doctors did surgery to open her skull and remove the tumor. During surgery, doctors used special tests to watch her nerve and muscle activity. The test results were not what doctors expected. After surgery, the patient had weakness in both her right arm and right leg. Lab tests confirmed the brain cancer diagnosis. The patient had a seizure after surgery. Because of the seizure, doctors could not do a follow-up nerve test. The patient left the hospital 13 days after surgery. Her weakness had not changed since right after surgery.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Information:
Patient: 15-year-old girl
Diagnosis: Congenital Hyperinsulinism (CHI), a condition where the body makes too much insulin, causing low blood sugar
Treatment: Diazoxide, Octreotide, Lanreotide

Hospital Course Summary:
The patient with CHI came to the children's hospital unit for a planned stay. The goal was to find a different medicine because diazoxide was causing unwanted hair growth.
The care team slowly lowered and then stopped diazoxide for 72 hours to see what would happen. However, this caused repeated episodes of low blood sugar with symptoms.
Octreotide was then started as a shot under the skin four times a day. This medicine helps control blood sugar.
The patient responded well to this dose. She was able to go without food for 24 hours with no low blood sugar.
Lanreotide was then started as a shot under the skin, 30 mg once a month. This is a long-acting medicine similar to octreotide. Octreotide was slowly lowered and then stopped.
A device that checks blood sugar all the time showed good blood sugar control after starting lanreotide. There were no episodes of low blood sugar.
The patient started having repeated low blood sugar episodes with symptoms after starting fluoxetine. Fluoxetine was stopped and the low blood sugar episodes went away within a week.
Two weeks after stopping fluoxetine, the patient's sad mood slowly got better over time with the help of talk therapy.

Final Diagnosis:
Congenital Hyperinsulinism (CHI)

Follow-up Plan:
No further specific follow-up needed at this time.

Discharge Summary:

This is a discharge summary for a 50-year-old female patient who came to our department with swelling inside the mouth on the left side of the lower jaw for six months. The patient had surgery to remove the growth and rebuild the area using skin and tissue from under the chin. The patient was asleep under general anesthesia during the procedure.

History of Present Illness: The patient came to our department with swelling and pain in the left lower jaw area for six months. The swelling grew quickly after the patient had back teeth removed on the lower left side. The patient did not have a fever or trouble swallowing.

Physical Examination: When looking at the outside of the face, the lower left side looked uneven compared to the right side. There were no swollen lymph nodes in the area. When looking inside the mouth, there was a growing mass that spread from front to back and side to side. It went from the area of the first small back tooth to the area behind the last molar. The mass measured about 6 by 4 centimeters. The skin covering the mass looked normal in color and feel.

Diagnostic Tests: A panoramic jaw x-ray showed a clear dark area going from the lower left first small back tooth to the area behind the last molar. CT scans, which are detailed pictures of the inside of the body, showed the growth was breaking down bone in the lower left jaw. This bone loss went from the small back teeth area into the back part of the jawbone. A small tissue sample was taken and looked at under a microscope. This test confirmed the growth was an aggressive central giant cell granuloma, which is a type of noncancerous but fast-growing jaw tumor.

Hospital Course: The patient had surgery to remove the growth and rebuild the area using skin and tissue from under the chin. The surgery was done from both outside and inside the mouth to remove all of the growth. The patient went home without any problems.

Follow-up: At checkup visits over the next year, there were no signs that the growth came back. This was checked by looking in the mouth and taking x-rays. The area under the chin where tissue was taken healed well with very little scarring. The small scar is not in a part of the face that people easily see.

Summary: A 50-year-old female patient came in with swelling inside the mouth on the left side of the lower jaw for six months. The patient was found to have an aggressive central giant cell granuloma, which is a type of noncancerous but fast-growing jaw tumor. The patient had surgery to remove the growth and rebuild the area using skin and tissue from under the chin. The patient was asleep under general anesthesia during the procedure. The patient went home without any problems. Checkup visits over the next year showed no signs that the growth came back.

Electronic Health Record - Discharge Summary

Patient Name: [Redacted]
Medical Record Number: [Redacted]
Date of Admission: [Redacted]
Date of Discharge: [Redacted]
Attending Physician: [Redacted]

Hospital Course:
The patient is a 4-month-old baby girl. She was brought to the hospital because she was not making eye contact. She was born 5 weeks early at 35 weeks of pregnancy. There were no known health problems in the family. The patient was found to have Leber congenital amaurosis, also called LCA. This is a rare eye condition that causes severe vision loss. The doctors found this because her eyes turned inward and moved back and forth on their own. A test that checks how the back of the eye responds to light showed no response in both eyes. The patient also had trouble focusing her eyes, which was treated. The doctors did several exams. They looked at the front and back of her eyes. They also checked her whole body for problems with her organs or body chemistry. These tests were normal except for the eye problems already mentioned.

The doctors did many tests to find the cause. They did genetic testing to look for changes in certain genes. These tests did not find any problems. A brain scan called an MRI was done. It showed extra fluid in the spaces around the front parts of the brain. It also showed that a thin wall in the middle of the brain was missing. This wall is called the septum pellucidum. No other brain problems were found. The main connection between the two sides of the brain looked normal. The protective covering around nerves in the brain was developing normally. Later brain scans still showed the missing wall in the middle of the brain. The extra fluid around the brain stayed the same and did not get worse. The doctors thought about a condition called septo-optic dysplasia. However, the eye nerves looked normal and the hormone gland at the base of the brain worked normally. This made the doctors unsure about that diagnosis.

Medical History:
The patient had no other health problems. Her only issues were the eye condition called LCA and the brain scan findings with extra fluid around the brain.

Hospital Course Summary:
The patient is a 4-month-old baby girl who came to the hospital for poor eye contact. She was found to have LCA, a condition that causes severe vision loss. The doctors did genetic testing and brain scans. Later brain scans still showed the missing wall in the middle of the brain. The extra fluid around the brain stayed the same. By age 3, the patient showed some delays in learning and development. No other health problems were found during her time in the hospital.

Hospital Course Summary:

Admission:
A 65-year-old female with a history of thyroid disease was admitted to the hospital. She had been feeling tired and sick to her stomach for one week. She had no history of mental health problems. Her blood tests showed low sodium levels. Her heart test showed some unusual patterns.

Course:
After admission, the patient became more alert at first. Four days later, she started seeing things that were not there. She also became very suspicious of others. She was confused and restless. Mental health doctors were called to help. They gave her a medicine called quetiapine to help calm her confusion. On the same day, she felt sick to her stomach again. She became pale and started sweating. Doctors thought her heart might be failing. They did an emergency heart procedure to check her blood vessels. They found she had a heart condition called broken heart syndrome. This is a type of heart problem often caused by stress. Doctors gave her a steroid medicine called hydrocortisone. Within 3 days, her sodium levels and confusion got much better. A heart imaging test was done 10 days after starting the steroid. It showed her heart was pumping much better than before.

Diagnosis:
Blood tests showed her body was not making enough of certain stress hormones. These hormones are called cortisol and ACTH. Her urine tests also showed low levels of cortisol. Doctors found the patient had a rare condition. Her body could not make enough ACTH hormone. A brain scan was done to check the gland that makes this hormone. The scan showed no growths or problems in that area.

Discharge:
The patient left the hospital in stable condition. She was told to keep taking hydrocortisone by mouth. She was told to see her regular doctor for follow-up care. She was also told to see a hormone specialist to manage her ACTH hormone problem.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Information:
Name: [Name Redacted]
Age: 65 years old
Gender: Female
Diagnosis: Skin cancer (melanoma) found in the urethra (the tube that carries urine out of the body). Some cancer cells were left at the edges after the first surgery.

Hospital Course:
The patient came to our hospital after having trouble urinating for 6 months. The patient also had a small growth at the opening where urine comes out. A physical exam showed a small tan growth sticking out from the urine opening. It looked like a common harmless bump. There were no signs of swollen glands in the groin area. Doctors removed the growth, and the patient recovered well from this surgery. Lab tests on the removed tissue showed it was skin cancer (melanoma) in the urethra. Some cancer cells were still at the edges of what was removed. More tests showed a small amount of cancer was still in the last half centimeter of the urethra. The upper part of the urethra and the bladder were normal. Doctors then did a second surgery to remove the entire urethra but kept the bladder. They created a new opening in the belly for the patient to empty the bladder using a thin tube. This surgery removed enough tissue to get 2.5 centimeters of healthy tissue around the cancer. The patient handled the surgery well and had no problems afterward.

Outcome:
The final lab report showed a very small spot (3 millimeters) of remaining skin cancer. This time, no cancer cells were found at the edges. Now, one year after surgery, the patient shows no signs of cancer.

Follow-up Recommendations:
The patient will need long-term checkups with regular tests and scans to watch for any return of the cancer. The patient must use a thin tube to empty the bladder on a regular schedule. The patient can control when to empty the bladder. The patient should see a cancer doctor and a bladder doctor for ongoing care and checkups.

Hospital Course:

The patient was admitted after being diagnosed with a rare genetic brain disease called CADASIL. This disease affects blood vessels in the brain. The patient came in with a history of dizziness, severe headaches, numbness and tingling in the hands and feet, memory loss, tiredness, sleeping too much, anxiety, and depression. After being admitted, a brain scan was done. The scan showed more damage to the white matter in the brain, including areas on both sides of the brain.

Treatment:

The patient did not receive any treatment during the first visit. The symptoms went away after a few months. Later, the patient developed severe headaches that did not get better with usual headache medicines. No treatment was given at that time. A brain doctor first thought the patient had multiple sclerosis. The patient was sent to a special clinic. A new brain scan showed damage in specific areas on both sides of the brain. This led to a diagnosis of CADASIL.

Consultations:

The patient saw a brain specialist who focuses on the immune system. The diagnosis was changed based on the new brain scan results. A genetic test for the NOTCH3 gene came back positive, which confirmed the diagnosis.

Follow Up:

The patient was told to see a brain doctor for ongoing care of their CADASIL.

Discharge:

The patient left the hospital with a diagnosis of CADASIL. The patient was told to follow up with a brain doctor. There were no problems during the hospital stay.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: N/A
Medical Record Number: N/A
Date of Admission: N/A
Date of Discharge: N/A
Admitting Physician: N/A
Attending Physician: N/A

Hospital Course:

The patient is a 50-year-old male farmer who was sent to our hospital for emergency care. The patient came in with stomach pain that came and went. Two days before, he had surgery at another hospital to fix a hole in his small intestine and treat an infection that had spread in his belly.

When the patient first went to the other hospital, his kidneys were not working well. He had low potassium levels in his blood. He also had bad belly pain and was making very little urine for 5 days. After surgery, the patient had swelling in his face and trouble breathing. He also had too much acid in his blood, low blood pressure, confusion, and fever. The patient was put on a breathing machine and given medicines to fight infection. These medicines included aztreonam and metronidazole given through a vein. Even with all this care, the patient got worse.

Blood tests showed the patient had a low red blood cell count with some oddly shaped cells. Other test results showed the following. The patient had too many white blood cells and not enough cells that help blood clot. Tests that show swelling in the body were high. Kidney function tests showed the kidneys were not working well. Salt and potassium levels in the blood were too high. Liver tests were also high. An imaging test of the belly showed mild kidney disease and a small fluid buildup near the spleen. It also showed swollen tubes in the liver. A urine test showed a small number of cells that fight infection. A test of fluid from the belly showed some cells that fight infection along with yeast and fungus. A blood test for germs came back clean after 24 hours.

A test of belly fluid found a fungus called Trichosporon beigelii. Based on these tests, the infection was treated using standard medical care. Even with treatment, the patient kept getting worse. He was then sent here for emergency care.

Given how sick the patient is, he will keep getting care to support his body. More treatment will be given as needed.

Discharge Diagnosis:

The patient was found to have an infection caused by a fungus called Trichosporon beigelii. This was treated during his hospital stay.

Follow-up Care:

The patient will keep getting follow-up care to make sure he gets the treatment he needs. Instructions for follow-up care will be given at future visits.

Discharge Summary

Patient: [INSERT NAME HERE]

Gender: Male

Age: 63

Main Problem: Red patches and scabbed sores on the scalp

What Happened Before Coming to This Hospital:

The patient went to a skin doctor with red patches and scabbed sores on the scalp that had been there for one month. The first diagnosis was a long-lasting open sore caused by an infection. After four weeks of treatment, the patient did not get better. The patient was then sent to a larger hospital for surgery to remove a tissue sample and for more care. The tissue sample showed a type of blood vessel cancer called angiosarcoma. The cancer cells had spread to the edges of the removed tissue.

What Happened During the Hospital Stay:

The patient had an MRI scan. The scan showed the tumor had grown into the fat layer under the skin. It also spread to the thin tissue covering the skull and the muscles around the skull. A PET-CT scan showed the cancer had spread across the scalp. The scan also showed small signs of cancer in lymph nodes on both sides of the neck. The patient had surgery to remove a large area of tissue. Doctors rebuilt the area using muscle from the back and a thin layer of skin from another part of the body. After surgery, another PET-CT scan found the cancer had spread to several lymph nodes. The patient received radiation treatment and cancer-fighting drugs. After these treatments, the scans showed the cancer signs were gone.

Summary:

In summary, the patient came to the hospital with a type of blood vessel cancer called angiosarcoma. The cancer cells had spread to the edges of the removed tissue. The treatment plan included surgery to remove a large area of tissue and rebuild the scalp. This was followed by radiation treatment and cancer-fighting drugs. After treatment, the cancer signs on the scans were gone. The patient left the hospital in stable condition. The patient was told to follow up with the regular doctor and cancer doctor for more check-ups and care.

Hospital Course:
The patient, an 8-year-old girl, was admitted because of vision loss in the right eye for 5 years. She also had headache and vomiting for 6 months. During the exam, the right eye could not see any light at all. The left eye had normal vision. A brain scan showed a fluid-filled sac on the right side of the brain. It measured about 8 by 9 by 6.5 centimeters. A small round lump was seen on the inner side of this sac, near the brain's fluid spaces. Doctors first thought it might be a type of brain tumor. Blood tests later showed that the thyroid gland was not working well due to a problem with hormone signals from the brain.

Treatment:
The patient had surgery to open the skull on the right side of the head. The surgeon drained the fluid-filled sac and created an opening so fluid would not build up again. The fluid inside was yellow and looked like thick oil. It contained fatty crystals and small bits, mostly on the inner side. Lab tests of the tissue showed the sac was a harmless cyst that had become swollen and irritated. The cyst wall was lined with flat to layered skin-like cells. It also had swollen blood vessels and signs of long-term irritation, including certain white blood cells grouped together.

Outcomes:
After surgery, the patient recovered without any problems. The headache and vomiting went away completely. The patient continues to see the doctor regularly. A brain scan done 6 months after surgery showed the cyst has not come back.

Discharge Summary:

The patient is a 43-year-old white male who was generally healthy before this illness. He was admitted to the hospital because of ongoing fever, belly pain, back chest pain, and ear pain. He was found to have an outer ear infection and sent home with amoxicillin-clavulanate and paracetamol, both taken by mouth. Blood tests at that time showed higher than normal levels of CRP, a marker of swelling in the body, and ALT, a liver enzyme.

After leaving the hospital, the patient came back with dark urine, pale stool, and yellow skin and eyes. Swollen lymph nodes were found on both sides of the neck. No other problems were found during the physical exam, chest X-ray, or belly ultrasound.

The patient's blood tests showed a rise in white blood cells, a mild rise in lipase, a digestive enzyme, and higher bilirubin levels. He was given two strong antibiotics called Piperacillin-Tazobactam and Tigecycline. However, his condition got worse. Several of his organs began to fail, and he was moved to the intensive care unit. Tests for immune system problems and immune cell levels came back normal. A liver tissue sample showed damaged liver tissue with changes in structure, scarring, and signs of swelling caused by certain white blood cells. The patient was then started on steroid medicines. This helped improve his condition. His liver function and signs of swelling in the body also got better.

The patient was sent home after 40 days in the hospital. He was given steroid medicine with the dose slowly going down over time. On day 47 after leaving the hospital, he had a heart scan using a special X-ray with dye. The results were normal. Eighteen months later, the patient had no symptoms at all.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [Redacted]
Age: 59
Admission date: [Redacted]
Discharge Date: [Redacted]
Final Diagnosis: COVID-19

Medical History:
The patient had no major health problems before this illness.

Hospital Course:
The patient came to the hospital with a cough that produced mucus, a runny nose, fever, and trouble breathing. A chest X-ray was done. The results showed infection in both lungs near the bottom. The patient was found to have COVID-19 and asthma. The patient received two antibiotics through an IV. These were ceftazidime 1 gram and levofloxacin 500 milligrams. The patient also received medicine to treat asthma symptoms.

Clinical Course:
The patient got much better during the hospital stay. The patient no longer had a fever. Breathing became much easier. The cough and runny nose also got better.

Follow-up:
The patient was told to stay home and away from others. The patient should keep watching for any symptoms. The patient's regular doctor will provide ongoing care.

DISCHARGE SUMMARY
Patient Name: [REDACTED]
Age: 84 years
Sex: Male
Date of Admission: [REDACTED]
Date of Discharge: [REDACTED]

HOSPITAL COURSE:
The patient came to the ear, nose, and throat clinic with a growth on the scalp. The growth had been getting bigger for 2 months after a skin cancer removal surgery. A tissue sample showed a type of skin cancer that had spread deeper into the skin. The skin also showed severe sun damage. The doctors removed the cancer through surgery. This left an open wound about 5 by 7 centimeters in size. The wound went down to the tough tissue covering the skull. The doctors talked about ways to help the wound heal. They chose to use a special skin graft material called vCPM. The vCPM was placed directly on the wound and covered with a non-stick bandage. The patient came back to the clinic 7 days after the first treatment. A second piece of vCPM was placed on the wound, which now had healthy new tissue growing. The patient returned on day 14. The wound had shrunk to about 3 by 5 centimeters. New skin was growing well over the wound. The doctors decided a third treatment was not needed. At the day 21 visit, the wound had fully closed with very little scarring. Six months after treatment, the wound stayed closed. The redness continued to fade. The patient had no problems and was very happy with the results.

DIAGNOSIS:
Skin cancer that spread deeper into the skin, with severe sun damage to the skin

DISCHARGE INSTRUCTIONS:
The patient should see the doctor for regular check-ups to watch how the wound heals. The patient should tell the doctor right away about any signs of infection or slow healing.

FOLLOW-UP:
The patient has appointments scheduled with the doctor to check on wound healing.

Hospital Course:
The patient is an 86-year-old man. He came to our pain clinic for ongoing lower back pain and pain in his left leg. He has had this pain for 2 years. Pain medicines taken by mouth did not help enough. They also caused unwanted side effects. A special scan of his lower back showed narrowing of the spine, worn-out joints, and breakdown of the spine bones. A nerve and spine doctor said that surgery would not help.

Assessment and Plan:
The care team found that the patient still has pain after past back surgery. He also has soreness in the joint where the left hip meets the spine. Good pain relief would mean the pain is cut in half or more. This relief should last at least 2 weeks after a pain shot. It should last at least 3 months after a heat treatment to block pain nerves. The patient said he did not get this level of pain relief.

Disposition:
The patient was sent home. No more treatments or procedures were recommended. The patient was told to see his regular doctor to help manage his ongoing pain.

Patient Identification:
Patient: 20-year-old Japanese woman with intellectual disability and seizure disorder

History and Physical Examination:
The patient came in with pain in her lower belly. Doctors found a growth with many fluid-filled sacs in her pelvic area. A special scan showed that both of her ovaries were swollen. Doctors removed her right ovary and took out a cyst from her left ovary. Two years and nine months later, a check-up found another growth with many sections in her pelvic area.

Hospital Course:
The patient had a second surgery. Doctors found a growth with many fluid-filled sacs of different sizes in her pelvic area. Doctors removed her uterus, left ovary, a fatty tissue layer near her stomach, some lymph nodes from her pelvic area, her appendix, and the growth from her belly. They were able to remove all of the growth. The patient started taking hormone medicine to replace what her ovaries used to make.

Diagnosis:
BMPM, a rare and fast-growing tumor

Follow-up:
Nine months after the second surgery, the tumor has not come back.

HOSPITAL COURSE SUMMARY:
Patient Name: [redacted]

Admission Date: [redacted]         Discharge Date: [redacted]
Length of Stay: [redacted]

Admitting Diagnosis:
Curved spine due to wear and tear, with the spine out of line both front-to-back and side-to-side, along with narrowing of the spinal canal in the lower back

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted with back pain and leg pain in both legs when walking. After testing, she was found to have a curved spine from wear and tear. Her spine was out of line both front-to-back and side-to-side. She also had narrowing of the spinal canal in the lower back. Surgery was needed because other treatments did not work. She had metal rods and screws placed from the middle back down to the pelvis. Bone was also fused at several levels through an opening in the back. After surgery, the patient was doing well and came back for regular check-ups.

During the six-year follow-up period, the patient came back with pain throughout her back. Testing showed that both metal rods had broken near where the middle and lower back meet. The left rod also broke between the screws near the base of the spine and pelvis. A CT scan showed gas bubbles in the disc space where the rod broke. The rest of the bone had healed well and fused together. The doctors chose to treat the patient without surgery. Treatment included pain shots into tight muscle areas, pain medicine, and physical therapy.

Outcome:
After five years of non-surgical treatment, the patient had no more symptoms. No further treatment was needed. The patient was discharged on [redacted] after a [redacted] day hospital stay. The patient should continue to come back for regular check-ups.

DISCHARGE SUMMARY

Patient Name: [patient name]
Admission Date: [admission date]
Discharge Date: [discharge date]

HOSPITAL COURSE:
The patient is a 65-year-old man with no past health problems. He came to the hospital with sudden, severe pain on the right side of his back. His blood pressure was dangerously low. A CT scan took pictures of his belly and lower body. The scan showed a large collection of blood around and behind his right kidney. This blood buildup was pressing on the kidney.

TREATMENT:
The medical team gave the patient fluids and care to stabilize him. Then doctors did a procedure to block the blood vessels and stop the bleeding. An MRI scan showed a growth in the area around the kidney. Doctors performed surgery to remove the entire right kidney. Tests on the removed kidney found a type of cancer called synovial sarcoma. The patient started cancer treatment with two medicines called docetaxel and gemcitabine. This treatment was given for six rounds.

FOLLOW-UP:
A cancer doctor checked on the patient over the year after surgery. A scan at nine months showed no signs that the cancer had come back.

DISCHARGE CONDITION:
The patient left the hospital in stable condition. He was told to continue his cancer treatment as directed. He should keep seeing his cancer doctor. He should tell his care team about any new symptoms right away.

DISCHARGE MEDICATIONS:
Please look at the most recent list of medicines given to the patient. Tell the doctor who prescribed the medicines about any changes.

FOLLOW-UP INSTRUCTIONS:
The patient should keep seeing his cancer doctor for checkups and treatment. The patient should report any symptoms to his care team right away.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [Redacted]
Sex: Male
Age: 36 years
Date of Admission: October 2007

Medical History: The patient came in with a history of bony growths and had surgeries before. He was diagnosed with schizophrenia, a mental illness that affects thinking and behavior. No one in his family has had similar mental health problems.

Hospital Course: The patient's treatment was difficult. His symptoms did not get better with different medicines for mental illness and mood. He tried many treatment options, including a therapy that uses small electrical currents to the brain. This led to several hospital stays.

Outcome: The patient got somewhat better with a mix of five medicines: Olanzapine, Haloperidol, Lamotrigine, clonazepam, and Zuclopenthixol. He left the hospital on [Redacted].

Follow-up Care: The patient needs to be watched closely for any mental health symptoms and other health problems. The care team should check the treatment plan often and make changes if needed.

Summary: The patient came to the hospital with schizophrenia. His stay was difficult because his symptoms did not respond well to medicines. A mix of medicines and other treatments helped him get somewhat better. He left the hospital with a plan for follow-up care.

Discharge Summary

Patient Name: Case 2
Date of Service: [DATE]

Hospital Course:

The patient is a 71-year-old man with lung cancer that has spread to other parts of his body. His cancer has a specific gene change called EGFR. He first received a cancer drug called afatinib. He also had radiation treatment to help with cancer that had spread to his spine at the T8 level. The main tumor in his left upper lung got smaller at first. However, the tumor grew bigger again after 7 months. The patient then received two chemotherapy drugs called pemetrexed and cisplatin. This treatment made the tumor shrink partly. The patient continued taking pemetrexed alone for two years with no major side effects. A scan of his chest showed the main tumor had grown again. The cancer had not spread to other parts of his body outside the chest. The patient started having trouble breathing during activity and chest pain. He received a focused radiation treatment called SABR to the tumor in his left upper lung. This treatment worked well. The area now shows scar tissue from the radiation but has not changed otherwise. The patient has now been on pemetrexed for more than 48 months. There are no signs that the cancer has come back.

Discharge Diagnosis:

Lung cancer with a specific gene change that has spread to other body parts. The main tumor in the lung had grown larger.

Hospital Course Summary:

The patient has lung cancer that has spread and has a gene change called EGFR. He received several treatments. These included the drug afatinib, radiation to ease symptoms, chemotherapy with pemetrexed and cisplatin, and ongoing pemetrexed. He also had focused radiation treatment called SABR to the tumor in his left upper lung. The patient had only mild side effects from chemotherapy. He handled the treatments well overall. He continues to take pemetrexed and is responding well to treatment.

Hospital Course:
A 66-year-old female patient came to the gum care department at M. S. Ramaiah Dental College and Hospital in Bangalore. She had a burning feeling in her gums and bleeding gums for the past month.

Medical History:
The patient was not taking any medicines and had no major health problems. She had never had dental treatment before.

Examination Findings:
The dentist looked at the outside of the patient's face and body. The patient had some skin patches on her scalp. She also had a thick, rough patch of skin behind her left ear. The dentist then looked inside the patient's mouth. The gums around the upper and lower front teeth were red. This included the gums at the edges, the gums attached to the teeth, and the gums between the teeth. In some areas, the top layer of gum tissue was peeling off.

Diagnosis:
Based on what the dentist saw and lab test results, the patient likely has discoid lupus erythematosus. This is a condition where the body's defense system attacks its own skin and gum tissue.

Treatment:
The dentist gently cleaned the teeth to remove buildup. This was done carefully to avoid hurting the gums. The patient was told to use a soft toothbrush and rinse with chlorhexidine 0.12 percent mouthwash. The patient was also told to apply triamcinolone acetonide paste inside the mouth two to three times per day. This paste helps reduce soreness and swelling.

Follow-up:
The patient was asked to come back for check-up visits and ongoing care.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [Name]

Discharge Date: [Discharge Date]

Diagnosis: Follicular Lymphoma (a slow-growing cancer of the white blood cells)

Hospital Course:

A 72-year-old man came in with a painless lump in his belly that did not bother him. Doctors found a large mass in the middle part of his belly using special scans. A small piece of the mass was removed and tested. The tests showed the patient had Follicular Lymphoma. The patient was treated with two cancer medicines called bendamustine and rituximab. The patient came back for check-ups after leaving the hospital. So far, the cancer has not come back.

Medical History:

The patient did not have any major health problems before this.

Discussion:

Tumors that start in the middle part of the belly are not common. Follicular Lymphoma is the most common type of these tumors. Scans can show different patterns for this kind of cancer. Some signs on scans may point to cancer, but they are not always reliable. This type of cancer often grows slowly, but finding it early is still very important. When doctors find a solid lump in the middle of the belly, they should first think about this type of cancer.

Recommendations:

The patient should keep seeing the cancer doctor for regular check-ups. The patient should tell the doctor right away about any new symptoms or problems.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Information:
Name: Louise
Age: 16
Gender: Female
Diagnosis: Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD), a condition that affects how a person communicates and interacts with others

Hospital Course:
Louise is a 16-year-old girl with autism. Testing showed she thinks and learns at the level of a 13-year-old. Louise grew up in a small country village in Italy with both parents until age nine. Her parents then split up. Her father moved her to Canada. There she went to school and got help from mental health doctors. She also received treatment for a related condition called OCD. OCD causes unwanted repeated thoughts and behaviors.

Over 5 years in Canada, Louise worked with many mental health helpers. She attended school with special changes made to help her learn. Later, a court ordered her to go back to Italy to live with her mother. The court did not find that living with her mother would cause serious harm. However, the mental health doctors disagreed. They believed moving Louise back to Italy could hurt her. The change in her surroundings and less access to mental health care for young people would likely make her symptoms worse.

The mental health doctors also looked into claims that the mother emotionally mistreated Louise. During her time in Italy, Louise was reportedly put down and called hurtful names. The doctors also noted that her OCD could make the move to Italy even harder for her.

The doctors conclude that Louise has a complicated situation because of her condition and history. She needs ongoing medical care and support. The mental health doctors say it is important for Louise to have access to mental health services for young people. She also needs special changes at school to help her learn. These services were available to her in Canada. They should also be available wherever she lives now. The doctors suggest watching her condition closely. They recommend regular visits with medical professionals to check her progress and change her treatment plan if needed.

Admission Diagnosis:
The patient was admitted with a hole in the heart wall, blood vessels connected to the wrong part of the heart, a slow heart rhythm that only beats every other time, slightly blue skin color, and fluid buildup in the lungs.

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted to the hospital for the conditions listed above. The first exam showed the patient had bluish skin and lower than normal oxygen levels between 85% and 94%. A heart ultrasound done after birth confirmed the blood vessels were connected wrong. It also showed two large veins in the upper body instead of one, a missing large vein in the lower body, and a hole in the wall between the upper heart chambers. The patient had successful heart surgery and received a device to help the heart beat regularly at 9 days old.

Diagnostic Assessments:
A blood test that looks at genes found a small extra copy of part of one chromosome. This copied section contains 11 genes. Seven of these genes are listed in a medical database. Four of them are linked to known health conditions.

Condition on Discharge:
The patient went home at 3 weeks old and was doing well. A checkup at 2 months showed no problems.

Discharge Instructions:
The patient's family learned why regular visits with a children's heart doctor are important. They were told to watch the baby's health at home. This includes checking oxygen levels every day and watching how the baby feeds. The family was also told to keep up with pacemaker checkups and get all vaccines the baby's doctor recommends.

Follow-up:
The patient will have regular visits with the children's heart doctor and regular doctor. These visits will check the heart condition, growth, and development. A visit with a genetics doctor will be suggested to understand how the chromosome change might affect the patient's health over time.

Disposition:
The patient went home in stable condition with improved heart symptoms and a good chance for healthy long-term results.

DISCHARGE SUMMARY:

Patient Name: [redacted]
Medical Record Number: [redacted]
Gender: Female
Age: 67 years

Hospital Course:
The 67-year-old female patient had a stage 3 hole in the macula, the central part of the eye. She came to the hospital on [redacted] because her left eye vision had gotten worse over the past month. The patient had eye surgery to remove the gel inside the eye and peel a thin layer from the retina. A special dye was used to help the surgeon see better. Gas was put in the eye to help it heal. Eye scans taken four weeks after surgery showed the light-sensing layer was still damaged over a wide area. The patient could see 20/100, which means her vision was still limited. At six weeks, the retina had pulled away from the back of the eye in some areas, but not the central vision area. There were several tears in the retina. She had another eye surgery to fix the detached retina. Laser treatment was used to seal the tears. Gas was again put in the eye. At six months, the patient could see 20/40. Eye scans showed the light-sensing layer was healing in many areas of the macula. There was still some damage under the very center of the macula. By one year, the patient could see 20/25, which is close to normal. Eye scans showed the light-sensing layer in the center of the macula had fully healed.

Diagnosis:
Stage 3 hole in the macula. Detached retina with several tears, but the central vision area was not affected.

Treatment:
Eye surgery to remove the gel inside the eye. Peeling of a thin layer from the retina using a special dye. Gas placed in the eye to help healing. Laser treatment to seal retina tears.

Condition on Discharge:
The patient has gotten much better. Her vision improved to 20/25, which is close to normal. The light-sensing layer in the center of the macula has fully healed.

Follow-up Care:
The patient will need regular check-ups to watch her vision and the health of her retina.

Summary:
The 67-year-old female patient had a stage 3 hole in the macula and came in with worse vision in her left eye. She had successful eye surgeries to fix the hole and later to repair a detached retina. Laser treatment sealed the retina tears. Eye scans after surgery showed the light-sensing layer was healing in many areas. There was some remaining damage under the very center of the macula at first. Over one year, the patient kept getting better. Her vision improved to 20/25, which is close to normal. The light-sensing layer in the center of the macula fully healed. The patient will need regular check-ups to watch her vision and retina health.

DISCHARGE SUMMARY:

PATIENT INFORMATION:

Name: [Patient Name]
Age: 65 years
Gender: Male
Admission Date: [Admission Date]
Discharge Date: [Discharge Date]
Reason for Admission: Painful growth at right lower back tooth area

HOSPITAL COURSE:

The patient came to our hospital because of a painful growth in the right lower back tooth area. The patient shared that he has been chewing pan for the past fifteen years. He chews about 3-5 packets per day. During the exam, doctors found a hard, painful growth about 4 by 3 cm in size. The growth was on the gum ridge where teeth 45 and 46 used to be. It spread into the jawbone and the inside of the right cheek. The edges of the growth were raised and the base felt hard when touched. Doctors also felt a firm lump about 3 by 2 cm under the right side of the jaw.

Doctors believed the growth was cancer affecting the right jawbone and cheek area near teeth 45 and 46. A special scan with dye was done to see inside the body. The scan showed a cancerous mass that had spread to nearby lymph nodes. A small tissue sample was taken and tested. The test confirmed the growth was a type of skin cancer called squamous cell carcinoma. It was a slow-growing type. Based on how far the cancer has spread, it was rated as stage IVA-T4a N1 M0. This means it is advanced but has not spread to distant body parts.

TREATMENT:

Doctors recommended surgery to remove the cancerous growth. The patient chose not to have the surgery. Because of how advanced the cancer is and the patient's choice, he was sent to a comfort care team. This team will help manage his pain and other symptoms.

DISCHARGE DIAGNOSIS:

Slow-growing skin cancer of the right jawbone and cheek area near teeth 45 and 46. The cancer has spread to nearby lymph nodes.

RECOMMENDATIONS:

The patient should see his cancer doctor regularly for help with pain and symptoms. The patient should stop using pan and all tobacco products. The patient learned why eating healthy foods and living a healthy lifestyle matters when dealing with cancer.

DISCHARGE MEDICATIONS:

None

FOLLOW-UP:

The patient has an appointment with his cancer doctor in two weeks. The patient should call the hospital if any new symptoms appear or current symptoms get worse. The patient's medical records have been sent to his cancer doctor for continued care.

Hospital Course:
The patient is a 61-year-old man with mouth cancer. He had surgery for early-stage cancer in 2011. He came back after not seeing doctors for over 4 years. He now had swollen lymph nodes in his neck and left armpit. A small tissue sample showed the cancer had spread to these lymph nodes. The patient joined a research study. He received three cancer drugs called carboplatin, 5-FU, and pembrolizumab at a dose of 200 mg. After 4 rounds of treatment, the cancer showed some shrinking. However, he came in feeling very tired and had low blood pressure with the top number at 70. Doctors found that his immune treatment caused his adrenal glands to stop working properly. These glands sit above the kidneys and make important hormones. He was given a strong steroid medicine called dexamethasone. Later, he switched to another steroid called hydrocortisone. A scan of his brain showed no swelling near the pituitary gland. The scan also showed no cancer spread to the brain. His tiredness went away after ten days. He then started taking pembrolizumab again. The patient continues to take hydrocortisone.

Reason for Admission:
The patient came in with a flaky, itchy scalp and hair loss for 2 years. The patient also had thick, scaly skin on both feet with cracks for 8 years.

Hospital Course:
A physical exam showed white flaky skin spread across the scalp. The soles of the feet had thick, widespread flaky skin. The mouth and nails looked normal.

A close-up exam of the scalp showed tube-shaped buildup around hairs, thin baby-fine hairs, and grey and white dots. There were also crystal-like shapes mainly around hair roots. A skin sample from the scalp was studied under a microscope. It showed a thick outer skin layer and blocked hair openings. There was damage to the bottom layer of skin cells. White blood cells had gathered in the upper skin layer around the hair roots. There was also color leaking into the skin. These findings matched a condition called LPP. A special dye test came back normal. A skin sample from the sole showed thick outer skin, thickened middle skin, and stretched tissue fibers in the upper skin layer. There were no signs of skin cell damage at the base.

Diagnosis:
The patient was found to have Lichen Planopilaris, also called LPP. This is a condition that causes swelling around hair roots and can lead to hair loss. The diagnosis was based on the skin sample findings.

Treatment:
The discharge summary does not contain any information about the patient's treatment plan.

Follow-up:
The patient will see her healthcare provider for care of her LPP.

Disposition:
The patient was sent home. The patient was told to keep seeing her healthcare provider.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [Redacted]
Date of Admission: [Redacted]
Date of Discharge: [Redacted]

Hospital Course:

The patient was admitted because of a low platelet count and mild bleeding symptoms. Platelets are blood cells that help stop bleeding. Many lab tests were done. These tests showed a low platelet count and red blood cells of different sizes. A blood test also showed very large platelets. The patient was found to have a rare genetic blood disorder called MYH9-related disease after genetic testing found a known gene change.

The patient had mild hearing loss and had nosebleeds and heavy periods since childhood. She had her spleen removed at age fifteen. She sometimes took a steroid medicine called prednisone when her platelet count dropped very low. The patient was correctly diagnosed with this blood disorder in 2016.

In 2018, she became pregnant and received very good care during pregnancy for herself and her babies. She received platelets one time at week 10 of pregnancy when her platelet count dropped a lot. At week 19 of pregnancy, scans of both twins showed a small fluid-filled sac in the brain of each baby. The babies' size, body parts, placenta position and shape, blood flow, and heart function were all normal. The twins were born at week 32 by surgery to deliver the babies. Both twins had low platelet counts, very large platelets, and medium-sized fluid-filled sacs in the brain at birth. Both babies were in good health, and one twin was smaller than most babies the same age. The mother received one dose of medicine to prevent bleeding before being put to sleep for surgery. Neither baby had any bleeding problems.

Discharge Diagnosis:

1. MYH9-Related Disease, a rare genetic blood disorder
2. Low platelet count
3. Very large platelets
4. Small fluid-filled sacs in the brain, found alone without other problems

Discharge Medications:

No medicines were prescribed when the patient left the hospital.

Discharge Condition:

The patient left the hospital with a low but stable platelet count. Both twins were moved to the newborn intensive care unit where they received the right care. They left the hospital after 28 days. All three are watched closely by their healthcare team and have regular checkups.

Follow-Up Plan:

The patient and her twins will be checked by their healthcare team every three months. They will also have regular blood tests. They will keep getting very good care and treatment when needed.

Follow-Up Tests:

1. Blood count test
2. Platelet count test
3. Checking the fluid-filled sacs in the brain

Summary:

The patient was admitted for a low platelet count and mild bleeding symptoms. Genetic testing showed she has a rare blood disorder called MYH9-related disease. During her pregnancy, the patient and her babies were watched very closely. The twins were born with low platelet counts, very large platelets, and medium-sized fluid-filled sacs in the brain. The patient left the hospital in stable condition. Both twins were moved to the newborn intensive care unit and left after 28 days. They all continue to have regular checkups with their healthcare team.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [Redacted]

Hospital Course:
A 9-year-old boy came to our hospital because he suddenly lost vision in his left eye 10 days earlier. This happened after he rubbed his eye very hard. When doctors checked his eyes, they found problems with both. The right eye had a bulging cornea (the clear front part of the eye) with stretch marks and a small surface scar. The left eye had severe swelling and a bulging cornea in the center. This showed a sudden fluid buildup. The doctors found that both eyes had a condition called keratoconus, where the cornea bulges outward. The left eye also had sudden swelling from fluid leaking into the cornea.

Treatment and Procedures:
The patient had a procedure on his left eye to fix the swelling. The doctor used a small needle to drain fluid from the front part of the eye in a clean, germ-free setting. Then the doctor filled this space with air. After that, the air was replaced with a special gas that filled two-thirds of the space. This gas helps push the cornea back into shape. The patient was given eye drops to prevent infection and reduce swelling. The patient was told to lie flat on his back after the procedure.

Outcome:
The patient has been checked by doctors for 12 months. The corneal swelling has completely gone away. The patient now has a light, cloudy scar on the cornea. With contact lenses, the patient can see 6/9, which is close to normal vision. The pressure inside the eye has stayed normal since the procedure.

Impressions and Plan:
The patient was treated for bulging corneas in both eyes and sudden swelling in the left eye. The special gas procedure was used to fix this. The corneal swelling has completely cleared up. The patient's vision has gotten better with contact lenses. The patient has been sent home and should keep seeing eye doctors for a long time.

Discharge Summary:
Patient Name: [redacted]
DOB: [redacted]
Admission Date: [redacted]
Discharge Date: [redacted]
Diagnosis: Diffuse Large B-cell Lymphoma (a type of blood cancer that affects white blood cells)

Hospital Course:
The patient came to the hospital with fever and neck pain. She had taken antibiotics for this before. The doctor found several swollen lymph nodes under the left arm. A CT scan showed swollen lymph nodes under the arm and bone damage in the spine. A PET scan showed the cancer had spread to many areas of the bone and bone marrow. A bone marrow test did not show large cancer cells. A small piece of tissue was taken from the lymph nodes under the left arm. The test showed cancer cells had spread throughout the tissue. Special lab tests confirmed the type of cancer. The patient was diagnosed with stage IV cancer that had spread to many parts of the body. The risk level was low to medium based on a standard scoring system.

The patient received radiation treatment for the neck area. She chose not to have regular chemotherapy because of the risk of a past lung infection coming back. She was started on two medicines called CAM and PSL. Her fever got better within a few days. The PSL dose started at 20 mg per day for 2 weeks. Then it was lowered to 15 mg per day for 2 weeks. The long-term dose was 10 mg per day. The patient noticed food tasted a little different. This was likely caused by taking CAM for a long time.

Scans taken 6 months later showed the cancer was gone. The swollen lymph nodes and bone problems had improved. The patient still has no signs of cancer 7 months after starting treatment.

Hospital Course Summary:
The patient came to the hospital with fever and neck pain. Doctors found several swollen lymph nodes under the left arm. Scans showed swollen lymph nodes, bone damage in the spine, and cancer in the bone and bone marrow. Tests confirmed stage IV blood cancer. The patient received radiation to the neck and started taking CAM and PSL. Scans after 6 months showed the cancer was gone. The patient still has no signs of cancer 7 months after starting treatment.

Diagnoses:
1. Sarcoidosis (a disease that causes small clumps of swelling in the body's organs)

Hospital Course Summary:
The patient came to the hospital with pain in the right side of the back, mild fever, upset stomach, loss of appetite, and weight loss without trying. These scans showed swollen lymph nodes in the chest, fluid around both lungs, and a growth in the pancreas about 2 inches in size.

More tests were done. These tests found small clusters of swelling in the tissue. Tests for cancer cells and germs came back negative. A blood test showed high levels of a certain enzyme. All of these findings led to a diagnosis of sarcoidosis. A needle was used to take a small sample from the pancreas growth. The sample showed this was a rare type of tumor called a Frantz tumor. More lab tests confirmed this diagnosis.

The patient had surgery to remove the tumor and parts of the pancreas and small intestine. The patient healed well after surgery. When leaving the hospital, the patient was in stable condition.

Instructions upon Discharge:
1. Keep taking all medicines as told by the doctor.
2. See the doctor for regular checkups to watch and manage the medical conditions.
3. Call the doctor right away if there are any new symptoms or concerns.

She has trouble adjusting to life changes, which causes worry and sadness. She has stress that does not fit into one category. She has been treated unfairly and harmed because of who she is. She was found to have trouble adjusting to life changes, with worry and sadness. She also has stress, has been treated unfairly and harmed, has lost family members, and has a history of other deeply upsetting events. Patient A is leaving in good health. Hospital Course:
The patient is a 40-year-old woman who came to our clinic for left back pain that lasted 2 months. The physical exam showed nothing unusual. Blood tests showed slightly high levels of adrenaline and another hormone called renin. A detailed scan of the belly area showed growths on both adrenal glands, which are small organs above the kidneys. Doctors first thought these growths might be adrenal gland cancer. The patient had surgery to remove the left adrenal gland and the left kidney. Tests on the removed tissue showed unusual immune cells. More lab tests found that the patient had a rare type of cancer called NK/T-cell lymphoma, which is linked to a virus called EBV. The patient then had a full body scan to see where the cancer had spread. The scan showed the cancer was in the left adrenal gland area, the right adrenal gland, and under the skin of the left thigh.

Discharge Summary:
The patient was found to have NK/T-cell lymphoma linked to the EBV virus. The patient had surgery to remove the left adrenal gland and left kidney. After surgery, the patient received 7 rounds of cancer-fighting drugs using a treatment plan called GLIDE. The patient also had a transplant using their own stem cells. Two follow-up body scans done within one year showed the cancer was gone. There were no signs of cancer in any of the areas where it had been found before. The patient left the hospital with instructions to come back for check-up visits and ongoing care. This summary gives a full record of the patient's health history, treatment, and expected outcome.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: N/A
Date of Discharge: N/A

Hospital Course:
The patient, a 60-year-old female, came to the hospital with pain in the upper right belly for 4 days. She was first treated with antibiotic pills for a suspected gallbladder infection. The patient had a history of Type-2 diabetes and high blood pressure. During the exam, doctors found her liver edge could be felt, her upper right belly was tender, and there were several dark spots on her liver. These spots suggested the cancer had spread to other parts of the body. More imaging tests showed a tumor about 6 by 7 centimeters in the lower right belly area. Doctors also found swollen lymph nodes near this area and near the main blood vessels in the belly.

During surgery, doctors found a large tumor that seemed to start from the right side of the large intestine. They removed the right side of the large intestine and reconnected the healthy parts. Lab tests showed the tumor had taken over the appendix but had not spread to the nearby pouch of the intestine. Special lab tests showed the cancer was a rare type called small cell cancer that affects hormone-making cells.

After the patient healed from surgery, she was moved to the cancer care team for treatment to ease symptoms. After one round of cancer medicine called carboplatin, she developed a pocket of infection in her right side. Doctors drained this infection through the skin using a needle. The patient was then sent to the comfort care team.

Two months after surgery, the patient passed away. No exam of the body was done after death.

Discharge Diagnoses:
Small cell cancer of the hormone-making cells

Discharge Instructions:
N/A (due to patient passing away)

HOSPITAL COURSE SUMMARY:

The patient is an 82-year-old Japanese male. He had small bumps and lumps on his belly, shoulders, arms, and legs for about 1 month. These bumps did not cause any pain or discomfort. The bumps on his forearms formed in clusters. The bumps on his belly appeared where he injects insulin for his type 2 diabetes. Blood tests showed signs of inflammation and high blood sugar levels over time. Calcium and ACE levels in the blood were normal.

The patient had an ultrasound test on the forearm bumps. The test showed areas around and inside blood vessels that may contain clumps of immune cells. A small piece of skin was taken from the belly bump for testing. The lab results showed clumps of immune cells without dead tissue in the deeper skin and fat layers.

The patient was diagnosed with sarcoidosis. This is a disease where clumps of immune cells form in different body parts. The disease affected his skin, muscles, and lymph nodes near both lungs. Doctors also found a single lump in a hip muscle using a special body scan. Eye and heart tests did not show any signs of the disease.

The patient was treated with a steroid cream. The belly skin bump almost went away. But the forearm bumps kept coming back along the veins over 1 year. The swollen lymph nodes near the lungs stayed the same size. One blood marker for inflammation did get better.

The patient should see specialists to keep checking on the sarcoidosis after leaving the hospital.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Identification:
The patient is a 16-year-old boy who came to the eye emergency room. He had sudden vision loss in the lower half of his left eye.

Hospital Course:
During the eye exam, doctors found the patient could not see in the lower part of his vision. The blood vessels in the left eye also looked narrower than normal. The patient was told he had a blocked blood vessel in the upper part of his left eye. He was started on Aspirin. The patient was quickly sent to the stroke team for more tests.

The patient had an ultrasound of his heart, brain scans, and scans of blood vessels in the brain and neck. All of these tests came back normal. Blood tests showed high levels of a substance called homocysteine. The patient also had low vitamin B12 and slightly low folate levels. Later, a gene test found a change in a gene called MTHFR. This gene change can affect how the body uses certain vitamins.

Treatment:
The patient was given vitamin B12 and folate supplements. This brought the homocysteine levels back to normal. The patient also kept taking Aspirin.

Outcome:
A vision test two months later showed the patient's eyesight had gotten a little better. No new blood vessel blockages happened.

Summary:
The patient came in with sudden vision loss in the lower half of his left eye. This was caused by a blocked blood vessel in the upper part of the eye. Tests found a gene change called MTHFR that affects how the body processes vitamins. The patient was treated with vitamin B12 and folate supplements. The patient also continued taking Aspirin. A follow-up test at two months showed some improvement in vision.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [REDACTED]

Date of Admission: [REDACTED]

Date of Discharge: [REDACTED]

Diagnosis: Fluid-filled sacs near the spine joints pressing on the bundle of nerves in the lower back

Hospital Course:

The patient was admitted after several weeks of worsening back and left leg pain. The patient also had new problems urinating and leaking urine. The physical exam showed weakness in the left leg due to pain. The patient also had less feeling from the upper left thigh down to the top of the left foot and toes. An MRI scan of the lower back showed the spinal canal was very narrow at the L3-L4 level. This was caused by fluid-filled sacs near the spine joints on both sides, worse on the left. These sacs were pressing on the bundle of nerves in the lower back. A CT scan without dye also showed severe narrowing at L3-L4. X-rays taken while bending forward and backward showed the spine was stable.

After talking about treatment choices, the patient had surgery to remove the sacs. The surgeon also placed a Coflex device to keep the spine flexible and stable. This approach avoided using screws and rods while lowering the chance of the sacs coming back. Surgery happened three days after the first clinic visit. The surgeon removed parts of the L3 and L4 bones and joint edges through a cut in the middle of the back. The fluid-filled sacs were seen on both sides and fully removed using a surgical microscope. After relieving pressure on the nerves, a Coflex device was placed between the remaining L3 and L4 bones. The tissue was then closed in the normal way. The patient lost about 35cc of blood, which is a very small amount.

Lab tests confirmed the sacs were fluid-filled cysts from near the spine joints. After surgery, the patient had quick relief of left leg pain and no problems. The patient was moved to a rehab center one day after surgery. At the one-year checkup, the patient still has complete relief of left leg pain and urinary problems.

Summary:

The patient is a 71-year-old man with a history of wear-and-tear arthritis in the left hip. The patient had a left hip replacement 2 months before this admission. The patient was admitted after several weeks of worsening back and left leg pain. The patient also had new problems urinating and leaking urine. An MRI scan of the lower back showed the spinal canal was very narrow at the L3-L4 level. This was caused by fluid-filled sacs near the spine joints pressing on the bundle of nerves in the lower back. The patient had surgery to remove the sacs and had a Coflex device placed to keep the spine flexible and stable. Lab tests confirmed the sacs were fluid-filled cysts from near the spine joints. After surgery, the patient had quick relief of left leg pain and no problems. At the one-year checkup, the patient still has complete relief of left leg pain and urinary problems.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [REDACTED]
Date of Admission: 26 September 2007
Date of Discharge: 24 October 2007

Clinical Course:

The patient, a 67-year-old male, was admitted on 26 September 2007. He had stomach swelling, weight loss, and weakness for three months. A full body scan was done on 28 September 2007 to check the blood vessels. On the same day, the patient had surgery to remove a large tumor from deep in the belly. The tumor had caused few symptoms. During surgery, the patient lost a lot of blood and his body temperature dropped too low. Doctors had to remove the spleen and pack the belly with gauze to stop the bleeding. Lab tests showed the tumor was an aggressive fatty tissue cancer.

The patient was moved to intensive care for 14 hours. There he was warmed up and given blood products. He received red blood cells, platelets, and blood fluid without clotting helpers. After imaging of his blood vessels, the patient had a second surgery on 29 September 2007. Doctors removed the packing and sealed the bleeding spots. They closed the belly and placed two tubes to drain fluids. After surgery, the patient had steady blood pressure, normal urine output, and stable blood levels. His kidney tubes were removed after five days. He needed a breathing machine for ten days due to mild lung problems. On 19 October 2007, a scan showed good blood flow to most of his horseshoe kidney. Urine was flowing normally from the kidneys to the bladder.

The patient was discharged on 24 October 2007. He started cancer treatment with chemotherapy drugs and a medicine to boost white blood cells.

Diagnosis:

Aggressive fatty tissue cancer

Hospital Course:

Admitted to hospital due to stomach swelling, weight loss, and weakness for three months. A full body scan was done to check the blood vessels. Had surgery on 28 September 2007 to remove a large tumor from deep in the belly. The tumor had caused few symptoms. Needed emergency stitching and belly packing due to heavy bleeding and low body temperature. Lab tests showed the tumor was an aggressive fatty tissue cancer. Moved to intensive care for 14 hours for warming, body chemistry fixes, and blood products. He received red blood cells, platelets, and blood fluid without clotting helpers. After blood vessel imaging, had a second surgery on 29 September 2007. Doctors removed the packing and sealed the bleeding spots. Discharged on 24 October 2007. He started cancer treatment with chemotherapy drugs and a medicine to boost white blood cells.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Information:
Name: [redacted] Ethnicity: Unknown Age: 81 Gender: Male
Date of admission: [redacted] Date of discharge: [redacted]
Length of stay: 40 days
Admitting Diagnosis: Infected pouches in the lower bowel, infected appendix, and a pocket of infection that spread behind the belly organs

Hospital Course:
The patient came to the hospital after 4 days of not wanting to eat and belly pain. The patient then fell and lay on the floor for 14 hours. This led to a pocket of infection on the left side of the body. The exam showed signs of belly lining swelling, fast heartbeat, low blood pressure, and fast breathing. These signs pointed to a serious body-wide infection. The patient also had long-term kidney problems and was overweight. A special scan of the belly and pelvis showed infected pouches in the lower bowel. This infection caused a pocket of pus that spread behind the belly organs. The patient also had an infected appendix.

Surgery was needed because the patient was very sick. The patient also had other health problems that made surgery risky. These included heart disease from poor blood flow, an uneven heartbeat, and late-stage kidney disease caused by cysts on the kidneys. The doctors removed part of the lower bowel, closed off the remaining part, and made a new opening in the belly for waste to leave the body. This is called Hartmann's procedure. The doctors also removed the appendix. A small amount of infection fluid was found on the left side of the belly. The area behind the belly organs was not opened during surgery. Tubes were placed to drain fluid from the left side of the belly and the pelvis.

After surgery, the patient was taken off the breathing machine on day 1. The patient stayed in the intensive care unit for 8 days. This was because the patient needed extra oxygen due to a lung infection. The patient then moved to the regular surgery ward. The patient later got a worse body-wide infection. Another scan showed a large pocket of infected fluid behind the belly organs on the left side. Two drain tubes were placed through the skin into this pocket of fluid. Even with infection-fighting medicine given through a vein and draining the fluid, the patient died on day 40 after surgery. The cause of death was the worsening body-wide infection.

Summary of Hospital Course:
The 81-year-old male patient came in with infected pouches in the lower bowel, an infected appendix, and a pocket of infection that spread behind the belly organs. These problems led to surgery. During the hospital stay, the patient got a lung infection that needed care in the intensive care unit. Later, the patient got a worse body-wide infection. The patient died on day 40 after surgery.

Discharge Diagnoses:
1. Infected pouches in the lower bowel
2. Infected appendix
3. Pocket of infection that spread behind the belly organs

Discharge Instructions:
The patient was released to the care of his regular doctor. The patient's family was told to watch for any changes in his health. This includes fever, pain, or discomfort. They should get medical help if these changes happen. They were also told to share his medical history, surgery details, and this hospital stay with any doctor who treats him soon after leaving the hospital. No other instructions are needed after leaving the hospital.

Hospital Course:
The patient, a 6-year-old girl, was admitted with problems walking normally, slow development of small movement skills, delayed speech, several missing baby front teeth, and trouble moving her eyes up and down. The patient was diagnosed with Pol III-related leukodystrophy, a rare brain disease caused by changes in both copies of the POL3B gene. A brain scan showed unusual signals in parts of the brain that control movement. The white matter in both sides of the brain also showed problems. These findings showed that the protective covering around nerve fibers in the brain did not develop properly. The scan also showed some shrinking in parts of the brain that control balance and coordination. The full exam confirmed the diagnosis and helped create a care plan.

Hospital Course Summary:
The patient was admitted with several health concerns, including problems walking normally, slow development of small movement skills, delayed speech, several missing baby front teeth, and trouble moving her eyes up and down. After a complete exam, the patient was diagnosed with Pol III-related leukodystrophy, a rare brain disease caused by changes in both copies of the POL3B gene. During the hospital stay, the patient received care to help with comfort and symptoms. The patient went home after her condition became stable. The care team talked with the patient and family about follow-up care and the treatment plan. When the patient left the hospital, she was sent to the right specialists for continued care.

The patient came to our hospital with an abnormal opening that formed a tunnel from the stomach to the skin. This happened after weight loss surgery. After surgery, the leaking stopped and very little fluid came out of the drainage tube. Scans showed no more leaking. The patient was very weak at first but slowly got better. The patient left the hospital after one month of watching and care.

The patient needs to see the care team to check for any problems after surgery and to discuss any symptoms.

None

The patient should make appointments with the care team. They will check healing and watch the recovery process.

DISCHARGE SUMMARY

PATIENT: 35-year old white woman with long-term belly pain and a history of repeated swelling of the pancreas

HOSPITAL COURSE:
The patient was admitted for severe long-term belly pain that did not get better with strong pain medicine. She also had nausea and vomiting.
She had a procedure called ERCP where doctors used a thin tube with a camera to look at her digestive system. This showed repeated swelling of the pancreas and a widened bile duct with no blockages.
Special imaging scans of her belly confirmed what the ERCP found.
Because the patient is young, doctors chose surgery to avoid more tube procedures in the future.
The patient had robot-assisted surgery to remove part of her pancreas and nearby organs. Doctors then reconnected her digestive system in several places so it could work properly.
During surgery, doctors also put special cells from her pancreas into her body to help control blood sugar.
The patient handled the surgery well and her recovery went smoothly without problems.
She went home nine days after surgery with less pain. She was taking a low dose of insulin to control blood sugar.
At her checkup 45 days after surgery, her blood sugar was normal without needing insulin shots. She said her pain was completely gone.

FOLLOW-UP:
The patient should see her regular doctor and any specialists as needed. They will keep checking on her care and how well her pancreas is working.

Hospital Course:
A 78-year-old female with diabetes, high blood pressure, and obesity was admitted to our hospital after a sudden stroke. The stroke caused slurred speech and weakness on the left side of her body. None specified.

The patient died on day 3 in the nursing home. The cause of death is not known. The family chose not to have an exam of the body after death.
