Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: IA, Mr.
Age: 85
Sex: Male

Hospital Course:
Mr. IA, an 85-year-old male, came to the mental health clinic. He was seeing things that were not there. He saw images of people in front of him. He had been treated for high pressure in his eyes for 7 years. This condition affects both eyes and can damage vision. He had been unable to see for the past 3 years. These strange visions had been happening for about 8 weeks before his visit. The doctor checked his eyes and found damage to the back of both eyes. The light-sensitive area in each eye had dried out and broken down. The nerve that connects the eye to the brain looked pale and showed signs of damage in both eyes. All other body and brain tests were normal for his age.

Treatment and Response:
The patient was told that he did not have a mental illness. He learned a way to make the images go away. He was told to close his eyes and blink over and over. This could make the images disappear for a short time before coming back. His family members learned about this condition called Charles Bonnet Syndrome. They were told not to think of it as a mental illness. At first, the patient came back every 2 weeks. Later, visits were spread out to every 4 weeks and then every 6 weeks. His eyesight did not get better during this time. However, the visions went away after 6 months without any medicine. He was then sent home from care.

Condition at Discharge:
Mr. IA left with a clear understanding of the eye-closing and blinking method used to help him. He was reminded not to think of this as a mental illness. He was told to close his eyes often and blink many times if the visions came back. His family members were happy with the information and advice they received. They agreed to watch and make sure the method was being used and working.

The patient came in at 12 weeks of pregnancy for testing and counseling about her baby's genes. Early pregnancy screening showed low risk for problems. A follow-up scan at 20 weeks found low fluid around the baby, slow baby growth, and small hands and feet. The patient had a test where fluid was taken from around the baby to check for gene problems. Testing found a missing piece of genetic material on chromosome 1. This missing piece was not found in the patient or her husband.

Diagnosis:

The baby has a missing piece of genetic material on chromosome 1. The baby also has a split lip and roof of mouth on both sides. The baby has a single crease across the right palm. The baby has a short neck. The baby has a wide, flat nose bridge. The baby has ears that are shaped differently and sit lower than usual. The baby has small hands and feet. The baby has weak muscle tone. The baby has a red birthmark on the back of the head.

Treatment:

The patient chose to continue the pregnancy after learning about the diagnosis. Surgery was done to repair the split lip and roof of mouth.

Follow-up:

The same gene test was done again using blood after birth. The test showed the same missing piece of genetic material on chromosome 1. This confirmed what was found during pregnancy.

Hospital Course Summary:

Admission: The patient came to the hospital with two weeks of pain in the side of the back and four days of dark brown urine. During the physical exam, the heart had a normal beat with an extra heart sound heard best on the left side of the chest. The patient had strong pain when the doctor pressed on the left side of the back near the kidney. The doctor also heard crackling sounds in the lower parts of both lungs. First blood tests showed low white blood cell count, low red blood cell count, and low platelet count. The tests also showed high creatinine levels, which means the kidneys were not working well. The urine test was not normal.

Diagnosis: The patient was found to have a blocked blood vessel in the spleen, which damaged part of the spleen. The patient also had a heart valve that formed with two flaps instead of three. This valve had a growth on it caused by an infection. The infection did not show up in blood tests that look for germs. A small tissue sample was taken from the kidney. It showed the immune system was causing swelling and damage in the kidney.

Treatment: The patient took two antibiotics called doxycycline and rifampin for 6 weeks. The patient also had surgery to replace the damaged heart valve. During treatment, the side pain got better. There were fewer red blood cells in the urine. The creatinine levels went down, which means the kidneys were working better.

Prognosis: The patient got better during treatment. However, a blood test for a certain protein linked to the immune system stayed high even after taking antibiotics.

Follow-up: The patient should see a regular doctor for checkups. More tests may be needed.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Information:
Name: [NAME]
Age: 69
Gender: Male

Diagnosis:
Heart attack affecting the front wall of the heart, Heart Failure

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted to the hospital in September 2017 for heart bypass surgery, repair of two heart valves, and replacement of another heart valve. A special wire was placed in the heart, and the heart device was upgraded to help the heart pump better and correct dangerous heart rhythms. A heart monitoring feature was set up and ready to use starting January 2018.

Progress Notes:
In January 2018, the patient had mild heart failure symptoms and normal fluid levels in the body. Blood tests showed reduced kidney function and high levels of a hormone that shows heart stress. The heart monitor score was 8, which is at the high end of normal. On February 5th, the heart monitor sent an alert because the score went above the warning level of 16. A review of the device data showed the score had slowly risen to 17 over two weeks. The patient was called and said he had no symptoms or signs of fluid buildup. A follow-up phone call was made two weeks later. Even though the heart monitor score rose to 25, the patient still felt fine. However, he admitted to drinking more fluids and eating more salt than advised. The patient was told to cut back on fluids and salt. The heart monitor score stopped rising but did not go down. An office visit was then scheduled.

At the office visit, the patient first said he had no symptoms. But during his exercise program, he had mild trouble breathing. The doctor found swollen neck veins and mild ankle swelling. Blood tests showed worse kidney function and higher levels of the heart stress hormone. The heart monitor score was 22. The patient was slowly building up extra fluid in his body. The dose of his water pill was increased. After this change, the patient could exercise better and finished his exercise program. The heart monitor score also dropped to 0.

Follow-up:
At a follow-up visit in April, the patient had no signs of fluid buildup. Blood tests showed better kidney function and lower levels of the heart stress hormone. The patient is now in stable condition with mild heart failure symptoms. The patient has not needed to go back to the hospital for worsening heart failure.

Impression:
The heart monitor was successfully used as part of the heart failure care plan. The monitor may also help guide changes to medicine for patients at home.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [Redacted]

Hospital Course:

The patient is a 45-year-old man. He came to the hospital with pain in his left side, numbness, and weakness in both legs. During the exam, the patient had weak muscles in both legs. The patient also had stronger than normal reflexes in the right knee. Tests showed that a bone tumor had caused breaks in the spine bones called T8 and T9. The tumor was also pressing on the spinal cord and causing nerve problems.

The patient had surgery to remove the damaged spine bone at T9. Doctors put in a metal cage to support the spine. They also placed screws at T8 through T10 to hold the spine steady. Lab tests of the removed tissue showed a condition called Langerhans cell histiocytosis. This is a rare disease where abnormal cells build up and can damage bones. The patient then had radiation treatment on the T8 through T10 area of the spine. After treatment, the leg weakness and numbness got much better.

The patient has been checked for almost 6 years with no sign of the tumor coming back. Discharge instructions included follow-up visits with the regular doctor. The patient should also get regular scans to make sure the bone tumor does not return.

Overall, the patient received excellent medical care from the healthcare team and responded well to treatment.

Discharge Summary:

Patient: 78-year-old Hispanic female

Clinical history: Type 2 diabetes, high blood pressure, underactive thyroid

Reason for admission: Confusion and changes in thinking

Diagnosis: Very high sodium levels in the blood caused by the body losing too much water due to very high blood sugar

Hospital course: The patient came in with a cough, trouble breathing, and confusion. The exam showed the patient looked very sick, was hard to wake up, and had weak breath sounds in the lower left lung. Lab tests showed very high blood sugar levels. The patient was given a large amount of salt water fluids in the emergency room. This caused sodium levels to rise for a short time. An insulin drip was started through the vein to lower the very high blood sugar. A brain wave test was done because of the confusion. The patient's kidneys got better. The infection in the lower left lung was treated as pneumonia caught outside the hospital. Feeding through a tube was started because the patient was too confused to eat. The patient's thinking got better and returned to normal. The patient was sent to a nursing care center after learning about diabetes care.

Plan: The patient was started on metformin, long-acting insulin glargine, and fast-acting insulin lispro as needed based on blood sugar levels. Follow-up with the patient was not possible because the patient went back to live in another country.

Discharge Summary
Patient: 39-year-old male

Medical History:
The patient had a history of hay fever. He reported many episodes of dizziness and patches of hives, with chest tightness that happened either with or shortly after exercise over the previous 3 months. Over time, the episodes had become more frequent and severe and required several treatments to relieve his symptoms. The patient was diagnosed with a condition that causes swelling in the food pipe due to a type of white blood cell. This was confirmed through a small tissue sample.

Hospital Course:
The patient was given several medications to treat his throat and chest tightness with exercise, but they did not completely resolve his symptoms. He later tried to avoid wheat and all food for up to 12 hours before exercise but to no avail.

To manage his condition, the patient chose to start a trial of omalizumab, which was given in doses of 300 mg every 2 weeks. No food restrictions were given during this time. The patient reported major improvement, and he was able to exercise three times a week without any symptoms. He had only one episode of mild hives, but it happened when he had missed one of his omalizumab injections. The patient continued to exercise normally, reporting any symptoms that he had and was followed up monthly.

The patient later experienced episodes of hives, greatly increased chest tightness, and swelling around the eyes after at least 15 minutes of exercise. He ultimately had an episode of a severe allergic reaction with hives, difficulty breathing, and facial swelling and was admitted to the emergency room, where he received several treatments to relieve his symptoms. After this episode, omalizumab was restarted at the same doses and intervals.

Follow-up and Outcome:
The patient continued on omalizumab with no further episodes of severe allergic reactions and no restrictions on his activity level. He is expected to continue being followed up monthly and continue exercising normally.

Patient: 37-year-old African-American female with sickle cell disease (a blood disorder)

Hospital Course:
The patient came to the clinic with sudden vision loss in her right eye. During the exam, she could only see hand movements with her right eye. Her left eye had normal 20/20 vision. Her pupils responded normally to light. There was heavy bleeding inside her right eye that blocked the doctor's view of the back of the eye. The patient also had some changes to the nerve and blood vessels at the back of her eye.

Treatment and Management:
The patient had surgery on her right eye to remove the blood and treat the bleeding. The doctor used a small camera and laser during the surgery. Some scar tissue was carefully cut away. Other scar tissue was left alone because it was stuck tightly to important blood vessels.

Follow-up:
At the 1-month follow-up visit, the patient reported sudden painless vision loss in her left eye 2 days before. Her right eye vision had improved to 20/100. Her left eye vision was 20/50. Her pupils still responded normally. The doctor looked at the back of her left eye and saw pale patches near the center. This meant some small blood vessels had become blocked. A scan done a few weeks later showed some leftover scar tissue in her right eye. The scan of her left eye showed damage to the inner layers from the blocked blood vessels.

Recommendations:
The doctor offered a special dye test to confirm what was wrong, but the patient said no. The patient should continue to be checked regularly to make sure her condition is managed well.

Discharge Summary:

This is a summary of admission details for a 20-year-old female with a medical history of post-traumatic stress syndrome and facial acne. The patient was admitted to the emergency department after swallowing seven pills of paroxetine.

The first check in the emergency department showed very few symptoms, steady body function measures, and a normal heart rhythm test. The patient was watched for six hours and said she felt warm and flushed and became restless. The patient had a seizure that staff saw happen, which lasted 90 seconds and stopped on its own. Cyproheptadine was given as a 12 mg pill one time, then 4 mg every eight hours if needed. The patient was moved to the intensive care unit for close watching with regular heart rhythm tests. The heart rhythm went back to normal 16 hours later, and no seizures were seen during the hospital stay.

Discharge Diagnosis:

Suspected serotonin syndrome

Treatment:

The patient was given fluids through a vein and lorazepam. Cyproheptadine was given as a 12 mg pill one time, then 4 mg every eight hours if needed.

Follow-up:

The patient was sent home in stable condition.

The patient came in with neck pain and vomiting that came and went. Scans showed a rare developmental cyst. The patient had surgery to remove almost all of the cyst. A scan showed only a very small piece of the cyst was left.

Diagnosis: Diffuse large B cell lymphoma (a type of blood cancer that affects white blood cells)

Hospital Course:
The patient, a 77-year-old woman, came to our clinic with trouble swallowing for two months. Both sides of her thyroid gland were enlarged. The right side felt firmer than the left side. Lumps were found along the right side of her neck. Her thyroid hormone levels were normal. A small camera was used to look at her throat and nothing unusual was seen.

An ultrasound showed a large mass over 4 cm in the right side of her thyroid. The mass had an uneven shape and looked solid with possible small calcium deposits inside. The mass had grown into the windpipe wall and wrapped around a major blood vessel in the neck. A thin needle was used to take a sample from the mass. The results suggested it might be an aggressive type of cancer.

A scan with dye was done to get a better look at the neck. It showed the mass in the back part of the right thyroid was growing toward the windpipe. A tissue sample was then removed through surgery. Lab tests on this sample showed it was diffuse large B cell lymphoma.

The patient received three rounds of cancer-fighting drugs called R-CHOP. She also received targeted radiation treatment with a total dose of 3,816 cGy. Four months after the first diagnosis, scans showed the cancer was completely gone.

Discharge condition:
The patient has been sent home with much improvement in her health.

Follow up care plan:
The right follow-up care plan has been explained to the patient. She has been told to come back to the clinic for a follow-up visit.

Summary:
The patient came in with trouble swallowing and an enlarged thyroid with signs that suggested aggressive cancer. A tissue sample was removed through surgery. Lab tests showed it was diffuse large B cell lymphoma. She was treated with R-CHOP cancer-fighting drugs and targeted radiation. Four months after the first diagnosis, scans showed the cancer was completely gone. The patient has been sent home with much improvement in her health. The right follow-up care plan has been explained to her.

Sex: Male

Medical History: None

Chief Complaint: Painless swelling on the right side of the neck

Hospital Course:

The patient came in with a painless lump on the right side of the neck. The lump had been there for one month. There was no injury, fever, or other illness. A physical exam showed one oval-shaped lump on the right side of the neck. It measured about 3 by 2 centimeters. Imaging tests of the neck showed a growth. Doctors thought it might be a tumor growing from nerve tissue.

Doctors made a cut along the front of the neck muscle to reach the tumor. The entire tumor was removed using standard surgery methods. The vagus nerve, which controls swallowing and voice, had to be cut during surgery. Doctors repaired this nerve using a piece of nerve taken from the lower leg.

After surgery, the patient had some trouble swallowing. This got better in two days. The patient noticed a small change in voice, but food and liquids did not go down the wrong way. A camera test of the throat showed the right vocal cord was not moving properly. The patient's voice got better with speech therapy.

Summary:

The patient came in with a painless lump on the right side of the neck. It turned out to be a tumor growing from the vagus nerve. Doctors removed the tumor with surgery. They repaired the vagus nerve using a piece of nerve from the lower leg. After surgery, the patient had some trouble swallowing and a small change in voice. These problems got better over time and with speech therapy. The patient should come back for checkups so doctors can track recovery.

During the hospital stay, the patient's low red blood cells and clotting cell counts returned to normal. The patient's kidneys started working normally again. Blood tests that measure swelling in the body also returned to normal within the first few weeks. The patient stayed healthy for 2 years without needing any medicine.

Follow-Up Care:
The patient received full information about his illness and treatment choices. The patient was told to see his regular doctor and his specialty doctors for blood, cancer, and kidney care. The patient was told to get regular blood tests and imaging scans to check on his health.

The patient was sent home without any medications.

Castleman's disease, a rare illness affecting many body systems, along with damage to small blood vessels in the kidneys and sudden kidney failure.

She also has weak bones, low iron in her blood, and cysts on her ovaries. The patient has low levels of uric acid and normal fat levels in her blood.

The patient has high levels of a protein that helps move fat in the blood. Other related proteins are at normal levels. She has been short and had learning difficulties since childhood. The patient is overweight and has fatty lumps under her skin. This is due to a high-starch diet and frequent doses of raw cornstarch to prevent low blood sugar.

The patient has a hard-to-treat form of seizures that happen every day. A brain scan showed scarring, shrinking of part of the right side of the brain, and deeper grooves in the brain. A test of brain waves showed abnormal electrical activity in the right front part of the brain.

The patient is currently taking medicine for seizures, depression, low iron, folic acid, and stomach acid.

Discharge Conditions:

The patient is being discharged with ongoing therapy and follow-up appointments arranged. They are to follow their prescribed treatment plan and update their medical care team with any concerns.

Discharge Diagnoses:

A rare disease that prevents the body from releasing stored sugar properly.
Hard-to-treat seizures.
Noncancerous liver growths.
Low iron in the blood.
Cysts on the ovaries.
Short height.

Discharge Medications:

N/A.

Hospital Course:

The patient is a 20-year-old female with high blood pressure in the lungs and a bleeding disorder. She came to the clinic when she was 13 weeks pregnant. The patient had an emergency surgery to deliver the baby at 26 weeks of pregnancy. This was done because her lung condition got worse and the baby's heart rate dropped too low. After the surgery, the patient's heart stopped beating. She was placed on a machine that pumped blood for her heart and added oxygen to her blood. She stayed in the intensive care unit for a long time. She needed medicines to help her heart pump and keep her blood pressure stable. After a long hospital stay, she went home 101 days after her surgery.

Discharge Diagnosis:

1. High blood pressure in the lungs
2. A bleeding disorder that prevents blood from clotting normally

Procedures:

1. Emergency surgery to deliver the baby
2. A machine to pump blood and add oxygen when the heart cannot work on its own
3. A small surgery to drain fluid from around the heart

Hospital Course Summary:

The patient was diagnosed with high blood pressure in the lungs and a bleeding disorder. She came to the clinic at 13 weeks of pregnancy. Doctors advised her about the risks, but she chose to continue her pregnancy. Doctors stopped medicines that could harm the baby. They kept her on two safe medicines for her lung condition. The patient was admitted to the hospital. Doctors changed one medicine given under her skin to a different medicine given through a vein. The patient did well on these medicines until 25 weeks of pregnancy. Then she came to the emergency room. She was coughing up blood and having trouble breathing. Doctors were worried her condition would get worse. They did emergency surgery and delivered a healthy baby. But during the surgery to close her womb, the patient's heart stopped beating. She was placed on a machine to pump her blood and add oxygen. The patient stayed in the intensive care unit for a long time. She needed medicines to help her heart pump and keep her blood pressure stable. After successful treatment, doctors slowly took her off the blood pumping machine. She stayed in the hospital for a long time to recover. The patient went home 101 days after her surgery.

Mucopolysaccharidosis type IIIA, which is a rare disease where the body cannot break down certain sugars properly

Stable

The patient came to Dongguan Children's Hospital 6 months ago because her breasts started developing. Doctors ran blood tests and took pictures of the inside of her body. They put the patient to sleep with a breathing tube during the procedure. They added fluid to her belly area to help see the growth better on the screen. The procedure went well. The patient should keep taking her medicines as directed. The patient should see her doctors for check-ups as planned. The patient may need regular visits and imaging tests to watch the treated area.

1. Early puberty

The patient was in stable condition when she left the hospital.

DISCHARGE SUMMARY:

Patient: 79-year-old male

Medications: None prescribed

Hospital Course:

The patient came in with pain in the right side of the back that had lasted for 1 year. During the exam, the patient's heart rate, blood pressure, and temperature were normal. The belly was soft and not painful when pressed. There was no swelling of organs or lumps that could be felt.

Blood tests and urine hormone tests came back normal. The urine test showed signs of possible infection. However, the lab test to grow bacteria found no germs after 24 hours.

A CT scan with dye showed a large growth behind the belly area near the right adrenal gland. The adrenal glands sit on top of the kidneys. The growth had brighter edges, dead tissue in the center, and small calcium spots. The dye washed out of the growth over time. An MRI scan with dye also showed a large uneven growth with dead tissue in the center above the right kidney. The edges of the growth showed up brighter on the scan.

Surgery was done to remove the right adrenal gland. The patient did well after surgery with no problems. Lab tests on the removed tissue showed the growth was a cavernous hemangioma. This is a non-cancerous tumor made of tangled blood vessels.

Follow-up:

The patient has healed well after surgery. The patient should schedule regular visits with the regular doctor. No other tests are needed. No medications have been prescribed at discharge.

The patient came to the Outpatients Department of the Ophthalmiatreio Eye Hospital of Athens. The patient had worsening vision in the right eye and saw flashing lights in both eyes. They looked at the front and back parts of both eyes using a special microscope. The patient had several tests done. These included tests to check side vision and tests using special dyes to look at blood vessels in the eyes. The patient also had scans to take detailed pictures of the back of the eyes. During this time, the symptoms and exam findings stayed the same in both eyes. The patient also had scans of the head and belly. These scans did not show any problems.

Diagnosis:
The patient was diagnosed with Acute Zonal Occult Outer Retinopathy, also called AZOOR. This is a rare condition that affects the outer layer of the back of the eye.

Plan:
The patient was sent home. The patient was told to come back for regular checkups and ongoing care.

Prognosis:
The symptoms and exam findings stayed stable in both eyes after 8 months of checkups.

Hospital Course:
The patient came to the hospital because her belly was bigger than normal. The doctor's exam showed her liver was larger than it should be. Her liver also had too much fat in it. The patient has Wolman Disease or CESD. This is a rare condition where the body cannot break down certain fats properly.

The patient was seen by a liver specialist and a doctor who studies inherited conditions.

The patient was in good overall health when she left the hospital. Her liver was still working well.

None listed in the report.

Discharge Instructions:
The patient's parents were told about the diagnosis. They received information about how this condition runs in families. The patient will need to see a liver specialist and a genetics doctor for ongoing care.

HOSPITAL COURSE SUMMARY:

Admission Date: [DATE]
Discharge Date: [DATE]

FINAL DIAGNOSIS:
Bladder cancer, a type called diffuse large B-cell lymphoma. This is a cancer of the immune system cells that started in the bladder.

HOSPITAL COURSE:
The patient came to the hospital with lower belly pain and pain during urination. These problems had been happening on and off for 3 months. A urine test showed an infection. An ultrasound showed swelling in the tubes that carry urine from the kidneys. It also showed a thick bladder wall and a growth in the pelvic area that had spread into the bladder.

Doctors used a small camera to look inside the bladder. They found a tumor in the area where urine drains out. They removed the tumor through a procedure done through the urinary opening. Lab tests on the removed tissue showed cancer cells with abnormal shapes. The cancer had grown into the bladder muscle and spread into blood and lymph vessels.

Special lab tests were done to identify the exact type of cancer. These tests checked for certain markers on the cancer cells. The results confirmed the cancer was a specific type of lymphoma called diffuse large B-cell type.

A full body scan was done to check for cancer spread. The scan showed a large active mass in the pelvic area. This mass involved the bladder, vagina, and rectum. The scan also showed cancer had spread to areas above and below the chest. There were also spots in the stomach, liver, and both lungs.

The patient started a cancer treatment plan called R-CHOP. This is a mix of medicines used to treat this type of lymphoma. After the first round of treatment, the patient's organs stopped working. The patient died from this organ failure.

DISCHARGE CONDITION:
Deceased.

FOLLOW-UP:
None necessary.

Patient Name: [REDACTED]

MR#: [REDACTED]

Date of Admission: [REDACTED]

Date of Discharge: [REDACTED]

Admitting Diagnosis: Advanced small cell lung cancer that has spread

Hospital Course Summary:

The patient is a 43-year-old woman who never smoked. The patient was admitted after having trouble breathing during activity for six months. The patient had several tests done to find the cause. These tests included a chest X-ray and CT scan of the chest. The patient also had a scope passed into the lungs to collect samples. Brain scans and full body scans were also done. These tests showed advanced small cell lung cancer that had spread. The patient started the first round of cancer-fighting drugs called cisplatin and etoposide. The tumor got much smaller with this treatment. After six rounds, the cancer started growing again. The patient then started a second set of drugs called carboplatin and irinotecan. After two rounds, the patient got a lung infection caused by a blockage. The treatment plan had to change. The cancer was no longer responding to standard treatments. The patient started a third set of drugs called CAV. This included three medicines: Adriamycin, vincristine, and cyclophosphamide. The patient received 11 rounds of this treatment. After the 11th round, the cancer started growing again. This treatment could not continue. The patient then started a fourth set of drugs called ICE. This included ifosfamide, carboplatin, and etoposide. The patient had to stop because of bad side effects. A new plan using ICE without etoposide was started as the fourth treatment. The cancer partly shrank with this treatment. The patient's pain slowly went away during this time. The patient chose to stop further treatment. Eight months after finishing five rounds of carboplatin and ifosfamide, the patient came to the emergency room. The patient had trouble breathing and rib pain. A chest CT scan showed the tumor had grown larger. Comfort care was started with a sixth round of carboplatin and ifosfamide. The patient's symptoms got better. Sadly, the patient died from a lung infection caused by food or liquid going into the lungs. This happened 11 days later. The patient lived for about 27 months after starting cancer treatment.

Discharge Diagnosis: Advanced small cell lung cancer that has spread

Discharge Medications: [REDACTED]

Summary of Hospitalization:

The patient was admitted with advanced small cell lung cancer that had spread. The patient received several different cancer-fighting drug treatments. These included cisplatin and etoposide, carboplatin and irinotecan, CAV, and ICE. The ICE treatment without etoposide worked partly. The tumor got smaller and was less active. The patient later came back to the hospital for comfort care. Trouble breathing and chest pain got better after a sixth round of carboplatin and ifosfamide. Sadly, the patient later died from a lung infection caused by food or liquid going into the lungs.

He had a surgery to remove the foreskin, which fixed his urination problems. The patient was started on a cancer medicine called venetoclax. PATIENT INFORMATION:
Patient 3 is a 1-year- and 10-month-old boy. He has Ohtahara syndrome, a rare brain condition that causes seizures. He also has serious delays in his growth and learning.

HOSPITAL COURSE:
The patient started having seizures one day after he was born. These seizures caused his arms and legs to stiffen and stretch out. They happened in groups about 10 times a day, with 2 to 3 seizures in each group. At 1 month old, he started having a different type of seizure with muscle stiffening. A brain wave test showed unusual patterns of activity and pauses. The test also showed seizures that moved from one part of the brain to another. A brain scan came back normal. The patient tried four different seizure medicines, but none of them worked. A fifth medicine called oxcarbazepine helped some, but the brain wave test showed a new problem pattern. Doctors did detailed gene testing and found a rare change in his genes. Because of this, doctors gave him a medicine called phenytoin. The seizures stopped after the dose was raised to 12.5 milligrams for each kilogram of body weight per day. The brain wave test got better and no longer showed the problem pattern.

MEDICATIONS:
The patient takes phenytoin. This medicine worked well to stop his seizures.

FOLLOW-UP:
The patient will keep seeing his doctors for regular checkups.

Sex: Female

Date of Discharge: [Discharge Date]
Admitting Physician: [Physician Name]
Primary Diagnosis: Hives

Hospital Course:

The patient came to the allergy clinic with a problem of hives that kept coming back all over her body. She also had a rash and swelling of her face. These problems got worse when she ate very spicy foods, heavily seasoned foods, or Chinese foods. In the past, she was treated for allergies that caused a stuffy or runny nose. She also had bad hives and a rash all over her body after taking pain medicines like ibuprofen. Blood tests showed she had higher than normal levels of certain allergy-related cells and proteins. A skin test showed small reactions to silkworm pupa, herring, cabbage, celery, and walnut. However, the patient had never gotten hives from eating any of these foods before.

The patient had a special blood test to check how her allergy cells react to different things. The test showed that her allergy cells reacted to MSG, a flavor enhancer often used in food. Her allergy cells did not react to any other food additives that were tested. Tests for thyroid hormone levels came back normal.

Hospital Course Summary:

History of Present Illness:
The patient is a healthy 3.5-year-old boy. The patient was admitted because of weakness and pale skin for five days. Two weeks before coming to the hospital, the patient had loose stools for three days. A physical exam showed yellow skin, pale skin, and an enlarged spleen. Blood tests showed low red blood cell levels. The blood sample also showed unusual red blood cells. The patient was diagnosed with a condition where the body attacks its own red blood cells. This is called warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia.

Hospital Course:
The patient received a blood transfusion. The patient then received a strong steroid medicine through an IV. The patient responded very well to this treatment. The patient took steroid pills for four weeks. The dose was slowly lowered over the next five months. The patient got sick again after catching a cold. The steroid pills were restarted and worked well. When the dose was lowered, the blood counts got worse again. A medicine called azathioprine was started. The blood counts got a little worse. After the parents agreed in writing, a medicine called rituximab was started. The patient received four doses, one each week. Two months later, the patient was doing well. After 12 months, blood tests showed the condition was gone. The patient has been healthy with no return of the illness for three years.

Discharge Diagnosis:
Warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia, a condition where the body attacks its own red blood cells

Discharge Medication:
None

Discharge Condition:
Stable

The patient should see the right doctors as needed.

The patient should eat healthy foods and get enough rest.

The patient was diagnosed with warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia. This is when the body attacks its own red blood cells. The patient was treated with blood transfusions and several medicines. These included steroids given by IV and by mouth, azathioprine, and rituximab. The patient responded well to treatment. The patient has been healthy with no return of the illness for three years.

Gender: Male
Age: 14 years
Date of Admission: [REDACTED]
Date of Discharge: [REDACTED]
Discharge Diagnosis: A non-cancerous sac filled with skin-like tissue near the lower end of the spinal cord

Hospital Course:

The patient was first told he had a spine infection called tuberculosis by a local doctor. He was given medicine for that illness. But the patient got worse, so he was moved to our hospital. He had pain in his lower back. He also had weakness and numbness in both legs. The patient's thinking and memory were normal. The nerves in his head and face were working fine.

Doctors found that the muscles in both lower legs had gotten smaller. The left side had loose muscle tone. Both legs had weak strength, rated 3 out of 5. Reflexes were missing in both legs. The patient had reduced feeling in parts of his right leg. He could not feel light touch or sharp pokes as well as normal. Feeling was also reduced in the area around his buttocks and upper thighs.

Scans showed a small, clearly shaped growth measuring about 1.5 by 0.6 centimeters. This growth was inside the spinal canal and pressing on the lower end of the spinal cord. The growth was located at the middle-to-lower back area. It had clear edges and different shades on the scan images.

Doctors did surgery through a straight cut in the middle of the back. They found the spinal cord was being squeezed by a growth inside it. They made a small opening in the spinal cord covering. Inside, they found a grayish-white sac with one pocket. This sac was growing in the lower end of the spinal cord. The doctors drained the sac and removed almost all of it. Lab tests showed the sac was a harmless cyst lined with skin cells.

After surgery, the patient slowly got stronger. Leg strength improved to 4 out of 5. Feeling for light touch and sharp pokes came back. One month later, the patient had no nerve problems. He could move around and walk with help.

Discharge Instructions:

The patient has been discharged on [REDACTED]. Please follow up with your primary care doctor or brain and nerve specialist for further consultation. In case of any return of symptoms, please return to our hospital immediately.

Discharge Summary

Patient Name: [REDACTED]
Age: 44
Gender: Female
Main Problem: Painful mouth sore

Hospital Stay:
The patient came to the hospital with a painful mouth sore that started 6 weeks before. She had a history of recurring mouth sores and was given steroid medicine that works throughout the body. Her condition got worse and she developed a red, bumpy rash on her body. She also had red eyes, fever, loose stools, and lost weight. Blood tests showed high levels of white blood cells and a type of white blood cell called eosinophils. Doctors thought she might have Stevens-Johnson Syndrome, a serious skin reaction. She was treated with steroids that work throughout the body. Her skin got a little better but her mouth sores did not improve.
A small sample of skin was tested and showed damage where the skin layers meet. It also showed blisters forming under the top skin layer. These findings matched a condition called paraneoplastic pemphigus. More tests showed that her immune system was attacking normal skin and organ tissue. The patient was finally found to have stage IV follicular lymphoma, a type of blood cancer that had spread. She also had a lung condition called bronchiolitis obliterans and a serious fungal lung infection called invasive pulmonary aspergillosis.
Cancer treatment led to complete disappearance of the lymphoma. This was confirmed through a special imaging scan that detects cancer activity. The patient's mouth sores and skin rash stayed under control with a low dose of steroid medicine for 8 months. However, she developed the lung condition and serious fungal lung infection. These caused her lungs to stop working.

Treatment Given:
Treatment included cancer-fighting drugs called rituximab, cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine, and prednisolone. These medicines led to complete disappearance of the patient's lymphoma. The patient also took a low dose of steroid medicine at 5mg per day. This kept her mouth sores and skin rash under control.

Follow-Up Care:
No follow-up care is needed because the patient died from lung failure.

Diagnosis:
The patient was found to have paraneoplastic pemphigus, a rare skin blistering disease. This was linked to stage IV follicular lymphoma, a blood cancer that had spread. She also had bronchiolitis obliterans, a lung condition, and invasive pulmonary aspergillosis, a serious fungal lung infection.

It showed swelling with many infection-fighting cells. It also showed swelling in small blood vessels but no broken-down cells.

Diagnosis:
Pyoderma gangrenosum of the penis. This is a rare skin condition that causes painful sores.

The patient was given a steroid medicine called prednisone. The pain got much better within a few days.

Diagnosis:
Retinitis pigmentosa (a condition that damages the back of the eye and affects vision)
Intermittent diplopia (double vision that comes and goes)

Hospital Course:
The patient came to the hospital with double vision that had been happening on and off for a few years. The double vision had recently gotten worse. An eye doctor looked at the back of the patient's eyes. The exam showed damage to the light-sensing tissue, narrowed blood vessels, and pale nerve areas in both eyes. This led to a diagnosis of retinitis pigmentosa. A vision field test showed the patient could only see in a small central area in both eyes. Eye alignment tests showed the left eye was higher than it should be and turned slightly outward. The muscles that move the left eye were not working properly. The patient tried special glasses with prisms that stopped the double vision. However, the patient did not want to wear these glasses and asked for surgery instead.

The patient had surgery to fix a muscle in the left eye. This helped improve the eye alignment. One month after surgery, the left eye was still slightly higher and turned outward. The patient only had double vision when looking up and to the right. There was no double vision when looking straight ahead or at close objects. At a check-up three months later, the eye measurements were the same. The patient was happy because the double vision no longer bothered daily activities.

Follow-Up Plan:
The patient will have regular check-ups with an eye doctor. These visits will track any changes in the eye condition. The doctor will also check if double vision comes back in the future.

Hospital Course:

The 27-year-old Japanese woman came to our hospital with a fever, pain in many joints, swelling in the lower legs and feet, confusion, and kidneys that were not working well. Tests showed high levels of creatinine, urea nitrogen, and lactate dehydrogenase in the blood. These are waste products that build up when the kidneys do not work properly. The patient also had low levels of white blood cells, red blood cells, and platelets. A urine test showed red blood cells in the urine. Tests of the immune system found two types of harmful proteins that attack the body. The tests also showed low levels of proteins that help fight infection. The patient did not have a blood clotting disorder called antiphospholipid syndrome. Based on these results, the patient was diagnosed with lupus nephritis and thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura. Lupus nephritis is a disease where the immune system attacks the kidneys. Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura is a blood disorder that causes small clots to form throughout the body. Treatment began with steroid medicines to calm the immune system. The patient also received plasma exchange, which replaces the liquid part of blood with healthy donor plasma. The patient also received dialysis to clean the blood because the kidneys were not working.

Hospital Course:
The patient is a 58-year-old male worker. He came in with a rough, scaly patch of skin on his right lower back. The patch started as a small ring-shaped spot. It grew outward into a larger patch. The patch stayed the same size for seven years. Then it started spreading again in the last two years. The patient often worked without a shirt for long hours. He felt itching and burning in hot weather.

Investigations:
The patients had many tests done. All test results came back normal. The patients tested negative for HIV. Their immune systems were working well. Doctors thought the skin problem was porokeratosis. A skin sample test confirmed this. The sample showed special features in the skin layers that matched this condition.

Treatment:
The patients were told to wear clothes that protect from the sun. They were given isotretinoin 20mg pills to take by mouth. They were also given halobetasol 0.05% cream to put on the skin at night. The patient with itching and burning in the sun had part of the patch removed. He also had freezing treatment. After that, he put on tretinoin 0.05% cream and fluorouracil 5% cream on different nights. This patient had side effects every 3-4 weeks. These included redness, itching, oozing, crusting, and swelling. After five months, the skin showed fair improvement.

Follow-up:
One of the three patients stopped coming to appointments. The other two patients showed no more signs of the skin problem. The patient who had side effects from treatment stopped coming because the side effects were bad and happened often.

Diagnosis:
Porokeratosis (a skin condition that causes rough, scaly patches)

Instructions:
The patient should wear clothes that protect the skin from direct sunlight. The patient should keep taking isotretinoin 20mg pills. The patient should keep using halobetasol 0.05% cream as directed.

Date of Admission: [insert date]

HISTORY:
The patient came in with headaches, neck pain, and vision problems. An eye exam showed that the patient had lost some vision in both eyes. Both pupils were wide open and not reacting to light. There was also severe swelling of the nerve at the back of both eyes.

DIAGNOSIS AND TREATMENT:
The patient had a brain scan using a special dye. The scan showed signs of long-term high pressure inside the skull. These signs included bending of the eye nerves, widening of fluid spaces around the brain, flattening at the back of the eyes, and an empty space where a gland should be. Another test looking at blood vessels in the brain showed that a growth was pressing on a major vein on the right side of the head. Because this growth was causing high pressure in the brain veins, the doctors decided to remove it with surgery. The surgery was done through a cut behind the right ear. The growth was fully removed, and the vein pressure went down right away. Lab tests showed the growth was a type of bone tumor called an osteoblastoma.

POSTOPERATIVE COURSE:
After surgery, the patient developed an infection in the bone behind the right ear. This infection was treated successfully. The headaches went away quickly. The patient's vision slowly got better over the following weeks. At a 4-week eye checkup, vision was 7 out of 10 in the right eye and 4 out of 10 in the left eye. The swelling at the back of the eyes was completely gone. There was some lasting damage to the left eye nerve. A brain scan 4 months later showed the pressed vein was now normal size. The signs of high pressure in the skull had greatly improved.

DISCHARGE PLAN:
The patient was sent home and told to come back for a follow-up visit. The patient and family were told to contact their doctor if the headaches, neck pain, or vision problems come back.

None.

A hospital visit to check on the patient's condition will be scheduled within the next month.

Hospital Course:

The patient came to our clinic with weakness in the left arm and leg that had lasted for 7 months. During the exam, the doctors found the left arm and leg could not move well. The left side of the face was also slightly weak. Brain scans showed several abnormal spots and areas in the brain. The doctors asked about the family health history. They learned that some family members also had similar physical problems, some worse than others. A blood test was done to look at the patient's genes. The test found a change in a gene called CCM3. This same gene change was found in the patient's brothers and mother. This means the condition runs in the family.

Diagnosis:

The patient has CCM, which stands for Cerebral Cavernous Malformation. This is a condition that is passed down in families. It causes small clusters of abnormal blood vessels to form in the brain.

Treatment:

There is no medicine that has been shown to work for CCM. This is especially true when there are many small problem areas. For now, the patient and family members will be treated for their symptoms. This includes keeping blood pressure under control and treating headaches.

Follow-up:

The patient should see the doctor and a genetic counselor on a regular basis. The patient should let them know if anything changes or if new symptoms appear.

Discharge Condition:

The patient left the hospital in stable condition.

Medication on Admission: The patient was taking dabigatran to prevent blood clots due to an irregular heartbeat.

Hospital Course: Emergency heart surgery was done using a machine to pump blood and cool the body. Blood flow was briefly stopped during the surgery. During the surgery, the patient was given medicine to help blood clot. The patient also received blood products and a medicine to reverse the blood thinner. After surgery, the patient went to the intensive care unit and was on a breathing machine. The breathing tube was removed after 17 hours. The patient needed medicine to remove extra fluid and lung exercises. The patient got a lung infection. Blood-thinning medicine called warfarin was started again. Eight days after surgery, the patient was moved to a nearby hospital.

Follow-Up: Thirty days after surgery, the patient was doing well with no problems.

Summary: An 83-year-old man came in with a bulge in the main blood vessel leaving the heart. The condition was made worse by a sudden tear in the blood vessel wall. Emergency heart surgery was done using a machine to pump blood and cool the body. Blood flow was briefly stopped during the surgery. The damaged part of the blood vessel was replaced. The surgery went well. The patient went to the intensive care unit and was on a breathing machine. The patient got a lung infection after surgery. Blood-thinning medicine called warfarin was started again. Eight days after surgery, the patient was moved to a nearby hospital for more care.

Hospital Course:
Josh is an 18 year old male. He has a history of alcohol and drug use problems. He also has struggled with understanding who he is. He has had problems in his relationship with his parents. In 2013, Josh tried to end his own life. After this, he stayed at a mental health care facility for 9 weeks. Doctors found that Josh has long-lasting low mood. He also has a personality disorder that does not fit one specific type. He shows some traits like needing a lot of attention, having unstable emotions, and thinking highly of himself. His ability to handle daily life was rated as serious to moderate difficulty.

Discharge Summary:
Josh left the mental health care facility with continued help in place. He still has mood changes from time to time. He has not spent much time with people his own age. He has had a few short friendships with other young men. Doctors noted problems with his main support system at home. They also noted problems with his social surroundings and school. His parents are musicians. They have their own mental health problems. This has made it hard for them to be part of his treatment.

Follow-up:
Josh will keep getting support and counseling. This will help with his mental health and drug use problems. His mood changes will need to be watched closely. He will be connected to school help and support groups.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [REDACTED]
DOB: [REDACTED]
Admission Date: [REDACTED]
Discharge Date: [REDACTED]
Diagnosis: Central giant cell tumor, a non-cancerous growth in the jaw bone

Hospital Course:
The patient came to our department for special care. The patient had a painless lump on the jaw that grew slowly over 3 years. The patient also lost some teeth during this time. The doctor found a large, sore lump that made the lower lip stick out. Inside the mouth, there was a hard lump about 2 inches wide. This lump pushed the teeth out of place so they did not line up right. Pictures of the jaw showed a large growth that was destroying bone and had a hollow space inside. A small tissue sample proved it was a central giant cell tumor, a non-cancerous growth.

The head doctor of our department did the surgery. The doctor removed a hollow growth that had no fluid inside. The outer wall of the jawbone had broken through, but the bone did not break during surgery. The patient took medicine to fight infection and control pain every day for 8 days. The patient healed well after surgery.

Recommendations:
The patient was told to get dental work to fix the teeth and mouth. The patient came back for check-up visits at 3, 6, and 12 months. There were no signs the growth came back.

Summary:
The 8-year-old girl had a central giant cell tumor, a non-cancerous growth in the jaw bone. She had surgery to remove it. At her check-up visits 3, 6, and 12 months later, there were no signs the growth came back. She was told to get dental work to fix her teeth and mouth after surgery.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Information:
Name: [Redacted]
Age: 65
Gender: Male
Admission Date: September 17, 2019
Date of Discharge: September 30, 2019

Hospital Course Summary:
The patient came to the hospital with an upset stomach, a swollen belly, and weight loss. The patient was found to have a long-term liver infection caused by the hepatitis B virus. The patient also had a large liver cancer on the left side of the liver that had spread to several spots. The patient had a treatment where medicine was sent through a tube in the blood vessels to the liver to fight the cancer. After each treatment, the patient had a fever but felt okay otherwise. The fever was treated with pain and fever medicine, which worked well. The patient had several scans to check if the cancer was getting better. The scans showed the cancer did not improve much even with treatment. The patient passed away in early February 2020. This happened because the cancer had spread too far and the liver had stopped working properly.

Discharge Instructions:
The patient has been sent home after finishing care at the hospital. Family members should get medical help right away if the patient has a fever or feels unwell. Family members should share the patient's health history with any new doctors or nurses. This will help them give the best care possible.

Follow-up Recommendations:
The patient's family members should make an appointment with the patient's regular doctor. The doctor may suggest other care based on how the patient is doing.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [Name]
Age: 56
Gender: Male
Admission Date: [Date]
Discharge Date: [Date]
Length of Stay: [Number] days

Hospital Course:
The patient came to the hospital with a bad headache and nausea that came and went. Brain scans showed a growth in the left side of the brain. Doctors at another hospital first removed this growth in 2002. After that surgery, the patient had several health problems. These included a bad reaction to a blood thinner, a blood clot in the lungs, a blood clot in the leg, and a small stroke. The stroke caused weakness on the right side of the body.

Two years after the first surgery, the patient had headaches, dizziness, and trouble with balance. A brain scan showed fluid building up in the brain. In 2004, doctors placed a small tube to drain this fluid into the belly. The patient got better after this treatment. In 2005, doctors found a bleeding growth near the back of the brain. They removed it. Tests showed it was a cluster of abnormal blood vessels that had bled several times.

In 2008, brain scans showed a new growth in the same spot as the first one from 2002. Doctors also found another growth in a different part of the brain. In 2009, doctors removed the growth on the left side of the brain. Tests showed this growth had two types of tissue mixed together. One part was the same type as before, and one part was abnormal blood vessels.

Brain scans after surgery showed no growth was left behind. The other growth in the brain seemed to be getting smaller on its own. Doctors did not suggest any extra treatment. Both types of growths were not cancer, and one was shrinking by itself. The patient left the hospital in good health.

Diagnoses:
1. A returning brain growth that can come back but is not cancer
2. A cluster of abnormal blood vessels that bled several times and changed over time
3. Fluid buildup in the brain

Procedures:
1. Placement of a small tube to drain fluid from the brain to the belly
2. Surgery to remove a growth from the left side of the brain
3. Surgery to remove a growth that had two types of tissue

Condition on Discharge:
The patient left the hospital in good health. Brain scans showed no signs of the growth coming back.

Follow-Up Plan:
The patient should get regular brain scans to check if the growth comes back. The patient should tell the doctor right away about any new health problems.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: N/A
Date of Admission: August 4, 2015
Sex: Male
Date of Discharge: N/A
Age: 6 years old
Length of Stay: N/A

History and Findings:
The patient is a 6-year-old boy who came in because he was losing vision in both eyes quickly over 38 days. The patient had mild trouble seeing at night starting one year before coming to the hospital. The patient's eyesight kept getting worse over time. When the patient arrived at the eye center, the pressure inside his eyes was normal. Doctors found many small bumps on the colored part of both eyes. The nerves at the back of both eyes looked pale, and the blood vessels in the eyes were thin. The middle outer areas of the back of both eyes looked spotted, but there were no dark bone-shaped spots. Other body exams showed no problems.

Diagnostic Tests and Results:
A special dye test of the eyes showed bright and dark spotted areas at the back of the eyes. A scan of the eye layers showed thinning and damage in the outer layer of the back of the eye, but the center vision area was still intact. Tests that measure how the eyes respond to light showed no activity in both eyes. No brain response to light flashes was found either. A brain scan showed several spots where the protective covering of nerves was damaged in the right front and side parts of the brain. Both eye nerves were also larger than normal.

Diagnosis and Treatment:
The patient was found to have a condition that damages the back of the eye and causes vision loss, along with swelling of the eye nerves. The patient was given a medicine to reduce swelling for 14 days, then the dose was slowly lowered. After treatment, the patient's vision with glasses slowly got better. The patient also had a gene test that found a change in a gene called OFD1, which was passed down from family members.

Hospital Course:
The patient got better 3 months later, with improved ability to see light in the center of his vision. Blood tests showed lower levels of certain substances that can cause swelling. The brain's response to light in both eyes became normal. However, the test measuring eye response to light still showed no activity.

Follow-up Recommendations:
The patient should keep checking his vision and have regular eye exams. The family should think about meeting with a doctor who can explain how this condition runs in families.

Discharge Summary:

Admission Date: [Date of admission]
Discharge Date: [Date of discharge]
Patient Name: [Patient's name]
Medical Record Number: [Patient's medical record number]

Hospital Course:

The patient is a 43-year-old man with no previous health problems. He came to the hospital with a headache, a drooping left eyelid, and double vision. He had no other brain or nerve problems. Eye doctors and brain doctors examined him. A scan of the head and blood vessels was done to check for a bulge in a brain artery. No bulge was found. More detailed scans of the head and eye area were also normal.

While in the hospital, the patient developed stomach pain that got worse after eating. A sound wave test of the belly showed the bowel wall might be thick. A detailed scan of the belly showed thickening and uneven edges of the small intestine wall. It also showed swollen glands in both groin areas. A scan of the chest was done to check for swollen glands there. It showed a large blockage in the right upper heart chamber. This blockage extended into the large vein leading to the heart. This finding suggested a type of blood cancer.

More tests were done, including a heart sound wave test and a detailed heart scan. These showed a growth inside the heart that matched blood cancer. A sample was taken from a swollen gland. The sample showed signs of a fast-growing blood cancer.

The patient was then moved to a cancer hospital for treatment. Treatment began with a drug plan called CHOP. This included four medicines: cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine, and prednisolone. Medicine was also given through a needle in the spine. At first, the patient got better. Later, the patient got worse and passed away.

Discharge Diagnosis:

The patient was found to have Burkitt lymphoma. This is a fast-growing blood cancer. It was found using the chest scan and the gland sample.

Discharge Instructions:

The patient was sent to a cancer comfort care center for end-of-life care. The family was told to keep giving the patient's medicines as directed. They were told to stay in contact with the comfort care team. The family was also told to call emergency services if any urgent health problems came up.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Information:

Name: [Redacted]
Age: 60 Years
Gender: Male
Admission Date: [Redacted]
Discharge Date: [Redacted]
Discharge Diagnosis: Membranous nephropathy (a kidney disease that causes protein to leak into the urine)

Hospital Course Summary:

The patient, a 60-year-old male, came to the hospital after feeling tired for two months. The patient also had mild swelling in the legs. The patient was having joint pain in both knees and hands. Tests showed that protein was leaking into the urine, which was a new problem. The patient was also waking up at night to urinate and going to the bathroom more often than usual.

A physical exam showed mild swelling in the legs. The heart, lungs, and belly were all normal. The patient had surgery to remove the gallbladder four months before this hospital stay. Blood tests showed the body had slightly higher than normal signs of swelling inside. A urine test showed high levels of protein but no signs of infection or sugar. The kidneys were working normally. The amount of protein lost in urine over one day was very high.

More tests were done to find out why protein was leaking from the kidneys. The patient was tested for diseases that attack the body's own tissues. These included tests for lupus and other immune system problems. All these test results came back normal or negative. Tests for hepatitis A, B, C, and HIV were also negative.

The patient had a scan of the chest and belly, which was normal. A small piece of kidney tissue was removed and looked at under a microscope. This test showed that the kidney's filters were damaged, causing protein to leak into the urine. A type of protein made by the immune system was found stuck to the kidney's tiny blood vessels.

Doctors found no signs of infection or other related health problems. The patient was diagnosed with membranous nephropathy.

The patient left the hospital in good condition. The diagnosis was membranous nephropathy. The patient did not need any medicines during the hospital stay.

Follow-Up Instructions:

The patient should contact a doctor if mild leg swelling or any other symptoms come back.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [Redacted]
Admission Date: [Redacted]
Discharge Date: [Redacted]
Diagnosis: Carbon (pencil lead) injury to the left eye

Hospital Course:
An 8-year-old boy with no past health problems came to our eye emergency clinic after a pencil hurt his left eye. The clear front layer of the eye was not broken. Small silver-gray pencil lead bits were found in the lower inner part of the clear front of the eye. The white part of the eye was slightly red. There were no signs of swelling or irritation inside the eye. The patient was given Vigamox eye drops to use 4 times a day for 3 weeks. The patient was also given artificial tears without added chemicals to use 4 times a day for 4 weeks.

The patient handled the treatment well and went home with no problems. Check-up visits at 1 week, 1 month, 4 months, and 6 months showed no signs of redness, swelling, or irritation.

Recommendations:
1. The patient should have regular vision checks to watch for any changes.
2. Regular eye exams are a good idea, especially after eye injuries.
3. The patient should avoid injuries that break through the eye surface.
4. The patient and caregivers should get medical help right away if an eye injury happens.

Primary Care Follow-up:
The patient should see a children's eye doctor for regular vision checks and eye exams. Any changes in vision, pain, or swelling should be reported right away to the regular doctor.

Hospital Course:

The patient, an 8-year-old girl, came to the hospital with pain behind her right eye and headaches. Scans showed a growth near the back of her right eye socket. This growth had spread into the brain area. A special brain scan with dye showed a mixed-looking growth in the area at the base of the brain. This growth had also spread upward. Doctors found the patient has a rare condition called RIM based on the scan pictures. The care team planned to treat it with a focused radiation treatment called gamma knife.

Hospital Course Summary:

Admission Date: [Date of admission]
Discharge Date: [Date of discharge]

Chief Complaint: Broken lower jaw and two missing front teeth

History of Present Illness: A 12-year-old girl was brought to the Oral Surgery Department after a roadside accident. She had a broken lower jaw near the chin area and was missing both lower front teeth. She had never had braces before. The doctors found that both lower eye teeth were stuck under the gums. Both her upper and lower teeth were also crowded.

Hospital Course: The doctors planned a treatment that would not require pulling any teeth. The goals were to fix the broken jaw, make room for replacement front teeth, fix the crowding, and keep the back teeth lined up correctly. On the same day, wires were placed to hold the broken jaw pieces together. When the patient was ready for surgery, a metal plate was attached to the bone. After the jaw healed, braces were placed on both the upper and lower teeth. The braces helped straighten the teeth and make space for the missing front teeth. The lower eye teeth were left in place because they were too close to the screw and hard to move due to where the break was. Temporary false teeth were made and attached to the braces with metal ties. The patient's appearance and smile looked much better after the false teeth were attached.

Summary: The 12-year-old girl had a broken lower jaw near the chin and two missing front teeth from a roadside accident. She completed a treatment plan that did not require pulling any teeth. After the broken jaw was fixed, braces were used to straighten the upper and lower teeth and make space for the front teeth. The lower eye teeth were left in place because of where the break was. The last step was attaching temporary false teeth to the braces. This greatly improved how the patient's smile looked.

Hospital Course:
The patient came to our hospital with swelling in his right cheek. The swelling had been there for two weeks. Doctors first thought it might be cancer in the mouth area. After a careful exam, doctors found an oval, firm lump about 1 inch by 0.8 inches in size. The lump was located near the right side of the jawbone. An ultrasound of the cheek showed the lump was a fluid-filled sac in the cheek muscle area. There was also some swelling in the tissue around it.

More tests were done, including an MRI scan of the face and neck. The MRI found a small structure inside the sac that looked like a tapeworm head. A small sample was taken from the lump using a thin needle. The sample showed no signs of cancer. X-rays of the chest, both arms, and both thighs were taken. An MRI of the head and eye area was also done. These tests showed no other problem areas in the body.

The patient was told to take pain medicine and medicine to reduce swelling for seven days. The lump slowly got smaller. Medicine to kill the parasite was also given.

Discharge Medications:
Albendazole

Discharge Diagnosis:
The patient had a parasitic infection called cysticercosis. This caused a fluid-filled sac to form in the cheek muscle area.

Follow-Up:
The patient should see his regular doctor for continued check-ups.

Discharge Condition:
The patient has gotten better since coming to the hospital. He is doing well and is ready to go home.

Discharge Instructions:
The patient should keep taking his albendazole medicine as directed. He should not use tobacco because it has been linked to this type of infection. He should see his regular doctor for continued check-ups. He should tell his doctor about any new or worrying symptoms.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Overview:
The patient is a 58-year-old man who came in with a painless bump on his right upper eyelid. He had this bump for 15 years and it did not bother him. He was also found to have a problem with his right lower eyelid turning inward. This is common in older adults. Surgery was planned to fix the eyelid turning inward.

History and Physical:
During the exam, the bump on the eyelid felt firm. It was not attached to the skin above it. The bump was about the size of a small pea and could be moved around. The skin over the bump was not broken or damaged. The patient had extra loose skin on his eyelid, which is normal with aging. Everything else about his eyes looked normal.

Hospital Course:
The patient had surgery to fix the eyelid that was turning inward. The doctor also removed the bump because the patient asked for it to be taken out. The patient healed well after surgery with no problems.

Outpatient Follow-up:
The patient came back for a checkup 3 months later. The bump had not come back.

Diagnosis:
Based on the medical report, no specific diagnosis was given for the bump.

Treatment:
The patient had surgery to fix the eyelid turning inward. The bump on the eyelid was also removed during the same surgery.

Prognosis:
The patient is expected to do well. At his last visit, there were no signs that the bump had come back.

Hospital Course:

The patient is a 37-year-old male with a history of anxiety and migraines who came to the emergency room with a constant, sharp pain on the right side of his head. The pain had lasted for 12 hours. The patient said the pain felt like his usual migraine but his regular migraine medicine, ibuprofen, and pain medicine had not helped.

During the physical exam, the doctor found tenderness at the back right side of the head when pressing on it. There was no tenderness along the spine or problems with the nerves in the head and face. The patient was first given medicine for nausea, fluids through an IV, and medicine for allergies that also helps with pain. After this, the patient said his pain went down from 10 out of 10 to 8 out of 10. Then, the doctor gave a numbing shot to the nerves at the back of the head using a numbing medicine. Three minutes later, the patient said the pain dropped to 2 out of 10.

A follow-up phone call on day 8 showed the patient's migraine symptoms were completely gone. The patient said he would prefer to get the numbing shot at the back of the head if another migraine happens.

Summary:

A 37-year-old male came in with 12 hours of severe pain on the right side of his head that matched his usual migraines. His regular migraine medicine had not worked. The first treatments with nausea medicine, IV fluids, and allergy medicine did not give enough relief. However, a numbing shot to the nerves at the back of the head made the symptoms go away. A follow-up phone call on day 8 showed the symptoms were still gone. The patient said he would prefer to get the numbing shot for future migraines.

Medical History:
The patient had several broken ribs and blood collecting in the right side of the chest after a car accident. A drainage tube was placed in the chest at the first hospital. She came to our hospital about one and a half months after the accident. Doctors found that part of the muscle wall between the chest and belly on the right side had died. The right lung had also collapsed.

Hospital Course:
The patient was put on a breathing machine and moved to the intensive care unit. New chest scans showed several broken ribs on both sides and blood with air pockets on the right side of the chest. The muscle wall between the chest and belly looked damaged. The patient had surgery to open the right side of the chest. During surgery, dead tissue and old blood clots were removed. The patient was stable after surgery but could not breathe on her own without the machine. A small opening was made in the throat to help with long-term breathing support. The patient was fed through a tube placed through the nose into the stomach. After three weeks, the patient was moved to the heart and chest surgery unit for more care. However, she was too weak for more surgery. The patient passed away one month later because her body was too weak to recover.

Condition at Discharge:
The patient had a sad outcome and could not leave the hospital.

Plan:
No further plan needed.

Follow-up:
None needed.

Sex: Female
