Main problem:
The patient had trouble swallowing that had gotten worse. She also noticed a growth on the left side of her neck.

Hospital stay:
The patient came to the hospital on [REDACTED]. She had mild trouble swallowing for two months that recently got worse. Blood tests showed her thyroid gland was working normally. An X-ray of her throat and food pipe showed a large pouch where the throat meets the food pipe. An ultrasound found an abnormal area behind both sides of the thyroid and a mass on the left side of the thyroid. A CT scan of the neck showed a thyroid lump, pouches on both sides of the lower throat, and an area that may have calcium buildup. Another swallowing test showed a large pouch on the left side and a small pouch on the right side.

The patient had surgery to remove the pouches and thyroid growth to help with swallowing. The surgeon made a curved cut on the left front of the neck. The pouches were found under a throat muscle. The left pouch was separated from the thyroid and the thyroid growth. The pouches were removed. The wound was closed in layers and a drain tube was placed to remove fluid.

Lab tests on the removed tissue showed the pouches were weak spots in the wall without muscle. The thyroid growth was found to be not cancer. The patient started drinking clear liquids on day 4 after surgery. Two years after surgery, the patient has no trouble swallowing.

Diagnosis:
Mild trouble swallowing
Pouches in the lower throat
Non-cancerous thyroid growth

Treatment:
Surgery to remove the throat pouches and thyroid growth

Follow-up:
The patient should keep seeing her regular doctor. No more visits to this hospital are needed.

DISCHARGE SUMMARY

Patient Name: [Name]
Medical Record Number: [Number]

Hospital Course:
The patient is a 38-year-old woman who came in with six months of worsening shortness of breath during activity and new fainting spells. Listening to the heart revealed an ongoing heart murmur on the left side of the chest. An ultrasound of the heart showed an abnormal blood vessel coming from a heart artery and connecting to the lung artery. This caused blood to flow the wrong way from the left side of the heart to the right side. There was mild widening of the right heart chambers and the heart was pumping at 60 percent strength. Special imaging and dye tests of the heart arteries confirmed an abnormal connection between a heart artery and another blood vessel. The amount of extra blood flow to the lungs was measured at 1.8 times higher than normal. Surgery was done through a small cut on the left side of the chest. The abnormal connections were found and closed with several stitches backed by small fabric patches. An ultrasound probe placed in the throat confirmed the abnormal connection was fully closed. There was no leftover abnormal blood flow and the heart wall was moving normally. A heart tracing showed no signs of poor blood flow to the heart muscle. The patient had the breathing tube removed one hour after surgery and went home two days after the procedure. At the six month and twelve month checkups, the patient had no heart or blood vessel symptoms. Heart ultrasounds showed no leftover abnormal blood flow. The small scar healed very well.

Hospital Course Summary:
A 38-year-old woman came in with shortness of breath, fainting spells, and a heart murmur heard during the exam. Testing showed an abnormal connection between a heart artery and the lung artery. This caused blood to flow the wrong way and mild widening of the right heart chambers. The patient had surgery through a small cut on the left side of the chest to close the abnormal connections. An ultrasound during surgery confirmed full closure with no leftover abnormal blood flow and normal heart wall movement. The patient had no symptoms at the six month and twelve month follow-up visits. Heart ultrasounds showed no leftover abnormal blood flow.

Hospital Course Summary:

The patient was a 71-year-old woman who came to our clinic after a heart test showed unusual results during a regular visit. She had a history of type 2 diabetes, high blood pressure, and high cholesterol. During the visit, the heart test showed extra heartbeats happening in an unusual pattern with a slow heart rate of 46 beats per minute. Because of this, several blood tests were ordered to find out what might be causing these heart changes. An urgent follow-up visit was set for one week later to go over these results. The patient was also told to get medical help right away if she felt her heart racing or felt dizzy.

During the second visit one week later, a new heart test showed a different irregular heart rhythm with a problem in how signals moved through the heart. Most blood test results were normal, except two tests that showed signs of swelling in the body were higher than normal. An urgent heart ultrasound showed that the left upper and lower chambers of the heart were larger than normal but were still squeezing well. A large solid growth measuring about 3.1 by 4.1 centimeters was found in the left upper chamber of the heart. The growth was attached to the heart wall by a stalk. The heart was pumping out 54 percent of its blood with each beat.

The patient was sent right away to a specialized heart clinic where another heart ultrasound was done. The doctors confirmed the growth was a type of non-cancerous heart tumor called a left atrial myxoma. The tumor measured about 2.9 by 3.1 centimeters. The heart test also showed episodes of an irregular heartbeat. Blood-thinning medicine called Warfarin was started to prevent blood clots with a goal to keep the blood at a certain thinness level between 2 and 3. Right now, the patient is being cared for by both her regular doctor and a team of specialists who are helping manage her blood-thinning treatment. The patient does not want to have surgery to remove the tumor.

The patient has been told to keep following the recommended treatment plan and to get medical help right away if she has any signs that her heart is not working well. The patient has been given learning materials to help manage her condition and to stay in touch with her healthcare team.

Hospital Course:

A 30-year-old man came to the hospital with a fever. He was moved from another hospital in Yunnan Province. Seven days before coming to this hospital, he had surgery to remove his appendix. The doctors found his appendix was badly infected. When he arrived, his body temperature was high at 39.5 degrees Celsius. His blood pressure was 108 over 78, which was normal. The rest of his body check was normal. Blood tests showed his white blood cell count was high. This means his body was fighting an infection. Another blood test called procalcitonin was also high. This test helps find serious infections. A special scan of his belly area was done using dye and x-rays. The scan showed a pocket of infection near where his appendix was removed. The pocket was about 2.3 cm by 2.9 cm in size. The doctors gave him an antibiotic medicine through a vein. The medicine was called moxifloxacin. They started this medicine before they knew exactly what germ was causing the infection.

Management and Treatment:

On Day 3, blood tests found a type of bacteria in his blood. The bacteria was called E. Lenta. The doctors then changed his medicine to one that works better against this germ. The patient received a strong antibiotic called meropenem through a vein. He got 1 gram of this medicine every 8 hours. The patient got better quickly with this treatment. The doctors did not need to drain the infection pocket with a needle or surgery. His fever went away. His blood test numbers went back to normal. He did not need any surgery.

Discharge Plan:

On Day 5, new blood tests showed no germs in his blood. On Day 10, a sound wave test of his belly area was normal. The patient kept getting the meropenem medicine through a vein for 6 more days. The patient got better and left the hospital. The patient has appointments set up to check on his healing. These visits will make sure he fully recovers.

Patient Name: [REDACTED]

Medical Record Number: [REDACTED]

Hospital Course:
The patient came to the hospital with weakness in both hands that had been getting worse for 2 years. The left hand was weaker than the right hand. The doctor found that muscles in the palms and between the fingers had shrunk, more on the left side. Tests of the nerves and muscles showed nerve damage in the lower neck area on both sides, worse on the left. Tests that check feeling in the hands were normal.

The patient had special scans of the neck in both a straight position and a bent position. These scans showed swelling of the spinal cord in the lower neck, worst at the C5-C6 level. The patient had surgery to open the back of the neck and take a small tissue sample from inside the spinal cord. This was done to make sure there was no tumor. The tissue sample showed reduced blood flow to part of the spinal cord. This matched a condition called Hirayama Disease.

The patient then had surgery from the front of the neck to take pressure off the spinal cord at the C5-C6 level. A scan after surgery showed the damaged area in the spinal cord had gotten smaller. The patient did not have any new problems after surgery. Scans done over the next two years showed the spinal cord slowly getting thinner at C5-C6. The front part of the spinal cord was most affected.

Discharge Diagnosis:
1. Hirayama Disease with reduced blood flow to the spinal cord.

Discharge Medications:
None

Follow-up:
The patient should see his nerve specialist for regular check-ups and ongoing care of his condition. More scans may be ordered to check if the disease is getting worse.

Discharge Condition:
The patient's condition has not improved. However, the hospital stay helped rule out a spinal cord tumor. It also confirmed that the patient has Hirayama Disease. The patient can now continue treatment with his nerve specialist without needing to stay in the hospital.

Discharge Summary:

This is a discharge summary for a 74-year-old woman with lung cancer that had spread to other parts of her body. The patient came to the hospital because of pain in the right lower chest wall. Tests showed the cancer had spread to the right lung, lymph nodes in the chest, liver, and the lining around the lungs.

The patient was given different medicines to treat her cancer, including gefitinib and osimertinib. After several months, these medicines stopped working and the cancer got worse.

In September 2017, the patient started getting two different medicines together called decitabine and camrelizumab. These medicines helped shrink the cancer in the chest lymph nodes, liver, and lung lining. But after 7 rounds of treatment, the cancer started growing again. The patient stopped taking these medicines.

During treatment, doctors checked different markers in the blood and body. Some of these markers went up and some went down while the patient was getting the two medicines together. Other markers stayed the same throughout treatment.

In May 2019, the patient died because several of her organs stopped working.

Hospital Course:

The patient came to the hospital with fever, muscle pain, throwing up, feeling sick to the stomach, headache, and belly pain. The doctor's exam showed an enlarged liver, enlarged spleen, a rash, and red eyes. Blood and urine tests showed the kidneys were not working well, protein in the urine, blood in the urine, and low platelet counts. The patient had been cutting trees in the forest eight days before but had not visited any other areas where this type of infection is common.

The patient had seizures on the third day in the hospital and was moved to the Intensive Care Unit. Brain scans showed unusual areas in the front, top, and back parts of the brain on both sides. There was no small bleeding in the brain. A test that measures brain waves showed slow activity in the left side of the brain near the temple and forehead.

Blood tests found signs of hantavirus infection, which confirmed the illness. Tests for other infections including Leptospira and liver viruses were negative. The patient chose not to have a spinal tap.

Treatment included supportive care with antibiotics, medicines to reduce swelling, medicines to prevent seizures, fluids through an IV, minerals, medicines to lower fever, and extra oxygen. The patient left the hospital after 16 days and had another brain scan two months later, which came back normal.

This patient was admitted to our facility for severe itching on her right arm. This problem had been going on for six months. She also had weakness in her right arm.

The patient has a known history of multiple myeloma. This is a type of blood cancer.

DIAGNOSTIC TESTS AND PROCEDURES

A CT scan of the neck, an MRI, and a nerve test of the shoulder and arm area were performed. These tests showed a bulging disc in the right side of the neck. This disc was pressing on nerves at the C6-C7 level. The tests also showed swelling of the nerves in the right shoulder and arm area. This condition is called Parsonage-Turner syndrome.

DISCHARGE MEDICATIONS

The patient was treated with methylprednisolone aceponate cream 0.1%. This is a steroid cream. She also took hydroxyzine 25mg by mouth every 8 hours. This helped only a little with the itching. Gabapentin was added at 900mg per day. After three months, this medicine controlled the itching well.

FOLLOW-UP INSTRUCTIONS

The patient was sent to see a brain and spine surgeon. She was also sent to see a cancer doctor for more treatment advice.

SUMMARY

The patient had nerve damage in the shoulder and arm area. This was caused by the spread of her blood cancer. The treatment plan included methylprednisolone aceponate cream 0.1% and hydroxyzine 25mg by mouth every 8 hours. Gabapentin at 900mg per day was also added. The patient was sent to a brain and spine surgeon and a cancer doctor for more care.

Clinical Summary
The patient is a 32-year-old man. He came to the hospital with trouble breathing, a mild fever, and weight loss. In the past, he had treatment for a type of infection that causes swollen glands. Doctors found that this infection had spread through his body and likely came back.

Hospital Course
While in the hospital, the patient had several tests done. These included blood tests, tests to check how well the liver works, and X-rays. The patient also had an ultrasound of the belly area. Doctors used a needle to take small samples from swollen glands in the neck and armpit areas. These tests helped doctors find out what was causing the illness.

Diagnosis
Test results from blood work, X-rays, and gland samples pointed to a fungal infection. Doctors grew the fungus from the gland sample in the lab. This confirmed the patient had a fungal infection called Cryptococcus.

Treatment
The patient received treatment for the fungal infection following the hospital's standard care plan. The patient did not have any problems during treatment.

Follow-Up Plan
The patient was told to take all medicines as directed. The patient has an appointment to come back in one month.

Prognosis
The patient is expected to do well. The patient must keep taking all medicines exactly as directed.

The patient was sent home with orders to take all prescribed medicines on schedule. The patient should return to the hospital right away if any bad reactions happen. The patient should also eat well, stay active, and drink plenty of water. The patient should keep seeing a doctor for regular check-ups.

Hospital Course:

The patient came to our hospital for a routine checkup. This was 2 years after surgery to remove the right kidney because of kidney cancer. The patient had no symptoms. However, a CT scan of the belly showed a growth on the left adrenal gland. The adrenal gland is a small organ that sits on top of the kidney. A team of doctors met to discuss the best treatment. They decided to remove the adrenal gland using a small camera and tiny cuts.

Procedure:

The patient had surgery to remove the left adrenal gland. The surgery was done while the patient was fully asleep under general anesthesia. The patient was placed on their side with the left side facing up. The doctors filled the belly with gas to create space to work. They used a small camera and three small openings to do the surgery. The doctors found the tumor and carefully separated it from surrounding tissue. Then they removed it.

Histological examination:

Doctors looked at the removed tissue under a microscope. The growth was cancer that had spread from the original kidney cancer. The edges of the removed tissue showed no signs of cancer. This means the doctors removed all of the tumor.

Outcome:

The patient recovered well after surgery with no problems. The patient left the hospital 2 days after the operation. At 18 months after this surgery, the patient is doing well. There are no signs that the cancer has come back. The patient also has no problems with the adrenal gland being gone.

Hospital Course:

The patient came to our hospital because of weakness and tingling in the left upper arm. The physical exam showed weakness on the left side of the body. The patient had reduced strength in the left arm and leg. There was also an abnormal toe reflex on the left side. A CT scan of the head showed damaged brain tissue in the front and side areas. This damage was caused by a stroke from blocked blood flow. An MRI scan of the head showed a blockage in a blood vessel in the brain.

Clinical Findings:

The patient reported a history of drug and alcohol use. This included regular use of heroin, methadone, cocaine, and alcohol. The patient also smoked crack cocaine the night before the symptoms started. Drug tests came back positive for cocaine and opioids. An ultrasound of the neck arteries showed a large buildup of soft fatty material. This buildup had an uneven surface and was inside a major neck artery that supplies blood to the brain.

Treatment and Management:

The patient was given two blood-thinning medicines called enoxaparin and warfarin. These medicines helped slowly break up the blood clot. The patient's symptoms slowly got better over the next few weeks. The patient left the hospital in good overall health.

Follow-Up:

The patient left the hospital in good overall health. However, the patient kept using drugs. One year later, the patient had another stroke.

Conclusion:

The patient came in with weakness on the left side of the body caused by a stroke. The patient had a history of drug use. Treatment with blood-thinning medicines helped break up the blood clot. The patient's symptoms got better over time. However, the patient kept using drugs. One year later, the patient came back to the hospital after having a second stroke.

Hospital Course:
The patient, [PATIENT NAME], was admitted to the hospital for a planned heart repair surgery. The patient has a rare heart condition present from birth called incomplete Shone syndrome. The patient came in with severe trouble breathing during normal activities. The patient was found to have a severely narrowed heart valve between the upper and lower left heart chambers. This was caused by a ring of tissue that should not be there. The patient also had a moderately leaky valve in the same area. The patient had a severe narrowing of the main blood vessel leaving the heart. There was also a large opening between two blood vessels that should have closed after birth. Next, through a cut in the chest bone, the doctors removed the extra ring of tissue near the heart valve. The heart was connected to a machine that pumped blood during this part of the surgery. After surgery, the heart valves had only mild leaking. The left lower heart chamber was pumping at 30 percent strength. The patient recovered well after surgery with no problems. The patient was sent home on [DATE].

The patient handled all treatments well with no problems and left the hospital in stable condition. The patient was told to see the healthcare team regularly for ongoing check-ups and care.

Hospital Course

This 51-year-old male weighing 131 kg came to the emergency room confused and with slurred speech. This happened after getting a pain injection in his neck. During the injection, he passed out and had a brief seizure. Emergency workers were called and found him barely awake with shallow breathing and low oxygen levels. He needed help breathing. When he arrived at the emergency room, his breathing was uneven and his oxygen levels were low. He stayed very drowsy with slurred speech. He could not answer questions correctly or follow directions. Heart monitors showed his heart was beating in an uneven pattern. A heart test showed he had a condition called atrial fibrillation, which means the heart beats in an irregular way. His heart rate was 82 beats per minute. His blood pressure and blood flow stayed normal. Within 60 minutes of arriving at the emergency room, the patient was thinking clearly again. He did not remember anything that happened after the procedure started. All imaging tests came back normal.

Hospital Course: Diagnosis and Treatment

The patient stayed in the hospital overnight for watching. He had no symptoms and no more heart rhythm problems. He only had chest wall pain. This was possibly from rubbing on his chest bone or from chest pushes that may have been done when he passed out. Blood tests checked for lidocaine and a related substance called MEGX. Lidocaine is a numbing medicine. These tests showed none of these substances in his blood. The patient was given aspirin 325 mg to take once a day. He was also given a referral to see a heart doctor as an outpatient.

Condition at Discharge

The patient was sent home with no symptoms and normal thinking.

Discharge Summary:

Patient 1 is a 21-year-old man with seizures affecting both sides of his brain, autism, and learning difficulties. He was admitted to the hospital because his seizures were not controlled by medicine. He has two types of seizures. One type causes him to lose awareness. The other type causes shaking of his whole body.

The patient takes two seizure medicines called lacosamide and levetiracetam. In the past, he tried three other seizure medicines called topiramate, carbamazepine, and lamotrigine. None of these fully stopped his seizures. He also tried a device that sends small electrical signals to his brain through a nerve in his neck. This device did not stop his seizures either. The patient has also had his shoulder pop out of place many times.

The patient had a test that records brain wave activity. This test showed abnormal electrical activity on both sides of his brain. He also had a brain scan. The scan looked mostly normal but showed his brain was slightly smaller than expected for his age. During his hospital stay, the patient was kept on his current medicines. The care team watched for any bad reactions to the medicines.

The patient was sent home and told to see his regular doctor within one week. His doctor will help manage his condition going forward.

When the patient left the hospital, his condition was stable. There were no new problems. The patient was told to avoid activities that could make his shoulder pop out of place. He was also told to keep taking his medicines as directed. The patient and his family learned why it is important to take medicines on time. They also learned how to watch for seizures and spot possible side effects from the seizure medicines.

This discharge summary gives a full report of what was found, how the patient was treated, and what to do next. It explains the patient's condition, his medicines, and limits on his activities. The patient is expected to take his medicines as directed, see his doctor for follow-up visits, and watch his condition closely.

The patient was asleep under general anesthesia during the surgery. The area was repaired using a skin graft taken from the upper arm. This graft included all layers of skin. The lab report showed no cancer cells. The patient had no regrowth during the 1-year follow-up period.

The patient came to the emergency room feeling unwell with a racing heart and tested positive for COVID-19. When admitted, the patient had a fever and chest x-rays showed signs of lung infection. The care team watched the patient's vital signs closely. The patient received diltiazem through an IV to help control the irregular heartbeat. The patient's heart rate got better after treatment. The patient then received a slow, steady dose of diltiazem through the IV at 5mg per hour. The patient received medicine to treat the fever. The patient was kept in a special room with safety measures to prevent spreading the virus.

Treatment:

The patient received diltiazem medicine through an IV and fluids through an IV. This helped lower the heart rate to about 100 beats per minute. After this, the patient received a slow, steady dose of diltiazem at 5 mg per hour to control the irregular heartbeat. The patient stayed in the hospital for more monitoring and tests.

Outcome:

The final diagnosis was irregular heartbeat with thickening of the heart muscle and COVID-19 infection. The patient's fast heart rate and fever went away during the hospital stay. The patient left the hospital in stable condition for follow-up care.

Recommendations:

The patient was told to stay home in isolation and complete 14 days of quarantine. The patient received a list of warning signs to report to the regular doctor if they happen. A follow-up visit with the regular doctor was scheduled after the quarantine period ends.

Overarching Risk Factors:

The patient had a history of high blood pressure that was not being treated.

Patient Name: [REDACTED]
Age: 25
Gender: Female
Admission Date: [REDACTED]
Discharge Date: [REDACTED]
Admitting Diagnosis: Adult-onset Still's disease and high blood pressure in the lungs
Final Diagnosis: Adult-onset Still's disease with a serious complication called macrophage activation syndrome and high blood pressure in the lungs

Hospital Course:
The patient came to the hospital for joint pain, fever, and rash that kept coming back. Blood tests showed high levels of inflammation and liver enzymes. The patient also had an enlarged spleen. These findings led doctors to diagnose Adult-onset Still's disease. The care team started treatment, but the patient got worse. Doctors then found a serious complication called macrophage activation syndrome. The patient received a strong steroid medicine called methylprednisolone. The patient got much better within a week. During the hospital stay, a chest scan and heart ultrasound showed high blood pressure in the lungs. This is a rare problem linked to Adult-onset Still's disease.

Imaging Findings:
A special scan of the blood vessels showed some problems with the heart and lungs. Blood vessels from the right lung were draining into the wrong part of the heart. The main blood vessel to the lungs was much larger than normal. There was also a small hole between the upper chambers of the heart.

Course of Treatment:
The patient received supportive care and the steroid medicine methylprednisolone for macrophage activation syndrome. No treatment was started for the high blood pressure in the lungs during this hospital stay.

Clinical Course and Follow-up:
The patient got much better with the steroid treatment and was sent home. The care team talked with the patient about plans to treat the high blood pressure in the lungs.

Summary:
This patient came to the hospital with Adult-onset Still's disease. Doctors also found a serious complication called macrophage activation syndrome. High blood pressure in the lungs was found by chance during testing. The patient received the right treatment and got much better. The care team talked with the patient about plans to treat the high blood pressure in the lungs.

This is a discharge summary for [Redacted], a 57-year-old female with a history of breast cancer that came back. She was admitted to our facility with pain and weakness in both thighs. She was first told she had breast cancer in her left breast at age 50. At that time, she had cancer drug treatment and surgery to remove her breast. She then took a cancer-blocking medicine called tamoxifen for 5 years. She was admitted to our facility because her muscles broke down after receiving cancer drugs called docetaxel and cyclophosphamide. At first, she did not want to do physical therapy. After meeting with the physical therapy team, they found she had overall weakness. This weakness was in her left upper arm, wrist, fingers, and hand muscles. Because of this, she was sent to our hospital's rehab unit for more care.

During her hospital stay, she went through a treatment plan with four parts. The first part focused on mental health exercises like deep breathing and relaxation methods. In the second part, she moved on to light strength exercises using stretchy bands and ankle weights. The third part focused on retraining her muscles and nerves. She also worked on balance while standing still and moving. She practiced walking on a balance beam while holding on for support. In the fourth and final part, she did walking activities that were more challenging. These included turning her head or body, changing her speed, and walking over or around objects. She went home 29 days after first coming to the hospital. She showed much better ability to do daily activities. She also said she felt more confident and had less pain.

When she left the hospital, the patient showed improvement with pain at 0 out of 10. Her upper leg and hip muscles got stronger on both sides. Her Timed Up and Go test improved to 10 seconds. This test measures how well someone can stand up, walk, and sit back down. She was able to walk long distances in the community using a walker when she left. Her balance test score improved to 55 out of 56. This means she has a low chance of falling. Follow-up appointments were scheduled to check on her progress.

The patient's discharge medicines were not available to include in this summary. This is because she was not given any medicine during her hospital stay.

Patient Name: [Redacted]
Age: 87 years
Date of admission: [Redacted]
Date of discharge: [Redacted]

Admission Diagnosis: Not eating well, lung infection, and low potassium levels
Discharge Diagnosis: Low potassium levels, possibly caused by a medication

Hospital Course:
The patient came to the hospital because of not eating well, low potassium levels, and a lung infection. The patient had stopped taking medication for an enlarged prostate. The patient was recently told about memory problems and started taking choline alfoscerate and donepezil. Tests showed low potassium levels and a mild lung infection. More tests were done to find out why potassium was low. The tests showed the kidneys were losing too much potassium. A CT scan showed nothing unusual. The care team looked at the memory medications and found donepezil might be causing the low potassium. Donepezil was stopped right away. The patient was given potassium through an IV and by mouth. The patient's potassium levels slowly went up. Three days after stopping donepezil, potassium reached a normal level of 3.5 mmol/L. The lung infection was also treated during this time. Blood pressure was high for 24 hours after coming to the hospital. The patient was started on amlodipine and olmesartan for this.

Discharge Medications:
Amlodipine and olmesartan were prescribed to control blood pressure.

Follow-up:
The patient left the hospital on the ninth day. The patient was told to keep taking potassium for 3 weeks total. The patient should keep taking olmesartan and amlodipine. The patient was told to check blood pressure regularly and see a primary care doctor.

Instructions to Patient:
The patient was told to eat less salt and fat and avoid foods high in potassium. The patient was told to take all prescribed medications. The patient should not take any store-bought medications without asking a doctor first. The patient was told to come back to the hospital if any worrying symptoms appear.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [INSERT NAME]
Sex: Female
Age: 65 years
Medical record number: [INSERT NUMBER]
Discharge Date: [INSERT DATE]

Hospital Course:
The patient came to the hospital with pain and swelling in her left hand. The swelling was near the base of her thumb and the fleshy part of her palm. She also had swollen glands in her neck. An X-ray showed a broken bone at the base of her thumb. The break happened because the bone was weak from disease. There was also a dark spot on the bone and cloudy tissue around it. An ultrasound showed a pocket of infection. An MRI scan suggested the pocket was most likely caused by infection and not cancer.

The patient had surgery to drain the infection and clean out the damaged tissue. The doctors also fixed the broken bone to keep it stable. During surgery, the doctors found thick cheese-like material in the soft tissue. The bone piece at the base of the thumb was loose and moving freely. The loose piece was taken out and sent to the lab for testing. The tissue around it was also sent for testing. A thin metal pin was placed through the thumb joint to hold it steady.

The lab results showed the patient had a bone infection caused by tuberculosis. The tissue samples showed dead tissue and signs of this specific infection. The patient was started on tuberculosis medicine right away while waiting for more test results. She was given four medicines called Isoniazid, Rifampicin, Pyrazinamide, and Ethambutol.

After 5 weeks, the metal pin started to come loose on its own. It was then taken out. The patient started doing exercises to move her thumb. The swollen neck glands went down after 3 months. At 7 months, the neck glands swelled up again one time. They went back down while the patient kept taking her tuberculosis medicine.

After one year, the patient could move her thumb almost as well as her other hand. There were no lasting problems from the tuberculosis. X-rays showed the joint had healed and reshaped itself after one year.

Discharge Medications:
The patient is given her regular home medicines.

Discharge Instructions:
The patient is told to see the bone doctor regularly and keep taking the medicines as directed. The patient is told to eat healthy foods and live a healthy lifestyle. Any signs that the infection is coming back or getting worse should be reported to the doctor right away. The patient is also told how important it is to keep all follow-up visits. These visits are very important for treating her condition.

Follow-up:
The patient is scheduled to see the bone doctor for follow-up visits. These visits are to check her healing and plan her ongoing care.

Hospital Course:

The patient came to the emergency room with severe bleeding from the stomach area. The patient was admitted to Habib Thameur Hospital. A physical exam showed very pale skin. The patient was fully alert and aware. The patient had a fast heartbeat, low blood pressure, and an enlarged spleen. The liver was normal in size. A rectal exam showed dark, tarry stools from internal bleeding. Blood tests showed low white blood cell count, low platelet count, and low red blood cells. There were minor signs that the liver was not working well, but protein levels were normal. The kidneys were also failing. Test results showed no signs of hepatitis B or hepatitis C infections.

The patient became stable after receiving fluids and two units of blood. The patient received medicine to reduce stomach acid (omeprazole) and medicine to slow bleeding (octreotide). A camera test looking at the throat and stomach showed swollen veins in the food pipe that were bleeding heavily. The stomach lining showed damage from high blood pressure in the veins. There were also swollen veins in the stomach. Rubber bands were placed on the bleeding veins to stop the bleeding.  An ultrasound of the belly showed many fluid-filled sacs in the liver caused by a parasite infection.

The patient had sudden, severe bleeding that started again. This caused the body to go into shock that could not be controlled. The blood also lost its ability to clot properly. The patient died after one week.

Impression:

Based on the patient's history, physical exam, and test results, the patient had a parasite infection in the liver and kidney failure. The patient received medicine to reduce stomach acid (omeprazole) and medicine to slow bleeding (octreotide) to try to control the bleeding. However, the patient had sudden, severe bleeding that started again. This caused shock that could not be controlled and the blood lost its ability to clot. The patient died.

Hospital Course:
A 24-year-old male came to the emergency room with several gunshot wounds. The exam showed that the patient had stable blood pressure and heart rate. No other problems were found.
More tests including CT scans found a bullet inside the right side of the heart. Heart surgeons and heart doctors were called in. They first tried to remove the bullet through a blood vessel. This did not work because the bullet was stuck in the muscle ridges inside the heart. The doctors then opened the chest through the breastbone. They used a heart-lung machine to take over for the heart. They gave medicine to stop the heart safely. The bullet was removed successfully. The patient was then moved to the intensive care unit to be watched closely.
On the sixth day after surgery, the patient got a fever. More scans showed a large buildup of fluid around the heart. There was also some fluid around the right lung. Part of the lower right lung had also collapsed. Doctors used a needle to drain the fluid from around the heart. A small tube was left in place to keep draining the fluid. The patient kept getting better. On the fifteenth day after surgery, the patient was well enough to move to a center for recovery and physical therapy.

Discharge Summary:

This is a 48-year-old female patient. She came to the hospital for surgery because her skin cancer on the left side of her lower jawbone had come back. The cancer type is called squamous cell carcinoma. The doctors removed the cancer and part of her jawbone. Then they rebuilt her jawbone, mouth floor, and tongue. They used a metal implant made of titanium and tissue taken from her thigh. The tissue from her thigh was connected to a blood vessel near the tongue and a large vein in the neck. After surgery, her face looked good and she could chew food.

The patient had radiation treatment and cancer-fighting drugs because the cancer came back after her first surgery. A follow-up scan showed no signs that the cancer had returned.

The metal implant was made using a 3D printer. It was made from a safe material containing titanium, aluminum, and vanadium. An x-ray taken after surgery showed the implant was in the right place.

The patient left the hospital. She was told to keep seeing her team of doctors for follow-up care. The doctors talked with the patient and her family about what to do next and when to come back.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: Not Disclosed
Gender: Female
Age: 80

Hospital Course:
The patient came in with a slow-growing, painless fluid-filled sac near the outer right eye area. This sac had been there for some time. It caused the eyelid to droop, the eye to bulge forward slightly, and the eye to sit a bit lower than normal. A special scan using magnets (MRI) showed a round growth that did not absorb the contrast dye. Another scan using X-rays (CT) showed changes to the eye socket bones. The bone had worn away near where two skull bones meet. These tests confirmed the growth was a dermoid cyst, a type of harmless sac present from birth. The patient chose not to have surgery to remove the cyst and repair the bone. Instead, the patient had the fluid drained from the cyst several times. After agreeing to treatment, the patient had a procedure to shrink the cyst using a special solution. The first treatment used a numbing medicine mixed with a drug to reduce bleeding. Then pure alcohol was put into the cyst to shrink it. The area was then rinsed with salt water. The patient had two more treatments three months apart. After the last treatment, the cyst became smaller. It stayed small for one year with no signs of growing back. The patient said the loose skin was blocking part of her vision. The doctors did eyelid surgery to remove extra skin. At the same time, they took a small sample of the cyst to study. Lab tests showed the sample contained skin tissue with sweat and oil glands. This confirmed it was a dermoid cyst.

Condition at Discharge:
The treatment to shrink the cyst and the tissue sample test were successful. When the patient left the hospital, there were no signs that the cyst was coming back.

Follow-Up Plan:
The patient will keep seeing her regular doctor near her home for check-ups. The patient should contact her doctor if any new problems come up.

Patient Name: [REDACTED]
Age: 56
Sex: Male
Admission Date: [REDACTED]
Discharge Date: [REDACTED]
Admitting Diagnosis: Chest pain

Hospital Course:
The patient, a 56-year-old male electrician, came to the hospital with chest pain that lasted about an hour. The patient had a history of high blood pressure that was being treated. The patient also had some chest pain in the past that did not follow a typical pattern. A heart stress test done two years ago did not show any problems with blood flow to the heart. When the patient arrived, he was breathing fast while resting. His blood oxygen level was 93 percent. A heart tracing test showed an irregular heartbeat at 90 beats per minute. His blood pressure was 175/95.

The doctors used an electric shock to help reset the heart rhythm back to normal. This was done because blood tests showed slightly high levels of heart enzymes called troponin T and creatine kinase. These tests help check for heart damage. The doctors also wanted to rule out blocked heart arteries. Next, a test was done to look at the heart arteries using dye and X-rays. This test showed that the patient may have an unusual heart artery setup. It looked like a single artery was coming from a part of the main blood vessel called the right sinus of Valsalva. The right heart artery looked normal with no blockages. A special scan also showed no fatty buildup in the arteries.

The pumping ability of the heart was normal at 60 percent. The patient was sent home with only blood pressure medicine. At a check-up two months later, the patient had no chest pain. The patient also had no trouble breathing during activity. The heart pumping ability was still normal. The patient was told to avoid heavy physical work and working on overhead power lines.

Hospital Course Summary:
The 56-year-old male electrician came to the hospital with chest pain that lasted about an hour. The doctors used an electric shock to reset the heart rhythm. A dye test and a special scan were done to look at the heart arteries. The tests showed that the patient may have an unusual heart artery setup with a single artery coming from a part of the main blood vessel. There were no blockages or fatty buildup in the arteries. The heart pumping ability was normal. The patient was sent home in stable condition with only blood pressure medicine. At a check-up two months later, the heart pumping ability was still normal. The patient had no chest pain or trouble breathing during activity. The patient was told to avoid heavy physical work and working on overhead power lines.

Hospital Course:
The 76-year-old male patient came in because of vision problems in his right eye. He had a cornea transplant in that eye 50 years ago. Before that surgery in the 1960s, an explosion had damaged both of his corneas and made them cloudy. The patient saw his eye doctor every year for 50 years after his first cornea transplant. In recent years, he also had checkups for a type of eye pressure problem called glaucoma. He had cataract surgery done at another location 42 years after his cornea transplant in the right eye. Six years after the cataract surgery, he noticed his vision getting worse. His eye doctor continued to see him regularly. About 48 years after the first cornea transplant, the doctor noticed buildup forming at the edges of the transplanted tissue. During an eye exam using a special microscope, the doctor measured the transplanted tissue in both eyes. The transplant was 6 mm wide in each eye. The center of the cornea was 584 micrometers thick in the right eye and 544 micrometers thick in the left eye. The original cornea around the transplant looked cloudy and gray. The layer of cells lining the inside of the cornea showed 1162 cells per square millimeter in the right eye and 1320 cells per square millimeter in the left eye. Because the patient's vision kept getting worse and the blurry vision was bothering him, the doctors suggested another cornea transplant on the right eye since it was worse. The patient agreed, and the surgery went well with no problems. The doctors removed the old transplanted cornea along with a small ring of the surrounding tissue. This tissue was sent to a lab to be studied under a microscope.

Hospital Course:

The patient is a 29-year-old woman. She was admitted to the hospital 21 weeks after giving birth. She had diarrhea with blood and stomach pain. A test using a camera to look inside the large intestine was done. It showed swelling and irritation from the rectum to part of the colon. There were also many yellow-white spots. These findings matched a bowel disease called ulcerative colitis. The patient was given a medicine called sulfasalazine. Her symptoms got better. She left the hospital after 2 weeks. Soon after leaving, her medicine was changed to mesalazine. The patient was then able to breastfeed again.

At 27 weeks after giving birth, the patient came back to the hospital. She stayed for 12 days to learn about managing her bowel disease. During this time, she was given meals based mostly on plants, eggs, and dairy. She also received teaching about eating a plant-based diet. A camera test of the large intestine was done at the end of the stay. It showed the bowel disease was no longer active. The patient's mesalazine dose was slowly lowered to 0.4 grams per day when she left.

During a talk and survey about lifestyle and eating habits, the patient shared some information. She said her diet changed after having her baby. She stayed at her parents' home for about 3 months after delivery. Her mother made traditional Japanese meals as suggested by the midwife. After going back to her own home, the patient said she ate less healthy foods. She also had trouble with bowel movements and upper stomach discomfort. Her eating habits were measured using a plant-based diet score.

Outcome:

The patient left the hospital in stable condition. She was told to keep eating a plant-based diet. The patient stopped taking her medicine 3 weeks after leaving the hospital. She has stayed well without medicine up to now.

Hospital Course:

Doctors found that the cancer had spread to his skull and was pressing on his brain. He had surgery to treat this and left the hospital in stable condition. The patient was told to see his cancer doctor for more treatment and care.

Chief Complaint:
The patient came in because of a lump on his scalp that had been growing quickly for 5 months.

A CT scan showed a growing bone mass in the front of the skull. An MRI scan with contrast dye showed a lens-shaped mass. The mass was growing outward through the skull and pressing inward on both sides of the front of the brain. It was also pressing on a major blood vessel in the brain.

Past Medical History:
The patient had cancer of the food pipe that spread to both adrenal glands near the kidneys.

Physical Examination:
The doctor's exam found a hard lump about 3 inches wide on the front of the head behind the hairline. The lump did not move and did not hurt when touched.

Diagnostic Studies:
A CT scan showed a growing bone mass in the front of the skull. An MRI scan with contrast dye showed a lens-shaped mass.

Hospital Course:
The patient had surgery and left the hospital in stable condition.

Follow-up Plans:
The patient should see his cancer doctor for more treatment and care.

Medical History:
The patient was a 26-year-old female who had been told she had colon cancer six years earlier. The patient came to the hospital for a regular checkup.

Hospital Course:
During the exam, the patient had no health concerns and no visible signs of illness. More tests were done, including a special scan using dye called a CCT scan. This scan found a growth near the center of the chest. The growth had smooth edges and looked the same throughout. Several swollen lymph nodes were also found in the chest area. The patient then had a PET/CT scan. This scan uses a small amount of a sugar-like substance to find active cells in the body. The scan showed the growth was slightly more active than normal tissue. The patient also had an MRI scan of the chest area. This scan uses magnets to create pictures of the inside of the body. The MRI showed a growth that looked a certain way on different types of images. Based on the scan results and the patient's health history, doctors thought the growth could be one of several things. These included cancer that spread from another part of the body, lung cancer, a blood cancer called lymphoma, or a condition called sarcoidosis.

Results:
Blood tests showed that the patient had a high level of a protein called IgG4. The level was 723, which is much higher than the normal level of 135.

Diagnosis:
Doctors did surgery to take a small piece of lung tissue to test. The test showed the patient had a disease called IgG4-related lung disease. This is a condition where the immune system causes swelling in the lungs.

Condition at Discharge:
When the patient left the hospital, the patient was in stable condition. The patient was given information about the diagnosis. The patient was told to see their regular doctor for ongoing care.

Follow-Up Care:
The patient should see their regular doctor for continued checkups and care of this condition.

Summary:
The patient, a 26-year-old female with a history of colon cancer, came to the hospital for a regular checkup. Tests found a growth near the center of the chest with several swollen lymph nodes. Blood tests showed a high level of a protein called IgG4. Doctors did surgery to take a small piece of lung tissue to test. The test showed the patient had IgG4-related lung disease. The patient was told to see their regular doctor for ongoing care.

Discharge Summary:

Patient: Female, 72 years old
Date of Admission: (Insert date of admission)
Date of Discharge: (Insert date of discharge)

Main Health Problem:
Lower back pain and shooting pain down the right leg that made walking very hard.

What Happened During the Hospital Stay:
The patient came to the hospital because of lower back pain and shooting pain in her right leg. This pain made it hard for her to walk. She had surgery to join bones in her spine together. The surgery connected bones from the middle back down to the base of the spine. Metal screws were placed in the lower spine. Bone spacers were also placed between the bones in the lower back. The surgery took 7 hours and 51 minutes. The patient lost about 1271 mL of blood during surgery. The patient received her own blood back during the surgery. She did not need blood from a donor. There were no major problems during the surgery.

Doctor Visits:
The surgery team checked on the patient before the surgery. The same team also checked on her after the surgery.

Treatments and Therapy:
The patient had spine surgery to join bones together using metal screws and bone spacers. On the fifth day after surgery, the patient started standing up using a tilting table. On the twentieth day after surgery, the patient was allowed to start walking. She wore a back brace that supported her middle and lower back.

How the Patient Got Better:
The lower back pain and shooting leg pain got better after surgery. One year after surgery, the patient could walk for more than 10 minutes using a cane. Tests showed the spine bones had joined together. However, the scans also showed the screws at the base of the spine had loosened a little.

Condition at Discharge:
The patient left the hospital in stable condition. She should go to follow-up visits as the surgery team told her.

Instructions and Medications:
None given.

Where the Patient Went:
The patient went home.

None

Hospital Course:
The patient came in with ongoing serious depression that had lasted 10 years. The patient had tried many depression medicines in the past. None of these medicines helped enough, even though the patient took them as directed.
The patient was given venlafaxine and mirtazapine. These medicines did not help much.
The patient then received ketamine shots into the muscle. This improved the patient's mood. But after the third shot, the patient had mood swings that were too high. Because of this, the ketamine was stopped.
The patient was then given lithium and a long-acting form of paroxetine. These medicines helped calm the high mood swings. They also helped with the depression that came back.

Diagnosis:
Ongoing serious depression without breaks from reality.

Treatment:
Venlafaxine and mirtazapine were given at first but later stopped.
Ketamine shots were given into the muscle. Lithium and paroxetine were also given.

Outcome:
The patient felt better from depression with the first treatment. But the patient had mood swings that were too high after getting ketamine.
The high mood swings went away within 16 to 18 days after stopping ketamine. Lithium and paroxetine helped with both the high mood swings and the depression that came back.

Follow-up:
The patient should keep taking lithium and paroxetine as directed.
The patient should see a regular doctor or mental health doctor as needed.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [REDACTED]
Date of Admission: [REDACTED]
Date of Discharge: [REDACTED]

Hospital Course:

A 44-year-old white male came to the emergency room after being trapped under a car part for an unknown amount of time. This caused injury to his chest and lungs. When he arrived, the patient was gasping for air, had a steady heartbeat, but had low blood pressure. Doctors quickly placed a breathing tube and connected him to a breathing machine. This was needed because he was confused and having trouble breathing. His chest and upper body were swollen, full of blood, and covered with tiny red spots from broken blood vessels. Both lungs had collapsed, and bloody fluid was removed from his lungs through the breathing tube. The patient got better after doctors placed tubes in both sides of his chest to drain air and blood. Blood tests showed his blood was more acidic than normal and had high levels of proteins released from damaged muscles. A body scan showed mild brain swelling and blood and air around both lungs with bruised lung tissue.

The patient was moved to the intensive care unit. He was kept on the breathing machine with settings that were slowly reduced. The oxygen level in his breathing air was lowered to 40 percent. The care team worked to protect his kidneys from damage caused by injured muscles releasing harmful substances. They also watched his brain swelling closely by giving medicine to reduce fluid and checking his brain function often. The patient got better quickly. The breathing tube was removed on day two, but he stayed confused and restless until day four. The tiny red spots on his face and chest slowly went away over the next three days. His muscle protein levels returned to normal on day seven. He was then moved to the chest surgery ward.

Recommendations:

The patient should keep all follow-up visits with his doctor to check on his healing. He should avoid activities that put too much strain on his chest and lungs. He should tell his doctor right away if his symptoms change. The patient should keep taking all medicines as directed. He should also follow healthy habits to help his body heal.

The patient should call his doctor right away if he has any of these warning signs: chest pain, feeling short of breath, trouble breathing, fever, or coughing up unusual mucus.

Treatment: Strong infection-fighting medicines given through a vein, surgery to remove the left kidney using small cuts, infection-fighting pills taken by mouth
Outcome: Feeling healthy and doing well, sent home after 7 days of infection-fighting pills taken by mouth

Hospital course: The patient was admitted with chest pain, fevers, night sweats, and weight loss. After careful testing, the patient was found to have a rare kidney infection that causes long-term swelling and damage. The patient also had another condition where unusual cells build up in the kidney. The patient was given strong infection-fighting medicines through a vein. The patient also had surgery to remove the left kidney using small cuts. Infection-fighting medicines were given for 7 days before surgery and 7 days after surgery. Hospital Course:

The 8-year-old female patient came in for a check on a slow-growing skin bump on her left chest. The bump was about 0.5 cm wide and had a light purple color. A sound wave scan showed a small oval-shaped growth under the skin. The growth reached into the skin layer and was close to the muscle below. The patient had surgery to remove the bump and test it. The test showed the tissue had a gray-white lump with cells arranged in a swirling pattern. Doctors thought it could be one of two types of skin tumors. Tests on the tissue confirmed it was a rare type of skin tumor called DFSP. This tumor grows slowly and rarely spreads to other body parts.

After finding this, the patient had scans and blood tests done. All results came back normal. Even though the edges around the removed bump looked healthy, doctors did a second surgery to remove more tissue. This was done to lower the chance of the tumor coming back. The patient healed well after surgery. She will be checked every 6 months for the next 3 years. Doctors will feel the scar area and check nearby glands to make sure the tumor has not come back or spread.

Impression and Plan:

The patient was found to have a rare slow-growing skin tumor called DFSP after testing the removed tissue. A second surgery was done to remove more tissue around the area. The patient will have regular check-up visits. No other treatment is needed at this time.

DISCHARGE SUMMARY

Patient Name: [Name]
Medical Record Number: [Number]
Date of Admission: [Date]
Date of Discharge: [Date]

HOSPITAL COURSE:

The patient is a 70-year-old male with a joint disease called rheumatoid arthritis. He came to the hospital because he had trouble breathing and was coughing up mucus. His joint disease had been well controlled with no joint pain or swelling before this visit. This meant his joint disease was not very active. Blood tests showed high levels of certain markers that point to swelling in the body. Tests also showed the patient had a past infection with a common virus called Epstein-Barr virus.

A scan of the chest showed lung swelling in the lower parts of both lungs with several small round spots. A test of the mucus coughed up from the lungs showed unusual immune cells that looked abnormal. A small piece of lung tissue was removed and tested. It showed unusual medium to large immune cells that looked abnormal. The patient was found to have a condition where the immune cells grow too much because of a medicine called methotrexate. This is a type of blood cancer.

A tube with a camera was used to look inside the airways. It showed swollen tissue with extra blood vessels that bled easily. The patient was treated by stopping the methotrexate medicine. Most of the spots in the lungs went away on their own about 3 weeks after stopping this medicine. After that, only a medicine called tacrolimus was used. The patient was watched for 15 months after stopping methotrexate. The disease did not get worse during this time.

DISCHARGE DIAGNOSES:

1. Immune cell overgrowth caused by methotrexate, a type of blood cancer

DISCHARGE INSTRUCTIONS:

1. The patient should keep taking prescribed medicines as told by the main doctor.
2. The patient should stay away from things in the air that can bother the lungs to prevent lung infections.
3. The patient should go to regular doctor visits to check health and how well the medicines are working.

FOLLOW-UP CARE:

The patient has been sent to a blood disease doctor for ongoing care of the immune cell overgrowth after stopping methotrexate.

Discharge Summary:

Patient: 51-year-old female

Admission Date: February 2013

Discharge Date: October 2015

Diagnosis: Returning jaw tumor (ameloblastoma)

Procedure: Surgery to remove part of the right lower jawbone and rebuild it using bone from the hip, followed by placing dental implants and a permanent set of replacement teeth

Hospital Course:

The patient came to the department in February 2013 because of pain in the lower jaw. She had a jaw tumor that kept coming back and had several surgeries before to drain it. The patient was not happy with her care at the other hospital and came to our department to have the tumor fully removed. After a complete checkup, we planned to remove all of the tumor and rebuild the jaw right away using bone from the hip. In March 2013, the patient had surgery to remove part of the right lower jawbone (teeth 43 to 46, about 35 mm long). The care team watched closely to make sure the tumor did not come back. Follow-up visits showed no signs of the tumor returning, but the patient still had trouble chewing on the right side. Because of this, we suggested a permanent set of replacement teeth. In November 2014, the metal plate was taken out of the new bone, and four dental implants were placed. After that, the patient had surgery to create more space in the mouth for the new teeth. All four implants joined well with the bone. The patient received the final set of permanent replacement teeth in October 2015. The patient has kept good mouth care habits. There are no signs of the tumor coming back or problems with the bone or implants. The patient was sent home in October 2015.

Discharge Instructions:

The patient should keep brushing and cleaning the mouth well and follow the regular care schedule. The patient should come to all follow-up visits so the care team can check for any return of the tumor and make sure the implants stay healthy. If the patient has any worries or questions, the patient should call the department for help.

Patient Name: [Insert Name]
Age: 29
Gender: Male
Date of Admission: [Insert Date]
Date of Discharge: [Insert Date]

Hospital Stay Summary:

The patient, a 29-year-old white male, was admitted to the hospital for shortness of breath, tiredness, swelling in the legs, and belly pain. The physical exam showed an enlarged left lower heart chamber with liver swelling due to heart backup. The patient had even swelling in both legs and trouble breathing while lying flat. The patient also had a loud heart murmur heard on the upper left chest. The neck veins were swollen, and heart sounds were normal. Heart scans showed an enlarged heart with the left lower chamber stretched and shaped like a ball. There were also several loose blood clots found in the lower part of the heart. The patient had episodes of fast, abnormal heart rhythms. The heart's electrical signals were blocked on the right side. There were frequent extra heartbeats. A heart valve was leaking because the heart chamber had changed shape. The left lower heart chamber was not pumping well and was too stiff when filling with blood. The patient also had damage to the liver and kidneys from blocked blood flow. A blood test showed high levels of a hormone that rises when the heart is stressed. Another heart valve was leaking a medium amount. Genetic tests for Fabry disease, Gaucher disease, and Niemann-Pick disease all came back normal.

During the hospital stay, the patient was treated with blood thinners, heart rhythm medicines, water pills, medicines to slow the heart rate, and medicines to relax blood vessels. After 2 months of blood thinners and heart failure treatment, a follow-up heart ultrasound showed no blood clots in the left lower heart chamber. The patient no longer showed signs of heart failure. A small device was placed in the chest to shock the heart if it stops or beats dangerously fast. The patient was recommended for a heart transplant.

In conclusion, a 29-year-old white male was admitted to the hospital with symptoms of an enlarged left lower heart chamber, liver swelling from heart backup, even swelling in both legs, and trouble breathing while lying flat. The patient had a stiff left lower heart chamber, damage to the liver and kidneys from blocked blood flow, and medium leaking of a heart valve. Treatment was started with blood thinners, heart rhythm medicines, water pills, medicines to slow the heart rate, and medicines to relax blood vessels. The patient was recommended for a heart transplant.

Discharge Summary:
Patient: 39-year-old female

Hospital Course:
The patient came to the hospital because her left eye felt like something was stuck in it. She also had watery eyes. An eye exam using a special microscope showed several soft, milky-white lumps on the clear front part of her left eye. There was also a slight cloudy area just below the surface. Doctors found that these lumps looked like a jelly-like growth. They were located where an eyelash was touching the eye. A special scan of the eye showed a large lump under the thin outer layer. The deeper protective layer of the eye was not damaged. The right eye had a line-shaped cloudy spot under the surface. This spot did not pick up yellow dye during the exam. A scan showed a dense spot in the protective layer. This spot matched where the eyelash touched and where the line appeared during the exam.

Treatment:
To fix the feeling of something stuck in her eye, the patient had surgery to replace part of the clear front layer of her eye. Doctors removed the affected eye tissue. They froze the removed tissue and cut it into thin slices for testing. They used special dyes and markers to study the tissue. The tests showed the material had a specific protein buildup. This buildup glowed apple-green under special light. The tissue also tested positive for a protein called lactoferrin in the same area.

Outcome:
The patient healed well after surgery. The protein buildup did not come back. Ten months after surgery, the patient's left eye vision with glasses was perfect at 20/20. The eyelashes in the problem area are removed regularly.

Hospital Course:

The patient came in with belly pain in the lower area that had lasted for 24 hours. The patient was found to have a blockage in the small intestine in the middle of the belly. The patient had a blockage in the small intestine in the middle of the belly. This was caused by thick scar tissue that had formed around the lining of the belly.

The patient had a rare case of a blocked small intestine caused by thick scar tissue in the belly lining. The patient needed surgery to fix this problem. The surgery went well. The patient healed without any problems. At the most recent check-up, there were no signs that the problem had come back.

Discharge Summary:
Patient Name: [REDACTED]
Medical Record Number: [REDACTED]

Hospital Course:
The patient is a 70-year-old male. He has a history of blood cancer, poor blood flow in the legs, low thyroid, lung disease, high cholesterol, and gout. He came to the hospital because he was confused and had belly pain. His blood pressure was too low and his heart was beating too fast. His bladder tube was blocked and showed signs of infection with pus. Lab tests showed his kidneys were not working well. He also had high white blood cell counts and too much acid in his blood. A scan of his belly showed air in his stomach wall and gas in the blood vessels of his liver.

Treatment and Management:
The patient was given three strong medicines to fight infection. Samples of his blood and urine were sent to check for germs. He was given fluids through a vein. He also needed medicine to raise his blood pressure when fluids did not help enough. Surgery and stomach doctors were asked to help. A camera was used to look inside his stomach. This showed poor blood flow and some dead tissue in the upper stomach. Small tissue samples showed bleeding and damage from poor blood flow. Doctors suggested removing part of the stomach. However, surgery was not safe for this patient because of his many health problems. He was treated without surgery instead.

Follow Up:
The patient's kidney problems got better after a few days. A new scan of his blood vessels showed no new problems. The patient slowly started to get better. Another camera look inside his stomach showed the tissue was now healthy and pink. There were no more signs of poor blood flow or dead tissue. The patient was slowly able to start eating again by mouth. He was moved to a regular hospital room after finishing all his infection medicines. The patient was then sent to a care facility for longer recovery.

Hospital Course Summary:

Admission Date: [date]
Discharge Date: [date]

Patient Name: [name]
Age: 68 years
Sex: Male

Medical History:
Prostate cancer treated with radiation therapy, 3 years ago
Removal of growths from the large intestine using a small camera tube, 1 year ago
Long-term difficulty having bowel movements

Hospital Course:
The patient came in with sudden pain in the upper belly. A scan showed a large lump between the stomach and pancreas. Doctors first thought it might be cancer that had spread, causing swelling in the belly lining. The patient was admitted for more tests and watching. The next day, doctors found bleeding inside the belly. The patient was moved to our hospital for emergency care.

When the patient arrived at our hospital, he was awake and thinking clearly. A physical exam showed pain in the left upper belly when pressed. The belly lining also showed signs of irritation. Blood tests showed a slightly high white blood cell count and low red blood cell count. Tests also showed high levels of a waste product in the blood and a digestive enzyme. A scan with dye showed a solid lump near the tail of the pancreas. There was also a large amount of fluid in the belly. This pointed to a blood clot and heavy bleeding inside the belly.

The patient needed emergency surgery to open and check the belly. Doctors found a 2-inch tear in the tissue that holds the large intestine in place. This tear started near where the small intestine meets the large intestine and went to the left. Doctors stopped the bleeding with stitches and special materials that help blood clot. The patient received blood during surgery. The surgery went well, but the bowels stopped moving for a short time afterward. The patient left the hospital in good health 20 days after surgery.

While in the hospital, doctors learned that the patient had ongoing trouble having bowel movements. The patient had been pressing on his belly to help pass stool. This likely caused the tear. Doctors told the patient to stop pressing on his belly. They also said to get medical help right away if he has any belly problems.

In summary, the patient has a history of prostate cancer, removal of growths from the large intestine, and long-term trouble having bowel movements. He came in with sudden upper belly pain. Doctors found bleeding inside the belly from a tear caused by pressing on his belly to help pass stool. The patient had emergency surgery to stop the bleeding. The surgery went well, but the bowels stopped moving for a short time afterward. The patient left the hospital 20 days after surgery. He was told not to press on his belly and to get medical help for any belly problems in the future.

Medical History:
The patient is a 24-year-old male with a serious bleeding disorder called Hemophilia A. This means his blood does not clot normally. He has been getting medicine called Factor VIII three times a week to help his blood clot. He reported missing his last three doses.

Hospital Course:
The patient came to the hospital with pain and swelling on the inner side of his left elbow. He also had pain and tingling in his ring finger and pinky finger. During the exam, the doctor found moderate swelling and tenderness on the inner elbow. The patient had less feeling in his pinky and ring fingers. These fingers are controlled by a nerve called the ulnar nerve. His hand strength was slightly weaker than normal. Tapping on the nerve at the elbow caused tingling, which is a sign of nerve irritation. The patient was given Factor VIII medicine and stayed in the hospital for monitoring. The next day, his symptoms got worse. He was taken to surgery to relieve pressure on the nerve. The surgeon released the trapped nerve at several spots around the elbow. There were no nerve growths or signs of long-term nerve damage.

Discharge Condition:
The patient left the hospital. The blood disorder team followed up with him to keep his Factor VIII levels in a healthy range.

Follow-up Plan:
At the 6-week checkup, the patient said he was doing well. He had no limits on his activities. His tingling had gone away completely. His grip strength was back to full normal.

Additional Information:
The patient gave written permission to share his information in this article.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [redacted]
DOB: [redacted]
Admission Date: [redacted]
Discharge Date: [redacted]
Attending Physician: [redacted]

Admission Diagnosis: West syndrome (a type of seizure disorder in infants)

Hospital Course:
The patient is a 2-month-old baby boy. He had heart surgery before this hospital stay to fix a hole between the lower chambers of his heart. He came to the hospital because he was crying a lot and could not be calmed. During these episodes, his neck would stretch back. His arms and body would become stiff. Sometimes he would swallow and throw up afterward. Doctors first thought the problem was acid reflux. They started medicine for acid reflux, but it did not help.

Over the next few weeks, the episodes happened more often and got worse. The patient's mother recorded a video of one episode. The video showed the patient having bending spasms. The patient then had surgery to help stop acid from coming back up. This surgery did not help either. The symptoms kept happening. The patient also had arm spasms during episodes. These signs finally pointed to West syndrome.

A brain wave test confirmed West syndrome. A brain scan showed no problems. The right treatment started when the patient was 8 months old. By then, there were already signs of developmental delays. West syndrome is rare. Doctors suspected it based on the patient's age and medical history after a full brain and nerve exam.

This is the first known case where West syndrome was mistaken for acid reflux. Focusing too much on acid reflux in children may cause doctors to miss other conditions. Doctors should consider acid reflux mainly in children at higher risk. This includes children with brain conditions that affect movement. It also includes children who had surgery for problems with their food pipe. Acid reflux should also be considered when symptoms clearly point to it. These symptoms include throwing up blood or long-term vomiting with poor growth.

Discharge Diagnosis: West syndrome (a type of seizure disorder in infants)

Final Condition at Discharge:
When the patient left the hospital, he still had symptoms of West syndrome. The right treatment had been started. The family was told to see the children's doctors. They will help manage medicines and do more tests.

Discharge Medications:
Not Applicable

Follow-Up:
The parents were told to see a children's doctor for regular checkups. They should watch the patient's condition closely. The patient also has appointments with a brain and nerve doctor for more tests and care.

Discharge Summary:

Patient: 52-year-old African American woman who has had multiple pregnancies

Diagnosis: Urethral diverticulum (a pouch or sac that forms in the tube that carries urine out of the body)

Hospital Course:

The patient was admitted after she fainted. She had heavy vaginal bleeding for 2 days before admission. She was passing large blood clots and had pain in her lower belly. A pelvic exam showed blood clots in the vagina. There was also a raw, damaged area on the vaginal wall near the urine tube. A CT scan (a special X-ray) showed a growth inside the vagina. It also showed a swollen lymph node near the right ovary. On day 2 in the hospital, the patient had a procedure while asleep. Doctors took tissue samples, but the results did not show a clear answer.

During days 3 through 5, the patient's bleeding slowed down a lot. On day 6, doctors did another procedure while the patient was asleep. The tissue samples showed no cancer. Doctors used a special clamp in the urine tube. The urology team (doctors who treat bladder and urine problems) was called in during the procedure. They confirmed the patient had a pouch in the urine tube. The pouch was removed. Doctors then repaired the area in layers around a urine drainage tube.

On day 9 after surgery, the patient came back with bleeding. Some stitches had come loose in the damaged tissue. These were removed. New stitches were placed to close the tissue. The final tissue tests showed the tissue was not cancerous.

Treatment:

Removal of the pouch in the urine tube and repair in layers around a urine drainage tube.

Follow-up:

The patient visited the urology clinic 2 weeks later. A special X-ray test was done to check the urine tube and bladder. It showed no leaking. A physical exam showed the vagina was healing well with no problems.

Disposition:

The patient left the hospital in stable condition.

Admitting Diagnosis: Stroke caused by a blocked blood vessel in the brain

The patient came to the emergency room with slurred speech, dizziness, and weakness on the left side of her body. These symptoms started about two hours before she arrived.
