Hospital Course:
The patient was a 33-year-old woman who came to the hospital with belly pain, loose stools, and fever. She was admitted and sent home after 2 days of taking an antibiotic pill called ciprofloxacin. She came back to the hospital two days later because her belly pain got worse and she had other problems.

Diagnostic Studies:
The patient had a special body scan. The scan showed a small fluid-filled sac on her left ovary that had burst. It was about 2 centimeters wide. There was a small amount of fluid in her lower belly area. The scan did not show any other problems inside her belly.

Treatment:
The patient received antibiotics through a needle in her vein. Doctors also did a surgery using a small camera to look inside her belly. They removed cloudy infected fluid from inside her belly. They saw that her appendix looked normal. The patient kept taking antibiotics for a serious infection in the lining of her belly caused by strep bacteria. She got better with care to help her symptoms. She went home after 10 days in the hospital.

Follow-Up:
The patient got better based on new blood tests. Her white blood cell count and infection levels went back to normal. She had some mild lower belly pain that went away on its own with basic care. She was set up to see the infection specialist team at the clinic.

Plan:
The patient will keep taking an antibiotic pill called clindamycin at home. This antibiotic was chosen based on lab tests of her infection. She will see the infection specialist team to make sure she keeps getting better and to continue her care.

Hospital Course:
The patient is a 23-year-old male with long-term hepatitis C virus infection. He came for treatment following Egypt's national guidelines for hepatitis C. The treatment plan included two medicines: a weekly injection called pegylated interferon and a daily pill called ribavirin. However, after 12 weeks of treatment, the doctors stopped the therapy. This happened because the virus levels did not drop enough.

Discharge Summary:
The patient found out he had hepatitis C during a job-related health check 2 years ago. The patient's body mass index was 27.5, which is slightly overweight. A liver tissue sample showed moderate liver damage and scarring but no fat buildup. During treatment, blood tests showed a hidden hepatitis B infection became active. The hepatitis B virus levels rose above 2000 units. To treat this, doctors gave the patient a medicine called lamivudine for 6 months. During this time, doctors kept checking both hepatitis B and hepatitis C virus levels. The hepatitis B virus became undetectable and the hepatitis C virus levels went down. The patient stopped taking lamivudine because he could not afford it. Six months later, tests showed hepatitis B was still undetectable. The hepatitis C virus level had dropped to 7062 units per milliliter.

Overall, the patient had hepatitis C and developed an active hepatitis B infection during treatment. The lamivudine medicine worked well to control the hepatitis B. The patient stopped lamivudine because of money problems. After stopping, no one checked the patient's hepatitis C virus levels. No additional treatment steps were planned when the patient left the hospital.

Discharge Summary:

Patient: 47-year-old female who has no natural teeth and wears a full upper denture

Chief Complaint: Upper denture that does not work properly

History of Present Illness: The patient came in because her upper denture was not working well. This problem happened because of radiation treatment she had on her neck area. She could not open her mouth very wide. She also did not have enough saliva, and her saliva did not flow well.

Hospital Course: The care team planned to make new full dentures with edges that fit better. They used bendable trays to take first molds of both the upper and lower mouth. They made custom trays for the final molds using a self-hardening plastic material. They took final upper molds using a rubber-like material on one half of the tray at a time. They made base plates and wax rims to help set the bite. They recorded how the jaws line up when closed and moved this information to a device that copies jaw movement. They checked the test dentures to make sure the jaw position and tooth placement were correct. After the patient agreed the fit was good, the team shaped and prepared the dentures in molds. They made the final dentures using the same design as the base plates. They removed the dentures from the molds, smoothed them, and shined them. The patient received instructions on how to clean, put in, and take out her dentures. She was asked to come back for checkup visits to make sure the dentures were in good shape and that she was adjusting to them.

Outcome: The patient had trouble putting in and taking out her denture at first. Over time, she got used to doing this.

Follow-up: The patient will keep coming to checkup visits. The care team will make sure her dentures are in good condition and that she is adjusting well to them.

Discharge Summary:

Admission Date: [Date]
Discharge Date: [Date]

Patient:
The patient is a 61-year-old Japanese man who was admitted with hip pain.

Presenting Issues:
The patient came in with hip pain. X-rays showed bony growths near the knee and shoulder joints. The patient had also developed wear and tear of the hip joint and severe pain in the right hip. The patient could not bend or move the right hip outward as much as normal.

Treatment:
The patient had surgery to replace the right hip joint. The doctors went in through the side of the hip. They found that the ball of the hip joint was very large. The soft tissue looked normal. The doctors cut into the tissue covering the joint. It was hard to move the hip out of place because the ball was so big. This caused a break in the bony bump on the side of the thigh bone. The bone in this area was weak and broke easily. A new hip socket was pressed into place without screws. The doctors cut the thigh bone lower than usual. They put in a smooth metal stem using bone cement. The broken bone piece was fixed back in place with wire and tape. The doctors then repaired the joint covering and the muscles around the hip.

Outcomes:
After surgery, the new hip parts were in good position. The bony growth on the thigh bone had been removed. The patient was allowed to walk and put full weight on the leg. There were no problems like the hip slipping out of place or infection. Thirteen months after surgery, the patient had no hip pain. The right hip still could not bend or move outward as much as normal. The patient did not limp and had no trouble with daily tasks. X-rays showed some extra bone had formed near the hip. The patient had gone back to work and had no problems with everyday activities.

Follow-Up Care:
The patient left the hospital using a crutch.

Discharge Summary

Patient Name: [REDACTED]
Age: 68
Sex: Male
Date of Admission: [REDACTED]

Diagnosis:
The patient has swelling and blisters on the clear front part of the eye after lens removal. The patient also has scarring on the clear front part of the eye.

Hospital Course:
The patient had surgery to replace the damaged clear front part of the eye with tissue from a donor. The first donor tissue showed a large sore right after it was placed. It was removed and replaced with new donor tissue. The patient received antiviral medicine through a vein during surgery. After surgery, the patient was given antiviral pills and eye drops. The patient also received antibiotic eye drops to prevent infection. After one week, the new tissue was clear and the surface had healed. The patient started taking acyclovir 400 mg pills for long term protection. Six months later, a sore appeared on the new tissue where it meets the original eye tissue. There was also clouding and small spots on the clear front part of the eye. The patient took acyclovir 400 mg pills and used antiviral eye drops five times a day for two weeks. The sore healed but left some scarring.

Summary:
The patient had swelling and scarring on the clear front part of the eye. The patient had surgery to replace this damaged tissue with donor tissue. The first donor tissue had to be replaced with a second one. After surgery, the patient took antiviral and antibiotic medicines. Later, a sore developed on the clear front part of the eye. This was treated successfully with antiviral medicines. The patient was sent home with instructions to return for a check-up within one week.

DISCHARGE SUMMARY:

Medical History: A 12-year-old female patient was admitted. She had been urinating a lot, feeling very thirsty, and her periods had stopped.

Clinical Findings: Doctors did hormone tests before surgery. The tests showed slightly high levels of a hormone called prolactin. The tests also showed her thyroid gland was underactive. Her body was not making enough stress hormones. Brain scans showed a large growth in the lower part of the brain. This growth was pressing on the nerves that control vision. It was also reaching into a fluid-filled space in the brain.

Diagnosis: Doctors first thought it might be one of two types of brain tumors. But based on the patient's symptoms, they believed it was a type called germinoma.

Procedure: The patient had surgery to remove the tumor. Doctors went through the nose using a small camera and tools. This allowed them to reach the tumor without opening the skull.

Postoperative Course: The patient got much better after surgery. She could see light with her left eye. Her side vision in her right eye also improved. There were no problems after surgery.

Postoperative Follow-up: Blood tests checked for certain markers. These results confirmed the tumor was a type of cancer called germinoma. The patient was sent to a children's cancer doctor for more treatment. She will need chemotherapy and radiation therapy.

Condition at Discharge: The patient left the hospital in normal condition. She is still taking a medicine called desmopressin acetate. This treats a condition where her body cannot control water balance.

Prognosis: The outlook for the patient is hopeful. She will need to come back for a follow-up visit.

Hospital Course:
The patient, a 71-year-old female, was admitted to our hospital due to loss of appetite, swelling in a lymph node in the left groin area, low platelet count, and elevated liver enzymes following a tick bite while harvesting. The patient was suspected to have a serious illness caused by the tick bite called severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome (SFTS). Diagnostic tests confirmed SFTS infection based on blood test results.

Clinical Findings:
On admission, the patient had a mild headache and swelling in a lymph node in the left groin area. There was no redness, rash, or raised bumps on the skin. Blood tests showed low platelet count and low white blood cell count. The tests also showed unusual white blood cells and elevated liver enzymes.

Treatment:
The patient was given fluids through an IV because she had mild low fluid levels in her body when she arrived. The patient was given an antibiotic called minocycline through an IV at first. Doctors thought she might have a different tick-borne illness. However, doctors stopped giving minocycline after tests confirmed the SFTS infection.

Outcome:
The platelet count went up a lot during the hospital stay. Liver enzyme levels returned to almost normal levels. The patient's appetite improved. The patient was sent home after 13 days. The patient did not have any fever during her hospital stay.

Follow-up Plan:
No specific follow-up plan was mentioned in the case report.

DISCHARGE SUMMARY

Patient Name: [REDACTED]

Admission Date: [REDACTED]
Discharge Date: [REDACTED]
Length of Stay: [REDACTED]

Medical History:
No relevant medical history was reported.

Hospital Course:
The patient came to the emergency clinic with sudden vision loss. This happened after a tennis ball hit the right eye. At first, the patient could only see hand movements and some light in all directions. The patient was treated without surgery at first. Treatment included steroid eye drops to reduce swelling, drops to relax the eye, and medicines to lower eye pressure. There was bleeding in the front and middle parts of the eye. This bleeding cleared up in three weeks. The patient's vision improved to 20/60. However, the pressure inside the eye stayed too high. A medicine called bimatoprost was added to help lower the eye pressure. The eye pressure did not get much better over the following weeks. The patient was told that surgery to drain fluid from the eye was needed. The doctors explained that vision results could not be guaranteed. During surgery, the gel inside the eye pushed forward when tissue was removed. This was fixed by removing some of the gel. One day after surgery, vision was 20/125 and eye pressure was too low to measure. Fluid collected under a layer at the back of the eye. This was treated with steroid medicine as drops and pills. The fluid went away in two weeks. Over time, the patient's vision and eye pressure got better. At the last checkup three months later, vision was 20/25 and eye pressure was 12, which is normal. The patient no longer needed any eye pressure medicine.

Summary:
An 18-year-old male came in after a tennis ball hit his right eye. This caused vision loss and high pressure inside the eye. The patient was first treated with steroid eye drops, drops to relax the eye, and medicines to lower eye pressure. Later, the patient had surgery to drain fluid from the eye. During surgery, the gel inside the eye pushed forward and some had to be removed. After surgery, fluid collected under a layer at the back of the eye. This was treated with steroid medicine and went away. The steroid medicine was slowly reduced over time. At the last checkup three months later, the patient's vision and eye pressure had improved.

Hospital Course:
The patient is a 54-year-old man who has a history of smoking and gallstones. He had two procedures done together. First, doctors used a thin tube with a camera to look at the bile ducts and remove any stones. Then they removed the gallbladder through small cuts. Doctors made a small opening to reach the gallbladder. Before surgery, the patient had yellow skin and eyes, and blood tests showed the liver was not working normally. The surgery took 92 minutes, and the patient was under sleep medicine for 108 minutes. For the first 12 hours after surgery, the patient did not need pain medicine. The patient rated the pain as less than 3 out of 10. At hour 13, the pain went up to 5 out of 10 when coughing and 3 out of 10 when resting. The patient needed extra pain medicine at that time. The patient went home after 24 hours with a prescription for pain medicine.
The rest of the hospital stay went well. There were no problems during recovery. The patient was told to schedule a visit with their regular doctor after leaving the hospital.

Discharge Summary:

Patient: [Name]
Sex: Female
Age: 61 years old
Date of admission: [Date]
Date of discharge: [Date]
Diagnosis: Papillary Fibroelastoma, a rare non-cancerous heart tumor

Hospital Course:

The patient came to the hospital with repeated sharp chest pain that got worse with breathing and serious trouble breathing. A CT scan of the lungs did not show any blood clots. Heart tests found a small growth attached to a flap in the right side of the heart. The growth measured about half an inch in size. The heart valve was also leaking slightly. Doctors thought the growth was most likely a papillary fibroelastoma or a myxoma, which are two types of non-cancerous heart tumors. Surgery was recommended because the tumor could break off and block blood flow. The size of the tumor, larger than one centimeter, also made surgery necessary.

Surgery:

Doctors removed the growth by carefully shaving it off the heart valve. The heart valve was also repaired using a special ring to help it close properly.

Postoperative Procedures:

The patient was watched closely after surgery and received proper care. The patient took blood-thinning medicine for 8 weeks after surgery. As of now, the patient has no symptoms during rest or physical activity.

Follow-Up:

The patient should live a healthy lifestyle. The patient should also keep all future appointments with the doctor.

Addendum:

The patient had no problems during the hospital stay. The patient was in stable condition at the time of discharge.

Hospital Course:

The patient is an 81-year-old woman with a history of prediabetes and kidney failure requiring dialysis. She had heart bypass surgery and a heart valve replacement. After surgery, she had several problems. Her chest wound opened up and needed special vacuum bandages to help it heal. She also had a pressure sore on her lower back. She had several infections that spread to her blood and had trouble breathing on her own.

Assessment and Plan:

For the first 45 days in the hospital, the patient's blood sugar was well controlled. She only needed 2 units of insulin total during that time. However, soon after starting vitamin C through an IV to help heal her chest wound, her blood sugar readings became very high. The readings went above 200. She needed 9 units of insulin in one day, and her blood sugar stayed high for several days. Doctors then found a big difference between two ways of measuring blood sugar. The difference was more than 100 points. One method showed high readings. The other method showed normal readings between 72 and 146. Doctors believed the vitamin C was causing false high readings on one type of test. They stopped the vitamin C, and her blood sugar readings went back to normal. The patient did not have low blood sugar from getting insulin she did not need.

Summary:

This discharge summary describes the hospital stay of an elderly woman with kidney disease and prediabetes. She had heart bypass surgery and a heart valve replacement with problems after surgery. Her blood sugar readings became high after starting vitamin C through an IV. Doctors believe these readings were falsely high. This led to insulin treatment she did not need. Her blood sugar readings returned to normal after stopping the vitamin C.

Discharge Summary:
Admission Date: [DATE]
Discharge Date: [DATE]
Patient Name: [NAME]
DOB: [DOB]
Gender: Male

Hospital Course:
The patient came to the hospital because one side of his face looked different from the other. He had trouble speaking and chewing because he could not move his lower jaw well. He also had pain on and off in the right jaw joint area. Over time, he could not open his mouth as wide, and his face became more uneven. He had no injuries that caused this. When doctors examined him, they saw his face was clearly uneven. X-rays showed a large growth on the right side of his lower jaw bone near the joint. A CT scan, which takes detailed pictures inside the body, confirmed a growth on the right jaw joint. Doctors planned surgery to remove the enlarged jaw joint through a cut made in front of the ear.

The doctors made a cut in front of the ear and removed the growth along with the jaw joint bone. They used a special dental drill to do this. The removed tissue was prepared and looked at under a microscope. The lab test showed the growth was made of cartilage and bone cells arranged in a normal pattern. There were no signs of cancer. The results showed the growth was a type of noncancerous bone tumor called a giant osteochondroma.

Recovery after surgery went smoothly with no problems. The patient was given regular follow-up visits. At his most recent visit, his face looked normal again and he could open his mouth normally. He had no more symptoms.

Discharge Condition:
The patient had successful surgery to remove a noncancerous bone growth. He has been sent home from the hospital and is recovering well.

Recommendations:
1. The patient should go to follow-up visits with his doctor as planned to check on healing and make sure he stays healthy.
2. If any new problems or symptoms come up, the patient should get medical help right away.
3. The patient should keep eating healthy foods and exercise regularly.
4. Surgery is not always the first choice for treatment. Other treatment options should be talked about fully with the patient and his family or caregiver.
5. Patients should learn all about their health condition and the different treatment choices available to them.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [redacted]
Sex: Male
Age: 39
Admission Date: [redacted]
Discharge Date: [redacted]
Diagnosis: Allergic to ketamine and morphine (two drugs used to make patients sleep during surgery)

Hospital Course:

The patient came to our hospital because of long-term sinus problems. Since the age of 11, the patient had several serious allergic reactions during surgeries and eye exams. These reactions happened when doctors gave medicine to make him sleep. The patient and his family were very scared to go to hospitals for 10 years. This fear started after his last serious allergic reaction at age 29 during eye removal surgery.

An allergy doctor checked the patient. The doctor did skin tests for morphine and ketamine using standard amounts. The first tests showed no allergy. But because the patient had such bad reactions before, doctors did more tests 6 weeks later. The second round of skin tests showed the patient is allergic to ketamine and morphine. We told the patient to never use ketamine or morphine for future surgeries. We updated the patient's drug allergy card. We tested other drugs that could be used instead. Those drugs did not cause a reaction. Doctors used these safe drugs for the patient's sinus surgery. The surgery went well with no allergic reactions.

The patient was told to watch carefully for allergy signs if given other sleep medicines in the future. The patient understood all the instructions. The patient went home feeling well. We gave the patient and his caregivers a full report about this hospital stay.

Discharge Medications:

None recommended.

Follow-up:

The patient should see the allergy doctor if needed.

Hospital Course:
The patient is a 16-year-old boy who was admitted to the hospital because of broken bones in his left lower leg and right forearm. The lower leg break was treated with a ring-shaped metal frame attached around the leg. The forearm break was fixed with flexible metal rods placed inside the bone. The patient needed another surgery because the metal rods shifted out of place. During this surgery, the extra metal was trimmed and pushed back into the bone. The holes where the rods came out were covered with a bone-like filling material.

Diagnosis:
The patient was diagnosed with a break near the metal hardware in his right forearm and a break in his left lower leg bone.

Procedure:
The patient had surgery to cut and reset the bone, create a channel inside the bone using a special drilling method, and insert flexible metal rods. The small metal pins were easy to remove because they had not attached to the bone. The metal wires were harder to take out but were removed in the end.

Treatment:
The patient received treatment using a ring-shaped metal frame and flexible metal rods inside the bone to fix his broken bones. Surgery was done because the metal rods moved out of place.

Follow-up:
Over 18 months, the flexible metal rods slowly shifted and caused some irritation to the nearby tissue. The patient's bones fully healed and he could do everything he did before the injury at his one-year checkup. His arm movement was checked. He could rotate his palm down 25 degrees and rotate his palm up 60 degrees. The patient said this matched how his arm moved before the injury and he was happy with the results. No more checkups were needed.

Discharge Summary

Patient Name: [REDACTED]
Medical Record Number: [REDACTED]
Date of Admission: [REDACTED]
Date of Discharge: [REDACTED]

Hospital Course:
The patient, a 78-year-old male, came to the emergency room with a dry cough, fever, and feeling unwell for 1 month. He was treated before with an antibiotic called amoxicillin, but it did not help. His health history included diabetes and high blood pressure. He had been taking metformin and amlodipine for these conditions for 7 years. When examined, the patient was slightly drowsy, had a fever, a slightly fast heartbeat, low oxygen levels, and crackling sounds in the middle and lower parts of his lungs. Blood tests showed signs of infection and swelling in the body. A chest x-ray showed cloudy patches in both lungs. A detailed lung scan showed widespread lung tissue damage with a hazy pattern. Tests of blood and mucus samples found no bacteria. Urine tests for two types of lung infection bacteria were negative. Blood tests for diseases where the body attacks itself were all negative. A camera was used to look inside the airways. Fluid and tissue samples from the lungs showed no cancer, bacteria, or fungus. The fluid samples did show more cells than normal with a mixed pattern. Based on all these results, the doctors believed the patient had a lung condition called Cryptogenic Organizing Pneumonia. This is a type of lung swelling with no known cause. The antibiotics were stopped. The patient was started on a steroid medicine called prednisone at 20mg once a day. The patient got better right away. The signs of swelling in the blood went down. The patient left the hospital after 5 days on prednisone. He was told to slowly lower his steroid dose over 6 to 12 months total.

Medical Condition:
Cryptogenic Organizing Pneumonia, a type of lung swelling with no known cause

Treatment:
Prednisone 20mg once a day

Follow-up:
The patient has had no return of symptoms at follow-up visits. His condition has fully cleared up based on exams and scans.

Hospital Course:

The patient came in with a high fever that came and went for three days. He also had bleeding gums and a mild headache. He then became more and more sleepy over time. Tests showed he had a very low platelet count and his red blood cells were breaking apart. The doctors found he had a rare blood disorder called TTP that causes these problems. He was quickly started on a treatment to replace his blood plasma. He also began taking a steroid medicine called prednisolone by mouth.

On the fifth day of being sick, the patient had two seizures where his whole body shook. These seizures then turned into ongoing brain activity problems. He needed to be put on a breathing machine in the intensive care unit. On day 18, he lost strength in both legs and could not control his bladder or bowels. A special scan showed bleeding at several spots along his spine.

The patient had 16 plasma replacement treatments and high doses of steroids. But his platelet count stayed very low. The doctors then looked for other causes. A blood test found high levels of a virus called CMV. He was started on an antiviral medicine called valganciclovir, 450 mg once a day for 21 days. About 6 days after starting this medicine, his platelet count went up. His red blood cells also stopped breaking apart.

The patient's blood tests later returned to normal. The virus was no longer found in his blood. He could walk again with some help. He could also control his bladder and bowels normally again. The patient was moved to a rehab center for more care.

The patient came to Monaldi Hospital to have a small wireless pacemaker put in. The procedure was stopped because readings and images showed the device may have moved. The patient left the hospital in good health. The patient was told to see a doctor for regular checks on the pacemaker.

The patient should see a doctor for regular checks on the pacemaker. No other follow-up steps were given.

None

Discharge Summary

Patient Name: [Redacted]
Date of Admission: [Redacted]
Date of Discharge: [Redacted]

Hospital Course:

The patient is a 68-year-old Japanese man. He had surgery to remove a rare muscle cancer found in the chest area between the lungs. The cancer had spread to the lining of the lungs. Because of this, the patient had radiation treatment and a second surgery. Ten months after surgery, the patient started having pain and numbness in his left arm. A special scan using dye showed two growths at the top of the left lung. One growth was solid and the other was filled with fluid. Radiation and chemotherapy did not work well. Surgery was too risky because it could cause heavy bleeding. So doctors used a heat treatment called RFA to destroy the growths. The doctor inserted a special needle with small hooks into the tumor. The needle sent heat into the tumor to kill the cancer cells. The doctor did this treatment three times total. The heat was started low and slowly increased every 2 minutes each time. The patient was kept awake with numbing medicine only. This let doctors know right away if the patient felt sharp pain in his left arm. The highest heat used was 80 W. The total treatment time was 57 minutes and 14 seconds. A scan done two days later showed the solid growth had gotten smaller. The patient had no pain for about 3 months. His arm also moved better during this time. But the pain in his left arm came back after 3 months. This happened because the tumor started growing again.

Condition at Discharge:

The patient's pain had come back. He was sent home from the hospital. He was told to see his doctor for follow-up care.

Instructions:

The patient should see his doctor to check on his condition.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [REDACTED]
Age: 45 years
Sex: Female
Admission Date: [REDACTED]
Discharge Date: [REDACTED]
Length of Stay: 7 days

Admitting Diagnosis:
A rare type of cancer made of long, thin cells affecting the pancreas

Hospital Course:
The patient was rushed to the hospital because of sudden, severe belly pain and collapse. Doctors found the patient had lost a large amount of blood and was in shock. The belly was swollen and painful to touch. The patient was given blood transfusions and fluids through a vein right away. Blood tests showed very low blood levels at 5g/dl. Imaging tests showed fluid in the belly and a growth near the upper part of the pancreas. Doctors then did emergency surgery to open the belly and find the bleeding. The bleeding came from a growth behind the pancreas that had burst through the lower edge of the pancreas. A tissue sample was taken and tested. The test showed a cancer made of bundles of long, thin cells. This cancer was diagnosed as a rare type called spindle cell sarcoma. The growth was removed during surgery.

Treatment:
The patient stayed in the intensive care unit for 4 days. The patient then received two cancer-fighting drugs called Ifosfamide and Doxorubicin for 6 months after surgery. Before starting these drugs, a special scan with dye was done. The scan showed a growth measuring about 7 by 4.8 by 4.9 centimeters with thin walls attached to the lower edge of the pancreas. The cancer had not spread to other parts of the body.

Outcome:
The patient got better after surgery and left the hospital 7 days after being admitted. The patient was sent to a cancer specialist. Doctors offered surgery to remove the pancreas and the growth. The patient said no to this surgery. The patient received six months of cancer-fighting drugs. The patient died from the disease 18 months after first coming to the hospital.

Summary:
The patient came to the hospital with a rare cancer affecting the pancreas. The cancer was treated with surgery and cancer-fighting drugs given after surgery. The patient left the hospital after staying for 7 days. The patient died from the disease 18 months later.

Discharge Summary

Patient Name: [Name]

Date of Admission: [Date of Admission]

Date of Discharge: [Date of Discharge]

Hospitalized for: Narrowing of the Left Arm Artery

Brief Hospital Course:

The patient, a 4-year-old boy, was admitted after doctors heard an unusual heart sound during a checkup. The doctor found that the pulse in the left arm was weak and blood pressure was low in that arm. The pulse in the right arm was normal. The patient was 100 cm tall. The left arm was 10 mm shorter than the right arm.

A heart ultrasound showed the heart structure was normal. However, it showed the main artery to the left arm was in an unusual position with uneven blood flow. A special scan of the blood vessels was done to confirm what was wrong. The scan showed the artery to the left arm was 70-80% blocked near where it starts. Because one arm was shorter than the other, treatment was needed. The patient was scheduled to have a small tube placed inside the artery to open it up.

The procedure went well, and the patient handled it without problems. A small metal tube was placed inside the narrowed part of the artery. Pictures taken after the procedure showed the tube was in the right place. Blood was flowing well through the left arm artery. The patient received blood-thinning medicine through an IV overnight. The patient went home with aspirin to take by mouth.

At check-up visits 3 and 6 months later, the pulse and blood pressure in the left arm were almost normal. The arm length had improved a lot. An ultrasound of the left arm showed smooth blood flow in the artery. The boy has been checked for 4 years now. There is no longer any difference in arm length.

Discharge Diagnosis: Narrowing of the Left Arm Artery.

Discharge Instructions:

The patient will keep taking aspirin as the doctor ordered. Follow-up visits should be scheduled as the doctor instructs. Parents should keep the patient's medical records up to date. Parents should bring these records to each visit.

Signed,

[Medical Institution]

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [redacted]
DOB: [redacted]
Admission Date: [redacted]
Discharge Date: [redacted]

Medical Diagnosis:
The patient was admitted because blood flow to the leg was suddenly blocked. The patient also had a serious body-wide infection caused by bacteria called Streptococcus dysgalactiae in the blood. Doctors checked for infection in the heart. Heart scans showed growths on the aortic valve and the valve was leaking badly.

Hospital Course:
The patient had emergency surgery to restore blood flow by removing a clot from the left hip area artery. The patient received antibiotics through a vein. Gentamicin was given for 10 days and ceftriaxone for six weeks. Heart surgeons were asked to help. The patient had surgery to replace the aortic valve. Once blood pressure and heart function became steady, the patient was sent to a rehab center. This was one month after first being admitted to the hospital.

Summary of Admission:
The patient is a 56-year-old man. His health history includes untreated hepatitis C liver infection and a bone infection that led to removal of his right fourth toe. He also has a history of alcohol abuse. He came to the hospital with tingling feelings and no pulse in his left leg. Blood tests showed low red blood cells, high white blood cells, low blood clotting cells, and poor kidney function. Blood tests found bacteria called Streptococcus dysgalactiae. A scan of the leg arteries showed major blockages. The patient was treated for blocked blood flow to the leg and serious body-wide infection. Testing confirmed growths on the heart valve.

Discharge Medications:
The patient's medications were ordered by the main doctor. They can be found in the patient's outpatient medical record.

Follow-up care:
The patient should keep seeing his regular doctor and heart surgeon. The patient should also do heart rehab exercises with help from his medical team.

Discharge condition:
The patient left the hospital with steady vital signs and better health. The patient and family were told to come back to the hospital if any new or worse symptoms continue.

Hospital Course:

A 47-year-old male was admitted after a car accident. The patient had a cut on the forehead and was confused. A brain scan and neck X-rays showed no bleeding or swelling in the brain. However, the images showed the neck bones were not stable at the lower neck area. The patient wore a neck brace and was watched closely. Two weeks after being admitted, the patient reported very bad pain in the back of the neck. The patient also had numbness in both arms and hands. Surgery was done to fix the unstable neck bones. During surgery, a metal plate was placed on the front of the neck. Holes were drilled to hold the plate in place. One hole in the upper left area was damaged from drilling too many times. Bone cement was used to fix this problem. This caused a lump to form in the space around the spinal cord. The surgical team quickly removed part of the damaged neck bone to take out the lump. The neck was rebuilt using a metal plate and a support cage from the fifth to seventh neck bones. After surgery, the patient had weakness on the left side. The patient also had trouble straightening the ring and pinky fingers on the left hand. These problems got better on their own without extra treatment.

Discharge Diagnosis:

Neck injury with pressure on the spinal cord. This led to surgery to remove part of a neck bone.

Hospital Course:

The patient was admitted to the hospital after a car accident. During the hospital stay, the patient had surgery to fix unstable bones in the lower neck. There were some problems during the surgery. These problems caused a lump near the spinal cord. Part of a neck bone had to be removed. After surgery, the patient had some weakness and trouble moving fingers on the left hand. These problems got better without extra treatment. The patient left the hospital in good condition. The patient has a follow-up visit scheduled with a spine doctor.

Hospital Course:

This 60-year-old male patient came to our outpatient clinic with skin bumps that had lasted for 1 year. The bumps were yellow, oval-shaped, and skin-colored. They appeared on the chest, back, groin area, arms, and legs. The patient said he first noticed itchy bumps. Then 2 to 3 months later, many more yellow and oval itchy bumps appeared. During the skin exam, doctors found firm, clear-edged, oval bumps. These bumps were skin-colored to yellow. They were located on the upper and lower arms and legs, chest, back, groin area, and belly.

Lab tests checked the blood cells, kidney function, and liver function. All test results came back normal. Doctors took a small skin sample from one bump on the trunk. The sample showed too many mast cells, which are a type of immune cell. These cells had oval and long-shaped centers with clear edges. They were found around tiny blood vessels. This finding matched a condition called mastocytosis. Based on the skin exam and lab results together, doctors determined the patient had a rare type called xanthelasmoid mastocytosis.

The patient received two allergy medicines to control the itching. Cetirizine 10 mg was taken by mouth each night. Fexofenadine 120 mg was taken each morning. These medicines helped stop the itching. However, the skin bumps stayed the same without any changes. Doctors also suggested light therapy treatment. The patient tried this for 1 year, but the bumps did not get much better.

The patient chose not to have more tests like a bone marrow sample. The patient also chose not to try other treatments. The patient decided to end care at this time. The patient was told to watch the bumps and see a doctor if they change or get worse. The patient left the hospital with no problems.

Discharge Summary

Patient: 4-month-old male unneutered Labrador

Hospital Course:

The patient came in with several small skin cuts on the lower legs, ankles, and base of the tail. During the exam, the dog appeared healthy with normal bone growth. Several fluid-filled bumps were found near the injured skin areas (ankles, tail base). Fluid samples from these bumps showed a moderate amount of red blood cells with some white blood cells and cell debris. These results suggested the bumps were pockets of blood or fluid, and the dog was given an antibiotic and a pain and swelling medication.

Two months later, the patient was seen again for ongoing fluid pockets and joint problems. The joints were found to bend too far, moving beyond the normal range. The skin also stretched too much and tore easily. A skin stretch test showed 23.5% stretch, which is higher than the normal limit of 14.5%. Blood tests showed slightly low red blood cells, low protein levels, and low albumin (a type of protein). Other blood results showed high phosphorus, slightly high liver enzyme levels, and low waste product levels. These other results were considered normal for a young dog.

Discharge Diagnosis:

The patient was believed to have an inherited disease affecting the body's connective tissue.

Treatment:

The patient received an antibiotic and a pain and swelling medication. The owners chose to humanely put the patient to sleep because of the ongoing joint looseness and skin cuts.

Follow-up Plan:

None.

Discharge Summary

Patient Name: [REDACTED]
Medical Record Number: [REDACTED]
Date of Admission: [REDACTED]
Date of Discharge: [REDACTED]

Hospital Course:
The patient came to a specialized center for a condition where tissue similar to the uterus lining grows in other places. The patient had pain during sex and belly pain. A physical exam, vaginal ultrasound, and MRI scan showed a growth deep in the tissue at the top of the vagina. The patient had surgery through small cuts in the belly to remove the growth using a special cutting tool. After the surgery, the patient came to the emergency room with vaginal pain and bloody discharge after having sex. The exam showed that the surgical cut at the top of the vagina had opened up. A small part of the intestine could be seen through the opening. Doctors closed the inner lining and put the intestine back in place. The patient came back for a check-up. The surgical cut at the top of the vagina had partly opened again. The inner lining could be seen through the opening. Doctors used a different method to fix it a second time. They trimmed the edges of the vaginal tissue to help it heal better. They closed the vagina in two layers. They also used a piece of fatty tissue from the belly to cover and protect the repair. This tissue was placed in the pelvis and attached loosely to the closure with stitches.

Diagnosis:
Deep tissue growth at the top of the vagina with opening of the surgical cut.

Treatment:
Surgery through small belly cuts to remove the tissue growth using a special cutting tool. Putting the intestine back in place. Trimming the vaginal edges and closing the vagina in two layers with a piece of fatty belly tissue to protect the repair.

Condition at Discharge:
Stable.

Follow-Up Care:
The patient was told to come to follow-up appointments, have regular check-ups, and follow the treatment plan.

Discharge Medications:
None prescribed.

Discharge Instructions:
The patient was told not to have sex for six weeks after the second repair. The patient was told to watch for any signs that the surgical cut at the top of the vagina might open again. The patient was told to come to the scheduled follow-up appointments. If there is an emergency, the patient was told to get medical help right away.

Discharge Summary:

This is a discharge summary for a 50-year-old male with a history of diabetes, high blood pressure, and kidney failure. He was admitted to the hospital in December 2020 with fever, less urine than normal, and pain on the right side below the ribs. First tests showed a big increase in infection-fighting cells and swelling markers in the blood.

A scan of the belly showed several swollen lymph nodes with dead tissue near the pancreas and liver. These nodes had grown larger compared to an earlier scan in March 2020. The patient was sent for a test where doctors used a camera and needle to take a small tissue sample from the swollen lymph nodes near the pancreas. The tissue sample showed signs of tuberculosis with clusters of special cells that form when the body fights this infection. A lab test on the tissue confirmed the patient had tuberculosis.

The patient started taking medicine to treat tuberculosis and this helped him feel much better. Follow-up scans showed the swollen lymph nodes near the pancreas and liver had gotten smaller. The patient felt much better with no more fevers or belly pain. A kidney transplant is planned for the patient after he finishes his tuberculosis treatment.

Overall, the patient was discharged in better health after being treated for tuberculosis. More doctor visits are needed to make sure the patient fully recovers.

Discharge Summary: Patient 2

Patient 2 is a 45-year-old woman. She came to the hospital in February 2016 with headaches and vomiting. Scans of her head showed a growth inside her brain. Doctors did surgery to remove the growth. Tests on the removed tissue showed a type of cancer called non-Hodgkin lymphoma. This is a cancer that affects the body's infection-fighting system.

In March 2016, the patient had radiation treatment to her whole brain. A brain scan after treatment showed the affected areas had gotten smaller. These areas were in the left side of her brain and in parts that connect the two sides.

In May 2016, the patient had two rounds of cancer-killing drug treatment. Two weeks later, the right side of her body became weak. This got worse until she could not move her right side at all. Doctors gave her medicines to reduce brain swelling. These medicines did not help much. A brain scan showed more swelling in the left side of her brain.

In July 2016, the patient started taking a pill called apatinib. Her right side weakness got much better. She could move normally again. Her headaches, upset stomach, and vomiting went away.

More information about the patient's health history, treatment, test results, medicines, and scans is in her medical record.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [REDACTED]
Date of Admission: [REDACTED]
Date of Discharge: [REDACTED]

Hospital Course Summary:

The patient was a 50-year-old Chinese male who came in with a cough and black mucus for about 2 weeks. Sometimes the patient also coughed up blood and had trouble breathing. A special X-ray scan of the chest showed a rough-edged mass about 32×22×10 mm in the upper part of the right lung. The patient had surgery to remove the upper part of the right lung and nearby lymph nodes. After surgery, doctors found a rare type of lung cancer called giant cell carcinoma-like tumor. Lab tests on the tumor cells showed positive results for certain markers called cytokeratin and vimentin. Tests for other markers called chromogranin A and synaptophysin were negative.

The patient had long-term health problems, including 10 years of swollen airways and damaged air sacs in the lungs. The patient smoked for many years, equal to one pack a day for 30 years. No one in the patient's family had lung cancer before. The patient received cancer-fighting drugs called gemcitabine and cisplatin for four rounds of treatment. The patient had full body scans every year at a local hospital. Seven years after surgery, the patient was still alive with no signs of the cancer coming back.

The patient did well during the hospital stay. The treatment worked well, and the patient was watched closely over many years. The patient talked clearly with the care team during the stay. The patient followed the treatment plan and helped plan for going home. The care team talked about the need to stop smoking and gave the patient information on how to quit.

Diagnoses:

1. Giant cell carcinoma-like tumor of the lung, a rare type of lung cancer.

Discharge Medications:

None.

Follow-Up Care:

The patient should keep going to yearly check-up visits at a local hospital to watch for any changes. The patient should also keep trying to stop smoking.

Discharge Summary:

Age: 30 years
Gender: Female
Date of Admission: [REDACTED]
Date of Discharge: [REDACTED]
Diagnosis: A fast-growing blood cancer that starts in certain white blood cells called T cells

Hospital Course:
The patient came to Ondokuz Mayis University Hospital because of lumps that could be felt in both breasts. Breast x-rays showed areas that looked denser than normal in the upper outer parts of both breasts. An ultrasound test showed lumps with uneven edges. Both armpits had swollen lymph nodes, thicker skin, and signs of fluid buildup in the breast tissue. This pointed to swelling in the breasts. The patient got much better after receiving the cancer-fighting drugs. The patient was ready to go home.

The patient should see their cancer doctor at the scheduled times for more care and checkups. The patient may need more imaging tests and blood tests if the doctor thinks they are needed. The patient should stay healthy, stay away from people who are sick, and exercise regularly.

The patient went home with instructions about how to take medicines and when to come back for checkups.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: XXX

Date of Admission: XX/XX/XXXX              Date of Discharge: XX/XX/XXXX

Admitting Diagnosis: Confusion

Hospital Course:

A 62-year-old African-American male with a history of schizophrenia and confusion was brought to the emergency room. During the exam, he was very sleepy, had low blood pressure, low blood sugar, and a fast heartbeat. Blood tests showed very low red blood cell counts, low blood cell counts overall, high iron storage levels, and high levels of a protein called CD25. A test of the bone marrow showed too many cells and signs that the body was attacking its own blood cells. This raised concern for a condition called HLH, where the immune system attacks the body. A heart ultrasound showed no signs of infection on the heart valves. Tests for viruses, HIV, hepatitis, and other infections all came back negative.

The patient was given a steroid medicine called dexamethasone because his liver was not working well. This treatment helped him get much better. The patient was taken off the breathing machine. The steroid medicine was slowly reduced over time. His liver test results, blood clotting tests, platelet counts, and iron levels all got better over time. After 31 days in the hospital, the patient was sent home.

Follow-Up Plan:

The patient was told to see his regular doctor for ongoing care. He was given a list of his current medicines. The patient was told to schedule a visit with his regular doctor to check on his health. This includes checking if he needs treatment to help his kidneys work.

Instructions to the Patient:

The patient was told to keep taking his medicines as directed. He should see his regular doctor for routine check-ups. The patient was told to live a healthy lifestyle and exercise regularly. This will help manage his condition and prevent future problems.

Summary:

The patient was found to have HLH, a condition where the immune system attacks the body. He was treated with a steroid medicine called dexamethasone. After 31 days in the hospital, the patient was sent home. He was told to follow up with his regular doctor. The patient was told to keep taking his medicines and live a healthy lifestyle to manage his condition and prevent future problems.

Hospital Course:

The ten-year-old female patient came to the hospital because she had trouble walking and stiffness in both legs for the past six months. During the physical exam, doctors found her muscles were stiff and jerky when moved. All four limbs had higher than normal muscle tightness. Her leg strength was slightly weak. She also had shaking when holding a position and muscle spasms that caused twisting movements. Her reflexes were stronger than normal when tested. Her ability to feel touch, her brain nerve function, and her balance were all normal. The patient was diagnosed with a movement disorder that responds to medicine called dopa-responsive dystonia. Doctors knew this because her symptoms got worse as the day went on. They gave her a test dose of levodopa and carbidopa medicine. Her muscle spasms got much better within two days. She was treated with three medicines called Levodopa, Carbidopa, and Trihexyphenidyl.

Discharge Summary:

The ten-year-old female patient came to the hospital with trouble walking and stiff legs that caused her to fall often. Her muscles were stiff and jerky when moved. She had increased muscle tightness, slight weakness, shaking when holding still, and twisting muscle spasms in all four limbs. Her reflexes were stronger than normal. Her ability to feel touch, brain nerve function, and balance were all normal. The patient was diagnosed with dopa-responsive dystonia. Her symptoms got worse as the day went on. She got much better after taking levodopa and carbidopa medicine. The medicine was continued and the patient kept getting better. A gene test was planned but could not be done because of limited resources. The patient left the hospital in good condition and will come back for a follow-up visit.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Identification:
The patient is a 38-year-old man who came to the hospital with painful joint swelling in his left wrist.

Admission and Hospital Course:
When the patient arrived, doctors checked his left wrist. They removed fluid from the joint and found tiny crystals that cause gout. The patient had gout before in his ankles and left knee. He also broke his left wrist in a car accident in the past. Doctors first tried a medicine called Colchicine at 2 mg per day. This did not help control his gout symptoms. Then doctors gave him a medicine called Anakinra. The patient got better quickly after this treatment. At a checkup 7 days after the first shot, his left wrist was still a little swollen and sore. His ankle and knee felt fine with no symptoms. Doctors then started him on a medicine called allopurinol.

Diagnosis:
The patient was diagnosed with gout, a type of joint swelling caused by crystal buildup.

Treatment:
The patient was treated with Anakinra and allopurinol.

Discharge Condition:
The patient's left wrist got better. It had only a little swelling and soreness when he left the hospital. The patient was told to keep taking allopurinol. He was also told to go to his follow-up visit with his doctor.

Follow-Up Care:
The patient was told to see his doctor about further care and treatment for his gout if needed.

Prognosis:
The patient's outlook is good. He responded well to Anakinra. His ankles and left knee have no symptoms.

Other:
Doctors reviewed the patient's health history. It relates to his current condition. The patient said he has no allergies to medicines or foods. The care team checked all medicines to make sure the prescriptions were correct when the patient left the hospital.

Hospital Course:
The patient, a 5-year-old Chinese girl, came to the emergency room with cough, fever, headache, vomiting, and unusual behavior with her parents. She was placed in the children's intensive care unit. Doctors found she had a serious blood infection and a lung infection. She received antibiotics to fight infection, medicine to boost her immune system, and limited fluids. The patient got worse and fell into a deep sleep state where she could not wake up. Her blood pressure dropped too low. Her heart beat in an uneven pattern and her oxygen levels fell too low. A heart test showed her heart's electrical signals were too slow. Blood tests showed she had an underactive thyroid gland that was never treated. This was caused by her own immune system attacking her thyroid gland. Doctors quickly started giving her thyroid medicine called levothyroxine through a tube in her nose to her stomach. She also received medicine to raise her blood pressure, a machine to help her breathe, and a machine to help clean her blood like her kidneys would. Two days after starting the thyroid medicine, she woke up and her body temperature went back to normal. The breathing tube was removed on the fifth day after starting the thyroid medicine. Her thyroid medicine dose was lowered before she went home. She left the hospital taking thyroid medicine once a day at a dose of 3 micrograms per kilogram per day.

Discharge Summary:

She developed a serious blood infection and a lung infection. She was treated with antibiotics to fight infection, medicine to boost her immune system, and limited fluids. She got worse and fell into a deep sleep state where she could not wake up. Her blood pressure dropped too low. Her heart beat in an uneven pattern and her oxygen levels fell too low. Doctors found she had an underactive thyroid gland that was never treated. This was caused by her own immune system attacking her thyroid gland. Doctors quickly started giving her thyroid medicine. The patient received thyroid medicine called levothyroxine, medicine to raise her blood pressure, a machine to help her breathe, and a machine to help clean her blood. Two days after starting the thyroid medicine, she woke up and her body temperature went back to normal. The breathing tube was removed on the fifth day after starting the thyroid medicine. She left the hospital taking thyroid medicine once a day at a dose of 3 micrograms per kilogram per day. Doctors told the family to get their thyroid glands tested. Her father and grandmother were found to have the same thyroid condition.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: Undisclosed

Date of Admission: Undisclosed

Date of Discharge: Undisclosed

Admission Diagnosis: Draining wounds on the lower front part of the belly

Discharge Diagnosis: Infection caused by two types of bacteria called Mycobacterium szulgai and M. intermedium

Hospital Course:

The patient is a 46-year-old woman. She had surgery to remove her appendix using small cuts in 1998. For the past two years, she had draining wounds on the lower front part of her belly. The cut from her surgery did not heal the right way. It opened up again after one month. She took many antibiotic medicines by mouth and by injection on and off. But doctors did not find the exact cause of the infection before this hospital stay. The patient had no history of injury to the area. She did not take medicines that weaken the body's defense system. She did not have tuberculosis.

When the patient came to the hospital, doctors saw an old surgery scar on the lower front part of her belly. A large raised scar had formed over it. There were six small tunnel openings on the lower front part of her belly. One of these tunnels was releasing thick fluid at the time. The area over and around these tunnels was sore to touch. Tests of the fluid showed bacteria. After testing which medicines would work best, doctors started the patient on three medicines called rifampicin, ethambutol, and clarithromycin.

After one month of treatment, the tunnel stopped releasing fluid. The patient was told to keep taking the medicines and come back in another month. After two months of treatment, the patient was doing well with no more fluid coming out.

Discharge Medications:

The patient was told to keep taking rifampicin 600 mg once a day, ethambutol 600 mg once a day, and clarithromycin 500 mg two times a day.

Follow-Up:

The patient was told to keep coming back for checkups. How often depends on how well she is healing and what tests show.

Patient Name: [Redacted]

Medical Record Number: [Redacted]

Date of Admission: February 2017

Date of Discharge: N/A

Chief Complaint:
Cancer that came back in the neck

History of Present Illness:
The patient is a 49-year-old woman. She was told she had thyroid cancer in September 2009. Thyroid cancer starts in the thyroid gland in the neck. She had four neck surgeries and two radiation treatments by May 2015. In August 2014, doctors found that radiation treatment no longer worked for her cancer. In February 2017, she came back to the hospital because the cancer returned in her neck. A special scan showed the cancer had come back in several spots in her neck. The scan also showed the cancer had spread to her lungs and behind her left shoulder blade.

Hospital Course:
From March to August 2017, the patient joined a research study testing a drug called anlotinib. This study compared the drug to a sugar pill with no medicine in it. The patient got the sugar pill at first. Her cancer got worse during this time.

In September 2017, the patient started taking the real anlotinib drug. Doctors checked her scans every two treatment rounds for the first 12 rounds. After that, they checked every four rounds. The treated tumors were under the muscle on the right side of her neck and behind her left shoulder blade. Other tumors in her neck and lungs were not treated.

The patient took anlotinib for 52 treatment rounds in total. The treated tumors shrank by almost 94 percent. No new tumors appeared. The patient had some side effects during the study. These included high blood pressure, fast heartbeat, twitching in hands and feet, loose stools, skin problems on hands and feet, and headaches. Most side effects were mild to moderate. Most were controlled with medicine.

Diagnosis:
Thyroid cancer that came back, with spread to the lungs and shoulder blade area

Treatment:
The patient had several neck surgeries and two radiation treatments before joining the anlotinib research study.

Hospital Course:

The patient is a five-year-old girl. She came to the hospital with a lump on her lower left back. A special scan called an MRI was done. The scan showed a growth with many small bumps under the skin. This growth was on her lower back, near the spine. Doctors did surgery to remove the growth. The removed tissue was looked at under a microscope. It showed a growth made of long, thin cells bundled together. The final diagnosis was plexiform schwannoma. This is a type of non-cancer nerve tumor. The patient had no symptoms after surgery. At her one-year checkup, the growth had not come back.

Discharge Summary:

The patient was diagnosed with plexiform schwannoma. This is a non-cancer nerve tumor. Surgery to remove it was successful. The patient had no symptoms after surgery. At the one-year checkup, the growth had not come back. More checkups are recommended based on standard guidelines. The family and patient were given information about future checkups. They were also told what warning signs to watch for. The patient left the hospital in stable condition.

Discharge Summary:

Medical History:
The patient is a 65-year-old man with a history of diabetes and long-term heavy alcohol use. He came to the emergency room because he was vomiting blood and had black, tarry stools for the past 24 hours. Doctors found that his liver was enlarged and showed signs of long-term liver damage. He had bleeding in his stomach and food pipe from swollen veins. He had a procedure to tie off the bleeding veins using a flexible tube with a camera.

Hospital Course:
The skin on both arms and both legs started turning black. This spread quickly and became large areas of dying tissue that leaked fluid. Doctors believed a medicine called terlipressin caused this problem. They stopped giving this medicine, and the skin damage stopped spreading further up the limbs. The patient received treatment including bandage changes, medicines to fight infection, and fluids through a vein. Doctors told the patient he needed surgery to remove his toes and fingers to stop the damage from spreading and prevent a serious blood infection. The patient said no to this surgery. Fifteen days later, the patient died at home from a serious blood infection.

Follow-up:
There is no follow-up information because the patient left the hospital against medical advice.

Discharge Summary

Hospital Course:

The patient is a 6-year-old girl with a partial form of Turner syndrome. Turner syndrome is a genetic condition that affects girls. She was sent to a heart doctor because of her genetic condition. During the physical exam, doctors noticed she was shorter than average. She also had moles on her skin and walked with her feet wider apart than usual. A heart ultrasound showed that parts of her heart muscle were too thick. The lower left part of her heart had a spongy look. The heart ultrasound raised concern for a condition where the heart muscle does not form properly. Doctors ordered a special heart scan using magnets to get a better look. This scan showed extra finger-like tissue in parts of the lower left heart chamber. The results confirmed that the patient has a heart condition where the muscle did not fully develop before birth.

Medical Management:

The patient is being watched carefully without treatment because she has no symptoms. Her follow-up visits with the heart doctor show her heart is pumping well. The right side of her heart pumps out 54 percent of its blood with each beat. The left side pumps out 53 percent. She is seeing several different specialists as an outpatient.

Plan:

The patient should keep seeing her heart doctor regularly to check how well her heart is working. She should continue seeing her team of different specialists as an outpatient.

Recommended Follow-up:

The patient should keep seeing her heart doctor regularly to check how well her heart is working.

Hospital Course:

The patient is a 70-year-old woman with heart failure, an irregular heartbeat, and kidney disease that needs dialysis. She came to the surgery clinic because a scan showed an abnormal tunnel between her gallbladder and part of her large intestine. Doctors found this tunnel by accident while checking for bleeding in her stomach area. She had pain in her upper right back that did not get worse after eating. Her belly did not hurt when pressed, and her liver tests came back normal.

Medical Management:

The patient stayed in the hospital to have surgery to fix the abnormal tunnel and remove her gallbladder. Doctors used a robotic surgery system for the operation. During surgery, they found swollen tissue connecting the bottom of the gallbladder to the large intestine. They carefully separated these two organs. The gallbladder was removed from top to bottom, and the surgeon made sure to clearly see all important parts. Small clips were placed on the tube and blood vessel connected to the gallbladder, and then these were cut. The small opening in the large intestine was closed with two layers of stitches.

Outcome:

The patient healed well with no problems. She went home two days after surgery. Lab tests on the removed tissue showed no cancer. The patient came back to the clinic for a follow-up visit and had no complaints or concerns.

Hospital Course Summary:

Admission Date: [insert date]
Discharge Date: [insert date]

Patient Information:
The patient is a 48-year-old male. He was admitted for treatment of kidney cancer that had spread to the liver. The patient was started on two medicines that help the immune system fight cancer, called ipilimumab and nivolumab. The patient also received targeted radiation treatment to the main tumor.

Medical History:
The patient had no other health problems before being diagnosed with kidney cancer.

Hospital Course:
During the hospital stay, the patient had signs that the kidneys were not working as well as they should. Blood tests showed higher waste levels and lower filtering ability. This was treated with two medicines called prednisone and mycophenolate. The patient's kidney function slowly got better over six weeks. Scans at that time showed very good results. All the tumors had gotten smaller. The patient chose to have surgery to remove the affected kidney.

Discharge Plan:
The patient received instructions before leaving the hospital. He was told to schedule regular visits with his kidney and bladder doctor. The patient is doing well with no signs of cancer. No more treatment is needed at this time.

Summary:
The patient was admitted for treatment of kidney cancer that had spread to the liver. The patient received two immune system medicines, ipilimumab and nivolumab, along with targeted radiation to the main tumor. The patient developed kidney problems, which were treated with prednisone and mycophenolate. Scans showed the tumors responded very well to treatment. The patient had surgery to remove the affected kidney. The patient is doing well with no signs of cancer. No more treatment is needed at this time.

Hospital Course:

The patient came to the emergency room feeling very weak and not eating well. Her health history includes diabetes, high blood pressure, severe joint pain from worn cartilage, and a recent bladder infection treated with antibiotics.

The physical exam showed she was low on body fluids and had low blood pressure. Blood tests showed high calcium levels, high waste product levels in the blood, and low magnesium levels. The patient was diagnosed with a serious blood infection from a bladder infection and moved to the intensive care unit. She received antibiotics and large amounts of fluids through an IV, which helped her vital signs become stable.

On the third day in the hospital, the patient's calcium level went down after receiving salt water fluids and a hormone medicine called calcitonin. However, the calcium level started going up again after three days of calcitonin treatment. More tests, including a special scan of the chest and belly and a full body bone scan, showed no cancer.

Blood tests showed that the systems controlling calcium and certain hormones were not working well, and low function of the adrenal glands may have caused her high calcium levels.

Treatment with a steroid medicine called hydrocortisone was started on the tenth day in the hospital and brought her calcium levels back to normal. Her weakness and poor appetite got better after that. The patient did not return for follow-up visits, and regular checks of bone strength were recommended.

The patient came to the hospital for treatment of a dangerous fast heart rhythm. He also has a condition where the heart muscle is too thick. Two months ago, he had a small device put in his chest. This device can shock the heart back to a normal rhythm if needed. He got this device after his identical twin brother died from a sudden heart stoppage. The patient fainted without warning while at work on a ladder. Before fainting, he felt dizzy.

Physical Examination:
The physical exam showed nothing unusual. All vital signs like blood pressure and heart rate were normal.

A heart ultrasound done two months before showed the heart was normal in size. The heart was pumping well. The wall between the heart chambers was too thick at 2.8 cm. There was no blockage of blood flow leaving the heart. An urgent test of the heart blood vessels showed no major blockages. A heart rhythm monitor worn three years ago showed no episodes of fast heart rhythm.

Hospital Course and Treatment:
The patient stayed in the intensive care unit with heart monitoring. He was started on a medicine called sotalol. No more dangerous fast heart rhythms were seen on the heart monitor. He went home on day 4 with a plan for follow-up visits.

Follow-Up Plan:
The patient has an appointment to see the doctor after leaving the hospital. The doctor will check his condition. The doctor will also keep managing his thick heart muscle disease and heart risk factors.

Summary:
This is a 62-year-old male who came in with a dangerous fast heart rhythm. He has a condition where the heart muscle is too thick. Two months ago, he had a small shocking device put in his chest. He got this device after his identical twin brother died from sudden heart stoppage. He stayed in the intensive care unit and was started on a medicine called sotalol. The patient went home after treatment. He has a follow-up appointment scheduled.

Hospital Course:
The patient is an 89-year-old man. He came to the hospital because he was coughing and coughing up blood. The patient had a lung condition called widened airways in the right middle part of his lung for 30 years. One month before coming to the hospital, the patient coughed up a large amount of blood. Doctors blocked the bleeding blood vessel to stop it. But the patient started coughing up blood again and came to our hospital. Doctors used a small camera to look inside the patient's airways. They saw active bleeding from the right middle part of the lung. They used cold treatment and medicine to stop the bleeding for a short time.

Management:
The next day, doctors placed a small tube called a stent to keep the airway open. The stent was about 8 mm wide and 3 cm long. They used a gripping tool and tried several times to put it in place. They also placed another custom-made tube in a lower part of the right lung. This second tube helped keep the first one from moving out of place. The bleeding stopped right away after the tubes were placed. The patient took medicine to fight infection. The patient did not develop lung blockage or infection.

Outcome:
One month after the tubes were placed, the right middle and lower parts of the lung collapsed. Fluid also built up around the right lung. The patient had another procedure to remove the tube from the lower right airway. Doctors also drained the fluid from around the lung using a needle. A scan of the chest showed the right lower part of the lung opened back up. The patient did not cough up any more blood during the next three months. The patient left the hospital ten days after the tube was removed.

The patient was sent home and told to continue pregnancy care with her regular doctor. No other tests were done to check for swollen veins in the food pipe or blood flow tests of the arms and legs. Hospital Course: The patient, a 50-year-old male, came to Dankook University Dental Hospital. He had pain and swelling at his left jaw joint. X-rays showed many small solid masses around the joint. The patient had pain on his own and when opening his mouth. He also had swelling at the left jaw joint. He did not have soreness when touched or trouble opening his mouth. Doctors did surgery while the patient was fully asleep. They removed about 120 loose pieces from the joint. Lab tests on the removed pieces confirmed the diagnosis of synovial chondromatosis. An X-ray taken after surgery showed some flat, thickened bone still in the joint area. No loose pieces remained. The patient felt better after surgery. Discharge Summary

Patient: 22-year-old male

Hospital Course:
The patient came in with muscle loss and shaking in both hands and forearms. These problems started slowly about 5 years ago. Cold weather made the symptoms worse. The doctor's exam showed muscle loss in both hands and forearms that looked the same on each side. The patient had weaker grip and trouble moving fingers and wrists. Reflexes in the affected areas were also lower than normal. Nerve and muscle tests showed long-term damage to the nerves that control movement in both arms. Pictures of the spine taken while the neck was straight showed the neck curve was flatter than normal. These pictures also showed the spinal cord was smaller than normal at the middle of the neck. Pictures taken while the neck was bent forward showed a wider space behind the spinal cord. This space lit up on the scan when dye was used. The space lit up less when the neck was straight. After looking at all the test results, the doctors found the patient has Hirayama Disease. The patient was treated without surgery.

Diagnosis:
Hirayama Disease, a rare condition that causes muscle weakness and loss in the hands and forearms

Summary:
The patient's symptoms matched Hirayama Disease. The diagnosis was confirmed by spine pictures taken while bending the neck forward. The patient was treated without surgery and is now going home. The patient should continue to be watched by doctors and come back for check-up visits.

Patient Information:
Name: [Patient's name]
Gender: Female
Age: 38 years

Hospital Course Summary:
The patient came in with painful, red, raised skin bumps on the right forearm along with fever. Over time, these bumps joined together to form larger patches. The patient had a cold before this happened and had similar skin problems three years ago. During the exam, doctors found a large red patch on the right upper arm. There were also smaller red patches on both arms, the right side of the neck, and the chest. Some patches had a bumpy surface that looked like a mountain range. All the patches felt warm to the touch. The nerves near the skin were normal and the patient could feel touch on the patches normally. A skin sample test showed a buildup of white blood cells called neutrophils in the upper layer of skin. There were no signs of blood vessel damage.

Treatment:
The patient first took a pill called dapsone 100 mg at bedtime. The skin got much better quickly. But the problem came back when the patient stopped taking the medicine. For the second round, the patient took dapsone along with a steroid pill called prednisolone. The prednisolone started at 30 mg per day. The dose was slowly lowered over 4 weeks. The patient's skin has now cleared up and the patient is going home.

Follow-Up Instructions:
The patient should see their regular doctor for more checkups and care.

Summary:
The patient came in with red, raised, painful skin bumps and fever after having a cold. A skin sample test showed a buildup of white blood cells in the upper layer of skin with no blood vessel damage. The patient first took dapsone 100 mg at bedtime and got better quickly. The problem came back when the medicine was stopped. For the second round, the patient took dapsone with prednisolone starting at 30 mg per day. The steroid dose was slowly lowered over 4 weeks. The patient's skin has now cleared up and the patient is going home. The patient should follow up with their regular doctor.

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted to the hospital to treat a very large liver tumor. She had surgery to remove the right side of her liver. During surgery, doctors removed two slow-growing liver cancers. The patient healed well after surgery and went home 17 days later.

Past Medical History:
The patient had no major health problems before this.

Hospital Course:
The patient felt bloating in her belly and did not want to eat. Doctors did an ultrasound of her belly and found a very large mass in the right side of her liver. A physical exam showed her liver was larger than normal. Blood tests showed bile was backing up in her liver but she was not yellow. Her liver enzyme levels were slightly high. Tests for liver infections came back negative. A blood test for a liver cancer marker showed very high levels. An ultrasound showed a very large dark mass in the right side of the liver measuring about 139 by 120 millimeters. A special scan with dye showed a huge mass taking up the right side of the liver. The mass lit up unevenly at first and then evenly as blood flowed through. A dark area in the center showed dead tissue inside the tumor. Based on these images, doctors believed it was liver cancer. The surgery team also found that the patient was born without a certain blood vessel in her liver called the portal vein type two.

Disposition and Follow-up:
The patient went home 17 days after surgery. Seven months later, doctors found a small new liver cancer spot. They treated it using heat therapy to destroy the cancer cells. The patient has been checked regularly for 6 months and shows no signs of more cancer coming back.
