Hospital Course:

The patient came in with pain on the thumb side of the left wrist. This was caused by a small wrist bone that did not heal properly and a broken metal screw inside. During the exam, the patient could move the wrist 30 degrees up and 40 degrees down. The patient could also tilt the wrist 20 degrees toward the thumb and 30 degrees toward the pinky. X-rays and a CT scan showed the broken bone and the broken screw. Two hand surgery specialists did the operation. They removed the old screw and put in a new one in a better position. The new screw was 2.8 millimeters wide. The surgeons also took a small piece of bone from the lower arm near the wrist. They packed this bone graft into the gap to help the bone heal.

The patient went home with a removable wrist and thumb splint to wear for two weeks. A hard cast was also put on after surgery. After three months, the wrist pain was gone. The patient could bend the wrist back 60 degrees and forward 40 degrees. X-rays at three months showed the bone was healing well with no bone loss. The patient went back to work five months after surgery and the wrist worked well. A CT scan at nine months showed new bone had grown across the break.

Diagnosis:

A small wrist bone that did not heal properly and a broken metal screw inside.

Treatment:

Two hand surgery specialists did the operation. They removed the old screw and put in a new one in a better position. The new screw was 2.8 millimeters wide. The surgeons also took a small piece of bone from the lower arm near the wrist. They packed this bone graft into the gap to help the bone heal.

Follow-up:

The patient was checked on for 14 months after surgery.

Discharge Summary:

Patient: 53-year-old male nurse found to have hepatitis C virus infection

Hospital Course:
In January 2011, the patient was seen at the Outpatient Infectious Diseases clinic because of abnormal liver test results. His hepatitis C virus level was 660,000 units per milliliter, type 3a. A small sample of liver tissue showed ongoing liver swelling with moderate damage and mild to moderate scarring. The patient was a good fit for treatment and began taking two medicines called PEG-IFN-α-2a and ribavirin in March 2011. The patient handled the treatment well. The virus was no longer found in the blood by week four. It stayed gone during the full 24 weeks of treatment. Liver test results returned to normal within the first 3 weeks. The patient had follow-up visits until September 2012. A new liver tissue sample showed less damage and less scarring than before.

Hospitalization:
Nine weeks after finishing the antiviral treatment, the patient developed joint swelling on both sides of the body. The patient had pain and swelling in the wrists, knees, shoulders, and finger joints. The patient also had stiffness in the morning that lasted a long time. An MRI scan showed bone damage and bone thinning near the joints in the wrist, knee, and hand. These findings led to a diagnosis of rheumatoid arthritis, a disease where the body attacks its own joints. Blood tests for rheumatoid factor and another marker for this disease were both positive.

Treatment:
The patient was treated with prednisone, a steroid, and pain relievers for two months. After that, the patient took methotrexate and sulfasalazine. The patient responded quickly and well to this treatment.

Discharge:
The patient went home in good condition with prescriptions for methotrexate and sulfasalazine. The patient should follow up with a joint specialist and a stomach and liver specialist.

Hospital Course:

The patient is a 79-year-old male with advanced prostate cancer who came to the hospital with a growth on the opening of his penis. A tissue sample showed a type of skin cancer called squamous cell carcinoma. The patient had surgery to remove part of his penis and nearby lymph nodes. Lymph nodes are small glands that help fight infection. The surgery found cancer in three out of seven lymph nodes on the right side of his groin. The cancer was staged as T2N2M0, meaning it had spread to nearby lymph nodes but not to other parts of the body. The patient received cancer-killing drugs called carboplatin and paclitaxel at low doses. He also received radiation treatment to the right groin area.

Nine months later, the cancer came back and spread to lymph nodes again. The patient received more cancer-killing drugs and radiation with the goal of curing the cancer. This included another round of low dose carboplatin and paclitaxel. Radiation was given to the left pelvic area. He responded well at first, but the cancer eventually grew again. The doctors then considered a different treatment called atezolizumab. This drug helps the body's defense system fight cancer.

After about two years on atezolizumab, the patient developed a skin condition called bullous pemphigoid. This causes blisters and is a known side effect of this type of drug. The patient was given a steroid medicine called prednisone. His blistering went away quickly.

At the time of this report, the cancer has almost completely gone away. The patient has stopped treatment for now. Follow-up appointments have been scheduled to check on his progress.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [REDACTED]

Age/Sex: 29/Female

Medical Record Number: [REDACTED]

Admission Date: [REDACTED]

Discharge Date: [REDACTED]

Admitting Diagnosis: Achalasia (a condition where the tube that carries food to the stomach does not work properly)

Hospital Course:

The patient was a 29-year-old female who had trouble swallowing that got worse over time. She came to the hospital because swallowing became very difficult. The patient was told she had achalasia three years ago but chose not to get treatment. About a month before coming to the hospital, her regular doctor gave her iron pills. After taking the pills for three weeks, her swallowing problems became much worse. She was sent to a stomach and digestive system doctor for more tests.

When the patient arrived, she had no pain when swallowing, no upset stomach, and no throwing up. The physical exam showed nothing unusual.

The patient had an X-ray test where she swallowed a special liquid. This showed a widened food tube with a narrowed bottom that looked like a bird's beak. It also showed something stuck in the lower part of the food tube. A camera test was done to look inside the food tube. This showed the food tube was widened. There was an oval-shaped, black mass stuck in the lower part of the food tube. The mass was made of the iron pills that had clumped together. There were no sores inside the food tube. The muscle at the bottom of the food tube was very tight.

The doctors tried to break up the mass and push it into the stomach. They had to stop because the tight muscle made it too risky. There was also a chance food could go into the lungs. The doctors used a small basket tool to pull the mass out instead.

A test was done to measure how well the food tube muscles work. The results matched the diagnosis of achalasia. In a later procedure, the doctors stretched the tight muscle using a balloon. The balloon was about 1.2 inches wide. The procedure worked well.

The patient had no symptoms during the 3 years of check-ups after treatment.

Discharge Condition:

The patient got better after the balloon stretching treatment. The patient left the hospital in good condition. The patient was told to see her stomach and digestive system doctor at her scheduled visits.

Discharge Medications:

None

Follow-up:

The patient was told to see her stomach and digestive system doctor at her scheduled visits.

Discharge Summary:

Patient: 79-year-old male

Reason for Admission: Trouble swallowing that was getting worse and weight loss

Medical History: None provided

Hospital Course:

When the patient came to the hospital, he had several symptoms. These included vomiting blood, dark or black stool, fever, cough, and yellow mucus. Blood tests showed he had very low red blood cell counts. His white blood cell counts were high, which can mean infection. He also had low protein levels in his blood. A test of his mucus showed a type of bacteria was present.

Doctors used a small camera to look inside the food pipe. They found a long growth on one side of the food pipe. The growth stretched about 15 centimeters along the food pipe. It covered half of the inside wall. A small tissue sample was taken and tested. The tests showed the growth was a serious type of skin cancer called melanoma. This cancer was growing inside the food pipe.

A scan of the body showed the patient had swelling in the lungs from infection. The scan showed the cancer had not spread to other parts of the body. Doctors also checked the skin, eyes, bottom, and other body areas. They found no dark spots or signs of cancer in those places.

The patient was 79 years old and had other health problems. These included low protein levels, infection, and very low red blood cell counts. Because of his age and these problems, doctors did not do surgery. They also did not give cancer-fighting drugs or radiation treatment. The patient left the hospital without receiving treatment for the cancer.

Follow-up:

About 1 month after leaving the hospital, the medical team learned that the patient had died.

Hospital Course:

The patient is a 50-year-old male with an itchy patch of skin on his left hand. He was admitted to the skin care department for evaluation. The patch started as a small, red bump. It slowly grew larger over several months and became a bigger, flaky patch. The patient also had itching and a tingling feeling. Skin cream with steroids helped for a short time, but the patch did not go away. A small tissue sample was taken because the patch looked unusual. The test showed a type of skin swelling called nummular dermatitis. Stronger steroid creams only made the patch flatten for a short time.

Several months later, the patient came back. The center of the patch had become an open sore. He also had lumps under the skin in a line from his left pinky finger up to his elbow. Testing a tissue sample found fish-tank granuloma, an infection caused by a germ called M. marinum. The patient said he had a salt-water fish tank at home. Several of his fish had died weeks after his skin problems started, but the fish were not tested.

Lab tests showed which medicines could kill the germ and which could not. The germ could be killed by amikacin, clarithromycin, doxycycline, ethambutol, moxifloxacin, rifabutin, and rifampin. The germ could not be killed by ciprofloxacin or trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole. Treatment with doxycycline and azithromycin did not help after 3 months. The medicines were changed to moxifloxacin and clarithromycin. The patient also put a reusable heat pack on the affected skin for several hours each day. The patient was sent to a surgeon to remove the lumps under the skin on his left hand, wrist, and arm. After 3 months on the new medicines and removal of the lumps, the open sore healed. The removed lumps did not come back.

The patient stayed in the hospital for 17 months until the disease was fully gone. The patient was sent home after tests showed the disease had cleared up. No further medical visits are needed.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [REDACTED]
Gender: Female
Date of Birth: [REDACTED]
Admission Date: [REDACTED]
Discharge Date: [REDACTED]
Reason for Admission: Shortness of breath

Hospital Course:
The patient came to the emergency room with shortness of breath that was getting worse. Doctors found a large growth on her thyroid gland. This growth was pressing on her windpipe and making it hard to breathe. The patient was moved quickly to the intensive care unit. There, doctors placed a breathing tube to help her breathe. Brain and chest scans showed the thyroid growth was very large and reaching into the upper chest area. Doctors removed the thyroid gland in surgery 48 hours after the patient arrived. Before waking the patient fully, doctors tested the windpipe. They found the windpipe walls were weak and floppy. The breathing tube stayed in place for 24 hours. It was removed the next day without any problems.

Course of Treatment:
The patient received a steroid medicine called dexamethasone before surgery. She took 12 mg per day for two days. This helped her baby's lungs develop faster. The surgery went well. Doctors did not need to make an opening in her windpipe. After surgery, the patient started taking thyroid hormone pills. The medicine is levothyroxin sodium tablets at 75 mcg per day.

Follow-Up Plan:
The patient left the hospital five days after surgery with no problems. Lab tests on the removed tissue showed a thyroid growth with many lumps. Some cells were growing in an unusual way. However, there was no cancer. The patient gave birth to a healthy baby four weeks later.

Recommendations:
The patient should keep taking levothyroxin sodium tablets at 75 mcg per day as directed. She should see her regular doctor for checkups. The doctor will monitor how well her thyroid medicine is working. The doctor will also watch for any problems from the thyroid removal surgery.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [Name]
Medical Record Number: [Number]

Hospital Course:
The patient is a 29-year-old man from Syria. He came to the hospital because of painless swelling in his right testicle. The swelling had been there for 12 months. During the exam, the right testicle was larger than normal but did not hurt when touched. Blood tests were done to check for cancer markers. These tests came back normal. An ultrasound of the scrotum showed a 7-centimeter mass in the right testicle. The mass had low echoes, many blood vessels, and fluid-filled areas. Surgery was done to remove the right testicle through a cut in the groin area. A full body scan showed no cancer spread to the lymph nodes or other parts of the body.

Hospital Course Summary:
The patient was found to have a rare type of testicular cancer called Sertoli cell sarcoma. There was also a fast-growing cancer that had no specific features. Both cancers were only in the testicle. The tumor had small, medium, and large cells grouped together in sheets. Large areas of dead tissue were also found. Some areas had oddly shaped cells that were dividing quickly. These cells were surrounded by tough, fiber-like tissue. The cancer did not grow through the outer covering of the testicle. The tube that carries sperm and the tissue next to the testicle were not affected. The cancer had not spread into blood vessels or lymph channels.

Treatment:
Tests confirmed the patient had Sertoli cell sarcoma with fast-growing cancer in the testicle only. Doctors strongly recommended additional cancer-killing drug treatment after surgery. However, the patient said no to this treatment and moved to a different area.

Follow-up:
The patient should see a doctor regularly to check if the cancer comes back. The patient should tell a doctor right away about any new symptoms that might be related to the cancer.

The 9-year-old male patient came to the clinic with several small raised bumps on his left cheek. Two years ago, the patient had a skin infection caused by a parasite on his nose. The patient's time in the hospital went smoothly. The patient did not have any problems or bad reactions to the medicine. The patient handled the treatment well and did not complain of pain or discomfort.

Follow-Up Plan:
The patient was told to keep the skin clean and stay away from sandflies. The patient has an appointment at the skin doctor's office in two months. This visit is to check if the skin bumps come back or if there are signs of the infection returning.

None

To watch for any return of the parasitic skin infection or new skin bumps on the left cheek.

Hospital Course:

The patient is a 21-year-old male. He came to our hospital with pain and swelling in the upper right part of his belly. During the exam, the doctor found tenderness in that area and could feel that his liver was enlarged. Tests showed high levels of a substance called CA 19-9, which can be a sign of cancer. An MRI scan showed two growths in the right side of his liver. A small tissue sample was taken from the growth. It showed a rare type of liver cancer called undifferentiated embryonal sarcoma of the liver. The tumor could not be removed with surgery. The patient started treatment with cancer-fighting drugs. During his fifth round of treatment, the patient had a liver transplant. He responded well to this treatment. The patient came back for check-up visits for 18 months. No new growths were found after the surgery.

Discharge Diagnosis:

Undifferentiated Embryonal Sarcoma of the Liver, a rare type of liver cancer.

Hospital Course Summary:

The patient came to our hospital with pain and swelling in the upper right part of his belly. Most test results were normal, except for high CA 19-9 levels. MRI scans showed two growths in the right side of his liver. A tissue sample showed a rare liver cancer. The tumor could not be removed with surgery. The patient started treatment with cancer-fighting drugs. During his fifth round of treatment, he had a liver transplant. He responded well. The patient came back for check-ups for 18 months. A CT scan showed no growths.

Impressions:

The patient had a rare liver cancer that could not be removed with surgery. He responded well to the cancer-fighting drugs and had a liver transplant. He had no problems after surgery. He came back for regular check-ups.

Plan:

The patient should keep coming back for check-up visits. He should have regular CT scans to check if the cancer has come back.

Hospital Course:
The patient came in with belly pain and swelling, a high number of white blood cells, and too many allergy-related cells in the blood. Blood tests also showed high levels of a protein linked to allergies. Scans showed a moderate amount of fluid buildup in the belly. Tissue samples showed too many allergy-related cells in the stomach and intestines. This pointed to a condition called eosinophilic gastroenteritis, where allergy cells cause gut inflammation. The patient was given a steroid pill called prednisone by mouth. This helped the symptoms go away. The fluid in the belly and the thickening of the gut walls also went away completely. After finishing the steroid treatment, the patient had no more symptoms. No other treatment was needed.

Hospital Course Summary:
A 28-year-old Saudi female with no major past health problems came in with two weeks of belly pain and swelling. During the physical exam, the doctor found tenderness all over the belly and a moderate amount of fluid buildup. Blood tests showed a high white blood cell count with too many allergy-related cells. A protein linked to allergies was also high. Scans showed moderate fluid in the belly, thickened gut walls, and swollen lymph nodes near the intestines. The patient had a scope test to look at the upper gut and another to look at the lower gut. Tissue samples from these tests confirmed too many allergy-related cells in the gut. This matched a diagnosis of eosinophilic gastroenteritis.

Treatment started with a steroid pill called prednisone by mouth. The patient's symptoms got better. The fluid in the belly and the thickened gut walls went away completely. After finishing the steroid treatment, the patient had no symptoms and did not need more treatment. Follow-up blood tests and scans showed the improvement lasted. The patient was sent home with instructions to see their regular doctor if needed.

Hospital Course:

This 58-year-old female came in with sudden painless vision loss in the left eye for 1 month. She had no history of straining or injury. Vision in the right eye was normal at 20/20 and the left eye was 20/200, which means much worse than normal.

Assessment and Findings:

Eye exams and imaging of the left eye showed bleeding under the retina at the center of vision. There was also bleeding under a thin layer of tissue in another part of the retina. Imaging confirmed that both eyes had thicker than normal blood vessel layers behind the retina. A special dye test could not show certain details in the left eye because the bleeding blocked the view.

Treatment and Outcome:

With a likely diagnosis of abnormal blood vessel growth in the eye, the patient was treated with a medicine injection into the left eye. At the 1-month follow-up visit, the left eye vision improved to 20/125. Eye exams showed that one area of bleeding had gone away and the other area of bleeding had gotten smaller. Imaging tests confirmed these improvements.

Conclusion:

The patient was discharged with improved vision after receiving the injection treatment in the left eye. Follow-up visits and monitoring may be necessary to make sure the patient's condition is properly managed going forward.

Treatment started right away, and the patient did well with the treatment. The patient had no serious problems during the hospital stay. A team of doctors and nurses watched the patient closely.

Discharge Summary:

Reason for Admission: Weight loss, yellowing of the skin and eyes, and belly pain
Diagnosis: A blockage causing yellowing of the skin due to a slow-growing cancer in the pancreas
Treatment: Three rounds of cancer-fighting drugs, radiation therapy, and a cancer drug called 5-fluorouracil given through a vein.
Outcome: The cancer shrank a lot in the area where it started. This allowed doctors to do surgery to remove it.
Post-operative Status: The edges of the tissue removed during surgery showed no signs of cancer.

Hospital Course:
The patient came to the hospital with weight loss, yellowing of the skin and eyes, and belly pain. These symptoms pointed to a blockage. Blood tests suggested cancer in the pancreas. The patient had a test where doctors used a thin needle guided by a special camera to take a small sample of tissue. This test confirmed a slow-growing cancer in the pancreas. At the same time, doctors placed a small tube to help drain bile.
The patient received three rounds of cancer-fighting drugs, radiation therapy, and a cancer drug given through a vein. The cancer shrank a lot in the area where it started. Because the treatment worked well, the patient had surgery to remove part of the pancreas and nearby organs. Tests on the removed tissue showed the edges were free of cancer.
The patient healed well without any problems and left the hospital. The patient was told to come back for a follow-up visit soon. The patient was also told to keep seeing the healthcare provider for ongoing check-ups and care.

Hospital Course Summary:

The patient was a 56-year-old man. He came to the hospital because he was not doing well and had lost a lot of weight. He had joint pain that moved around his body and did not respond to treatment. He also had belly pain and diarrhea from time to time. Early tests showed signs of infection and swelling in his body.

The patient came to the hospital several times. His health kept getting worse. He developed low levels of blood cells that help with clotting. He also had a type of blood problem where his red blood cells were too large. Doctors found that blood vessels in his neck were narrowed or blocked on both sides.

The patient's health kept getting worse even with treatment. He was moved to comfort care. He died while receiving this care.

The patient had many health problems that were hard to understand and treat. Doctors tried many tests and treatments but could not help him get better.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Information: Mrs. X, 96-year-old female.

Chief Complaint: Memory loss condition, physical restraints, and feeding tube through the nose.

Hospital Course:

Mrs. X was admitted to the hospital with a history of memory loss condition, physical restraints, and receiving nutrition through a feeding tube in her nose for the past three years. She wore mittens on her hands to stop her from pulling out the feeding tube. She had a high risk of food or liquids going into her lungs. Tests showed she took 9.5 seconds to swallow, which is too slow. Another swallowing test also showed she could choke easily.

Treatment and Intervention:

The patient received a traditional Chinese herbal medicine called Banxia Houpu Tang through her feeding tube for four weeks. Her swallowing got much better. Her swallowing time went down from 9.5 seconds to 3.5 seconds. The other swallowing test also showed improvement. The patient then started eating by mouth again. She began with soft jelly-like foods and moved to smooth blended foods of about 800 calories. The feeding tube and mittens were then removed.

Outcome:

Mrs. X was able to eat much better by mouth after receiving the herbal medicine. This allowed the care team to remove her feeding tube and physical restraints. She left the hospital in stable condition. She was told to keep taking her medicine and see her regular doctor.

Follow-up:

Mrs. X was told to keep taking her medicine and eat healthy, well-balanced meals. She should see her regular doctor and go to scheduled appointments to check her swallowing ability.

Hospital Course:
The patient, a 33-year-old Malaysian male, came to the hospital after having a seizure during sleep. Before coming to the hospital, the patient had symptoms like the flu, no appetite, and muscle aches. When he arrived, he was confused but did not have weakness on one side of his body. After each seizure, the patient was confused for about 30 minutes. During the third seizure, his heart stopped beating for 21 seconds. Doctors put in a device called a pacemaker to keep his heart beating normally.

The patient's brain and nerve exam was mostly normal. He did have jerky eye movements, likely caused by a seizure medicine called phenytoin. Even after getting seizure medicine and adjusting the dose, the patient kept having seizures. He also started having pain on the right side of his head and right ear. He felt tenderness and heard a strange sound in his right ear. This later turned into hearing music that was not real. The patient also had a type of seizure that affects awareness and behavior. These signs pointed to a possible brain infection caused by the herpes virus.

Investigations:
Doctors took fluid from the spine two times. The tests were mostly normal but showed slightly high protein levels. Brain scans with dye were normal. A special scan showed slightly less blood flow on the left side of the brain than the right. A second brain wave test showed something slightly off in the right side of the brain near the ear.

Treatment:
The patient started taking a medicine called acyclovir to fight the virus. After one week, he got much better. The seizures and headaches stopped, but he still heard music that was not real for a few more days. The patient left the hospital to finish three weeks of acyclovir at home. When doctors tried to lower the seizure medicine, the seizures came back. So the patient is still taking two seizure medicines called levetiracetam and phenytoin.

Summary:
The patient was diagnosed with a possible brain infection caused by the herpes virus. The infection was treated well with acyclovir. The patient left the hospital with orders to finish all the medicine and keep taking the seizure medicines.

Hospital Course:
The patient is a 36-year-old woman. She came to the hospital with dull pain in her left back that had lasted 4 years. She also had a foreign object on the left side of her spine. She did not have blood in her urine, pain when urinating, or a need to urinate often. The patient was admitted to the hospital. A CT scan took pictures of her belly and lower body. The scan showed that her left kidney was swollen with fluid buildup. Doctors did surgery to remove a 3-cm sewing needle. The needle was found near the upper part of the tube that carries urine from the kidney to the bladder. A small tube called a stent was placed to help urine flow better. After 6 months of checkups, the blockage and swelling in the kidney were much better. The stent was then removed.

Hospital Course Summary:
The patient came to the hospital with dull pain in her left back that had lasted 4 years. She also had a foreign object on the left side of her spine. She did not have blood in her urine, pain when urinating, or a need to urinate often. A CT scan showed that her left kidney was swollen with fluid buildup. Doctors did surgery to remove a 3-cm sewing needle found near the upper part of the tube that carries urine from the kidney to the bladder. A small tube called a stent was placed to help urine flow better. After 6 months of checkups, the blockage and swelling in the kidney were much better. The stent was then removed.

Hospital Course: A 73-year-old male patient came to the hospital with very high blood pressure after heart bypass surgery. The patient had a history of type 2 diabetes, high cholesterol, heart disease, prostate cancer, and high blood pressure that had been harder to control over the past 2 years. The patient's family history was normal, except for some sudden deaths among relatives on the mother's side. A CT scan showed a small growth on the right adrenal gland, which sits on top of the kidney. Blood tests showed high levels of certain hormones, with no signs of inherited conditions. A special imaging scan showed a small growth about 2 by 2 by 3 centimeters on the right adrenal gland with no spread to other parts of the body. The patient had surgery to remove the adrenal gland. Tests after surgery confirmed the growth was a pheochromocytoma, a type of tumor. The patient has been sent home and will continue care with regular doctor visits.

Summary of Hospital Stay: The patient was admitted because of very high blood pressure after surgery that was hard to control even with medicine. After more tests, doctors confirmed the patient had a pheochromocytoma, a type of tumor. The patient had surgery to remove the adrenal gland, and there were no problems during the procedure. The patient has been sent home and will see doctors at regular office visits.

Diagnosis: Pheochromocytoma is a tumor that grows in the adrenal gland. It makes the body produce too many stress hormones. This can cause high blood pressure, fast or pounding heartbeat, headaches, sweating, and blurry vision.

Treatment: The patient had surgery to remove the tumor, and there were no problems. The patient will keep taking medicine and making healthy lifestyle changes to manage ongoing health issues. These include diabetes, high cholesterol, and high blood pressure.

Prognosis: How well the patient does depends on the size of the tumor, whether it is cancerous, and other health problems. In this case, the growth was small. Lab tests showed the tumor cells were growing very slowly. Because of this, the patient's outlook is good.

Follow-up: The patient has been sent home and will return for regular doctor visits. These visits will help manage ongoing health issues and check if the tumor comes back or spreads. The patient will have blood and urine tests to check hormone levels and track recovery.

DISCHARGE SUMMARY

Patient Name: [REDACTED]
Age: 8 years old
Gender: Male
Medical Record Number: [REDACTED]

Admission Date: [REDACTED]
Discharge Date: [REDACTED]

MAIN PROBLEM:
Poor feeding, repeated colds and lung infections, and trouble speaking due to a large opening in the roof of the mouth.

WHAT HAPPENED DURING THE HOSPITAL STAY:
An 8-year-old boy with Seckel syndrome and slow growth before birth was seen at our clinic. He had a large opening in the roof of his mouth. After a full checkup and tests, doctors decided to do surgery to close the opening. The patient was put to sleep using a breathing gas called sevoflurane. The patient stayed asleep with oxygen, air, sevoflurane, and a muscle relaxer called atracurium. The surgery closed the opening in the roof of the mouth. The surgery went well with no problems. It took about 75 minutes. After surgery, the patient was watched closely in the intensive care unit. Doctors checked for breathing pauses, breathing problems, or bleeding from the mouth. Recovery went well with no problems. The patient's heart rate, breathing, and other body signs stayed normal.

DIAGNOSIS AT DISCHARGE:
Large opening in the roof of the mouth in a patient with Seckel syndrome and slow growth before birth.

DISCHARGE INSTRUCTIONS:
The patient went home in good condition. The patient should eat soft foods and foods mashed into a smooth paste. These foods are easy to swallow. The patient should not eat hard or crunchy foods. The patient should not eat foods that need a lot of chewing. Children with Seckel syndrome should be watched for slow development and other health problems. The patient should see a children's doctor and a specialist for more checkups and care.

FOLLOW-UP:
The patient should make appointments with the children's doctor and specialists for more checkups and care.

DISCHARGE MEDICATIONS:
None.

DIAGNOSES AND PROCEDURES AT DISCHARGE:
Large opening in the roof of the mouth and surgery to close it.

Hospital Course:
The patient came in with a feeling of fullness in the belly and nausea that had been happening on and off for 2 years. These symptoms got better after 10 minutes on their own. A special camera test using sound waves showed the stomach wall was thicker than normal. The inner layer of the upper part of the stomach looked different than expected. Another test that looks at the bile duct found a bile duct stone. The stone was removed without any problems.

Diagnostic Assessment:
A camera test looking inside the stomach found a bump in the upper part of the stomach. The bump was removed during a procedure that takes out tissue from under the stomach lining. A lab test done during the procedure showed the stomach tissue was not arranged normally. Some small tubes in the stomach lining were larger than usual. There were no signs of cancer.

Diagnostic Impression:
Based on the patient's symptoms and test results, the patient was found to have a growth in the upper stomach with a worn surface. The patient also had gallstones in the gallbladder and a stone in the bile duct.

Therapeutic Intervention:
A procedure was done to remove the bile duct stone. Another procedure was done to remove the growth from the upper part of the stomach.

Condition on Discharge:
The patient got much better after the procedures. The patient went home without any problems.

Follow-up:
The patient was told to eat foods low in fat. The patient should make an appointment with the stomach doctor. The doctor will check for any new symptoms and plan any treatment that may be needed.

Discharge Summary:

Patient: [Name], [Age], [Gender]

Admission date: [Date]
Discharge date: [Date]

Admission diagnosis: Belly pain
Discharge diagnosis: Infected pocket of pus in tissue left over from before birth near the belly button

Hospital course:

The patient came to the emergency room with bad belly pain along with fever and feeling sick to the stomach. The patient did not have problems with peeing. The physical exam showed pain and tightness when touching the belly button area. Blood tests showed a high number of white blood cells, which means the body was fighting an infection. Pictures of the belly confirmed an infected pocket of pus in tissue left over from before birth near the belly button.

The patient had treatment with medicine and surgery. There were no problems after the surgery. Tests on the removed tissue showed it was not cancer. The pus contained a common germ called E. coli. This infection was treated with an antibiotic called ciprofloxacin.

The patient had no symptoms during the rest of the hospital stay. At a check-up two years later, the patient felt fine and the belly area looked normal.

Instructions at discharge: The patient was told how to take medicines and care for the wound. The patient was also told when to come back for check-up visits. The patient was told to call the doctor if there were any worrying symptoms or problems.

Follow-up plan: The patient was told to come back for regular check-up visits. These visits are to make sure healing is going well and the infection does not come back.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: Mr C
Age: 60s
Sex: Male
Admission Date: not provided
Discharge Date: not provided

Hospital Course:

Mr C came to the hospital for talk therapy. He has post-traumatic stress disorder, also called PTSD. This is a mental health condition that can happen after a very upsetting event. Mr C developed PTSD after working as a military police officer in Northern Ireland in the 1960s. When he arrived, he said he kept seeing broken pieces of a scary memory in the corner of his right eye. He had been trying to avoid this memory for years. He also said his moods changed a lot. Sometimes he felt numb or cut off from his feelings. Other times he felt very worried and anxious when something reminded him of the event. He also felt sad and down. In the past, Mr C drank alcohol to help deal with these feelings.

During his stay, Mr C had trouble taking part in trauma-focused talk therapy. He used several sessions to talk about his worries. He tried different calming methods in the therapy room. But he either talked about things without showing any feelings or could not handle reliving his scary memory. When asked to close his eyes and go back to the memory, he felt too much panic in his body. This made him feel disconnected from what was happening around him.

Mr C's PTSD symptoms stayed the same because he kept avoiding his scary memory. In both sessions where he tried to relive the memory, he could not reach the thoughts and beliefs he had during the original event.

Outcome:

Mr C left the hospital after finishing his talk therapy. The care team gave him some ways to cope that could help him handle his PTSD symptoms if they come back. No other treatment was suggested when he left.

Prognosis:

The outlook for Mr C is fair. But his PTSD symptoms will likely come back if he keeps avoiding his scary memory. The care team suggests he keep using his coping methods to manage his PTSD symptoms. No follow-up visits were scheduled.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [REDACTED]
Date of Admission: [REDACTED]
Date of Discharge: [REDACTED]
Admitting Diagnosis: Pain in the left hand for 2 months

Hospital Course:

The patient came in with left hand pain that had lasted for 2 months. The patient was sent to our hospital after an X-ray at another clinic showed a growth in a hand bone. This bone is called the second metacarpal and is located below the pointer finger. During the hospital stay, the patient had many tests done. These included blood tests and urine tests. All test results came back normal. The tests showed no signs of other health problems.

A physical exam showed stiffness and soreness on top of the hand bone. The patient had X-rays, a CT scan, and an MRI done. These scans showed a growth in the hand bone. The bone wall had expanded and there was a clear dark spot inside. There was also some hardening around the growth and calcium buildup in the center. The MRI showed the growth had clear edges. The growth appeared dark on one type of image and bright on other types. When dye was used, only the edges of the growth showed up brighter. The bone and soft tissue around the growth looked normal.

The patient was sent to a doctor who specializes in this type of problem. We told the patient to see this specialist at their office for more care.

Discharge Diagnosis: Not yet known. The patient needs more tests and treatment.

Follow-up: The patient should see a specialist to find out what the growth is and get treatment.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [REDACTED]
DOB: [REDACTED]
Admission Date: [REDACTED]
Discharge Date: [REDACTED]

History of Presenting Illness:
The patient came in with chest pain that had been happening for two months. This chest pain was steady and happened during activity. The patient had a history of diabetes and high cholesterol. He was a smoker with no past heart problems. A stress test on a treadmill showed a problem. A test using dye to look at the heart arteries was done. This test showed a tear in the wall of one of the small heart arteries. The tear started near the beginning of the artery and went to the end.

Hospital Course:
The patient was given medicine to slow the heart rate and aspirin to thin the blood. A procedure to open the artery was not possible. The artery was too narrow and hard to reach. The patient stayed stable during the hospital stay. The patient was sent home with instructions to see his regular doctor.

Summary:
The patient is a 52-year-old man who came in with steady chest pain. A test with dye showed a tear in the wall of a small heart artery. He was treated with medicine to slow the heart rate and aspirin. A procedure to open the artery could not be done because of the size and location of the artery. The patient was sent home to follow up with his regular doctor.

Discharge Summary:

The patient is a 55-year-old man who came to the emergency room with sudden chest pain. A nose swab test showed the patient had COVID-19. The patient has family members who have had heart attacks and high blood pressure. The patient was also living at home with two family members who had COVID-19 at the time.

During the exam, the doctor heard a rubbing sound from the sac around the heart. Heart test readings showed signs of swelling in most areas. An ultrasound of the heart showed a small to medium amount of fluid around the heart. The patient was diagnosed with swelling of the sac around the heart caused by COVID-19.

The doctors gave the patient two medicines called indomethacin and aspirin. They also planned a procedure to drain fluid from around the heart. The patient had not received any treatment before coming to the emergency room. The patient left the hospital in stable condition. The patient should keep taking all medicines as directed. The patient should see their doctor to manage high blood pressure. The patient should also see their doctor to manage COVID-19 and watch for any warning signs of other problems.

Hospital Course:

The 16-year-old Bangladeshi girl came to our hospital because her voice had become hoarse. This problem had been getting worse over the past 4 months. Her local doctor had treated her with antibiotics. Doctors used a thin, flexible camera to look at her throat. They found a growth on the front part of her right voice box. Her right voice box was also not moving properly. The patient had surgery to remove the growth. Lab tests showed the growth was a type of cancer called squamous cell carcinoma. It was a slow-growing type. She was sent to the cancer clinic for more care.

The patient had never used tobacco or alcohol. She had not been around radiation or cancer-causing substances. No one in her family had cancer. A special scan of her neck showed a problem with her right voice box. No spread to the neck glands was found. The lab tests confirmed cancer. The cancer was at an early stage and had not spread to other parts of the body.

The patient was scheduled for radiation therapy to destroy the cancer. The treatment followed standard guidelines used before. The neck glands were not treated because this type of early cancer rarely spreads there. The patient received radiation therapy using a special machine. The patient handled the radiation treatment well. She is now coming back for regular check-ups.

Discharge Medications:

N/A

Follow-Up Plans:

The patient is advised to come back for check-up visits every 6 months so doctors can watch her progress.

Date of Admission: [Date of admission]

Admitting Diagnosis: Painless lump in the scrotum

Hospital Course:
The patient came to [Hospital Name] because of a painless lump on the left side of the scrotum. The patient had no major health problems in the past. The patient found the lump one month before coming to the hospital. A physical exam showed a 2 cm firm lump at the top of the left testicle. The lump had clear edges. The right testicle and the bottom of the left testicle felt normal. Blood tests came back normal. Tests for cancer markers in the blood were also normal. These included Alpha-fetoprotein, pregnancy hormone (hCG), and lactate dehydrogenase (LDH). An ultrasound of the scrotum showed a mass outside the testicle. The mass was attached to the top of the testicle. The mass looked similar to testicle tissue and had poor blood flow. The patient had surgery to remove the left testicle through a cut in the groin. Lab tests on the removed tissue showed the lump was made of normal spleen tissue. There were no signs of cancer. The spleen tissue had its own covering and was separate from the testicle. The testicle tissue and its outer layers looked normal under the microscope. The patient left the hospital two days after surgery.

Discharge Diagnosis: Painless lump in the scrotum

Summary:
A 38-year-old North African man came in with a painless lump on the left side of his scrotum. An ultrasound showed a mass outside the testicle, attached to the top of the testicle. The patient had surgery to remove the testicle through the groin. Lab tests showed the lump was made of spleen tissue with no signs of cancer. The patient left the hospital two days after surgery. The patient came back for checkups at 3 weeks and 2 months. At those visits, the spleen was in its normal place with normal size and appearance.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: Not provided
Medical Record Number: Not provided

Hospital Course: The patient is a 50-year-old woman who has had type 2 diabetes for 16 years. She was admitted to the hospital because of problems in her left eye. She had abnormal blood vessel growth on the nerve at the back of her eye. She also had swelling in the center of her vision with fluid buildup under the eye's light-sensing layer. Before coming to the hospital, she had received an eye injection of a medicine called bevacizumab. This treatment did not help much.

Treatment: The patient had eye surgery. The doctor removed the gel inside her eye. The doctor also removed a thin layer from the surface of the center of her vision. Laser treatment was applied to the back of her eye to stop abnormal blood vessel growth. A slow-release steroid medicine implant was placed inside her eye to reduce swelling.

Outcome: The patient stayed in the hospital so doctors could watch her recovery. After 12 months, her vision in that eye measured 20/63. The swelling in the center of her vision went down a lot. It went from 712 to 280 on the thickness measurement. A special eye scan at 12 months showed lasting damage to a layer of cells that sense light.

Recommendations: The patient should keep going to her follow-up eye exams. She should continue to get regular eye care.

Follow-up care: The patient should keep taking any medicines her doctor prescribed. She should follow a healthy lifestyle to control her blood sugar and blood pressure. She should get medical help right away if the swelling in her eye gets worse.

DISCHARGE SUMMARY

Hospital Course:
The patient is a 44-year-old Hispanic male who was admitted for eye swelling in both eyes. This happened while he was being treated with a cancer drug called ipilimumab for skin cancer that had spread to other parts of his body. He had received his third treatment two months before coming to the hospital. The cancer treatment caused side effects throughout his body including a skin rash, loose stools, fever, and ongoing sores near his bottom.

Physical Exam:
When the patient arrived, he had a blind spot in the center of his left eye. Both eyes showed color deposits on the inner surface of the clear front layer of the eye. There were no clumps of cells stuck to this layer. The doctor looked at the back of both eyes and found swelling of the nerve that connects the eye to the brain. There were also curved lines around this nerve caused by the swelling. The central part of the back of the eye was also swollen. A special scan of the eye found small pockets of fluid in and under the center of the back of the eye.

Treatment:
The patient was first treated with steroid eye drops called prednisolone acetate. He was then sent to doctors who specialize in eye swelling for more care. He was given prednisolone acetate 1% eye drops for both eyes four times a day. He also received eye drops twice a day to lower eye pressure. These drops contained brimonidine tartrate 0.2% and timolol maleate 0.5%. His treatment was increased to include 80 mg of prednisone pills taken by mouth each day. The doctors kept checking on the patient and changed his medicine amounts to help him heal.

Improvement and Discharge:
Over the next three weeks, the patient's vision got steadily better. The swelling in the eye nerve and back of the eye went away. A star-shaped pattern then appeared in the central part of the back of the eye. At a check-up two months later, his vision in both eyes improved to nearly normal at 20/25. The swelling inside the front of his eyes became stable with only mild signs of irritation while using prednisolone acetate eye drops four times a day. The patient then stopped coming to his appointments.

Discharge Summary

Patient Name: Not specified
Medical Record Number: Not specified

Admission Date: Not specified
Discharge Date: Not specified

Admitting Diagnosis: Wet age-related macular degeneration with a fluid-filled blister under the center of the retina and a related hole in the macula

Hospital Course: The 73-year-old Caucasian female was admitted with decreased vision and wavy or distorted vision for 6 months in her left eye. Initial examination showed the sharpest vision with glasses was 20/80 in the left eye and 20/25 in the right eye. A detailed eye exam showed wet age-related macular degeneration with a fluid-filled blister under the center of the retina and a related hole in the macula. A special imaging scan of the retina confirmed a hole going all the way through the macula with attached edges. It also showed a partly detached gel layer on top of the raised blister. Treatment with eye injections to stop abnormal blood vessel growth was started. The patient received three monthly injections of bevacizumab (1.25 mg) into the eye. After 4 weeks, the first injection made the fluid-filled blister go away and brought the edges of the hole closer together. However, vision got worse to 20/160. At the follow-up visit, the second injection was given after four weeks. The imaging scan showed the hole had closed completely and vision improved greatly to 20/50. During later follow-up visits, the fluid-filled blister came back, but the hole in the macula stayed closed. Ongoing eye injections with bevacizumab given as needed made the blister go away and kept vision stable.

Discharge Diagnosis: Wet age-related macular degeneration with a fluid-filled blister under the center of the retina and a related hole in the macula

Discharge Education: The patient was told about the importance of continued eye checkups and taking medication as directed. The possible side effects of the medication were explained. The patient was also told to report any new symptoms right away.

Follow-Up Care: The patient will follow-up with her eye doctor in three months.

Discharge Summary:

Patient 1 is a 94-year-old man who had several skin cancers on his face. These were a common type called basal cell carcinoma. The patient came to our facility for treatment. The patient did not want surgery to remove the cancers. Instead, the patient was treated with medicine.

The patient used a skin cream that helps the body fight cancer cells. This treatment worked well and all the skin cancers went away. However, after one year, the cancer on the nose came back. A new growth also appeared on the forehead that looked like it might be a different type of skin problem.

The patient used the skin cream again, but the nose cancer got bigger. The patient then started taking a pill called everolimus. The dose was slowly increased over 12 months of treatment. At first, the nose cancer formed an open sore. After eight months on this medicine, the nose cancer went away completely. The growth on the forehead did not change with medicine. Doctors removed it with surgery. Tests showed it was a different type of skin cancer that had grown deeper into the skin.

The nose cancer stayed gone for eight months after the patient stopped taking everolimus. The patient later died of natural causes.

The patient was watched closely and received very good medical care at our facility. The medical team followed all proper steps for finding and treating the patient's condition. The patient was given everything needed for their medical care.

The patient's condition was handled well and the team was happy to provide excellent medical care.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Information:
24-year-old white man who came in with a broken hip socket on the right side. The bone was broken into several pieces in the back part of the hip socket. The patient plays amateur rugby at a high level.

History of Present Illness:
The patient was tackled during a game. He landed on his bent right knee. This caused immediate pain. He could not put weight on his leg. Scans at the local hospital showed a broken bone. The patient was moved to our hospital for treatment.

Hospital Course:
The patient had surgery to put the broken bones back in place. Metal hardware was used to hold the bones together. The surgeon went in through the back of the hip. Bone from the top of the thigh bone was used to support the joint surface. The patient healed well after surgery. He left the hospital three days after the operation.

Treatment:
The patient could not put weight on his right leg for six weeks. He used crutches during this time. After six weeks, he slowly started putting full weight on his leg as he did physical therapy. Six months after surgery, the patient was doing well. He could put full weight on his leg. He was doing light exercise at the gym. X-rays showed the bone had healed.

Follow-up Plan:
The patient will continue to have checkups over time.

Hospital Course:
The patient is a 71-year-old Japanese woman. She had left hip pain for 10 years and swelling in her left leg for 1 year. A physical exam showed she could not move her left hip normally. Her hip could only bend to 80 degrees and had limited movement in other directions. X-rays showed severe joint damage in her left hip. This was caused by a hip problem she was born with. CT scans and MRI scans showed that blood vessels in her leg were being pressed by a growth. This growth was not there 8 years ago on an earlier X-ray. Doctors found that the growth was a piece of bone that had broken off due to the joint damage. The patient had surgery to replace her hip and remove the growth. Right after surgery, the swelling in her left leg went down. Her recovery went smoothly with no problems. At her last check-up, 3 years after surgery, the patient could walk without help. She could do all daily activities on her own. The growth had not come back.

Diagnoses:
Severe joint damage in the left hip caused by a hip problem present since birth.

Procedures performed:
Full hip replacement surgery with removal of the growth. Doctors used a short stem that fits into the thigh bone, a ceramic ball measuring 32mm, and a 48mm socket that attaches without cement. The socket has a plastic lining.

Tissue study findings:
The outer layer was made of cartilage. The center had normal bone tissue. No cancer cells were found.

Discharge condition:
Stable.

Functional status at discharge:
The patient was able to walk on her own and the growth had not come back.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [Insert Name]

Medical Record Number: [Insert Number]

Admission Date: [Insert Date]

Discharge Date: [Insert Date]

Diagnosis:

Birth defect causing a hole in the left side of the muscle that separates the chest from the belly. This hole allowed the stomach, spleen, part of the large intestine, and part of the small intestine to move up into the chest. The stomach and spleen became twisted and blocked.

Hospital Course:

The patient came to the hospital with less hunger than usual, trouble swallowing, pain in the upper belly, and trouble breathing. A chest X-ray and CT scan showed a stretched stomach and enlarged spleen. These organs had pushed into the chest and shifted the heart and nearby parts to the right side. This pointed to a type of birth defect called a hole in the muscle below the lungs.

The patient had surgery. Doctors first tried to operate using small cuts and a camera. They had to switch to a larger cut to complete the repair. During surgery, doctors found a large hole in the muscle below the lungs on the left side. The spleen and stomach had moved into the chest and become twisted. Doctors moved these organs back to where they belong. They used a special patch to close the hole in the muscle.

The patient healed well with no problems. The patient left the hospital 10 days after surgery. The patient was told to see their regular doctor for follow-up care. The patient was told to keep taking medicine as directed.

Hospital Course Summary:

The patient had signs of a birth defect causing a hole in the muscle below the lungs. Tests confirmed this problem. Doctors first tried surgery with small cuts and a camera. They had to switch to a larger cut. Doctors moved the organs back into place and used a special patch to close the hole. The patient healed well and left the hospital. The patient was told to keep taking medicine as directed and see their regular doctor.
